text:
Four states (Arizona, New Mexico, Oregon and Washington) joined last week the 17 others already facing lawsuits from the Donald Trump administration for allowing undocumented students to access public universities without being excluded from resident tuition rates. As part of its aggressive immigration agenda, the administration has targeted states that permit students to pay in-state tuition regardless of their immigration status.

In a country where the cost of higher education is so high that many families struggle to afford it, access to in-state tuition rates, which are substantially lower than those charged to out-of-state students, can determine whether a student is able to continue their studies. This is especially true for families of undocumented migrants, who tend to accept lower-paid jobs.

“Washington state won’t be bullied into changing how we provide opportunities for young people in our state. We’ll see them in court, and we expect to win,” Washington Governor Bob Ferguson responded on social media.

The gap between resident and nonresident tuition rates at public universities in the four states is significant. According to the lawsuit, for the 2026-27 academic year, Washington residents would pay $13,406 at the University of Washington, compared with $44,460 for out-of-state students.

The laws in the states being sued allow students without legal immigration status to qualify for in-state tuition if they meet certain requirements, many of them similar across states. In most cases, students must have graduated from a high school in the state, in addition to meeting conditions such as residing there for a specified period and committing to apply for permanent residency once they become eligible.

Several governors, state lawmakers and attorneys general in the affected states have denounced what they see as federal interference in an area under state jurisdiction. They have also argued that denying students access to higher education on the basis of their immigration status would amount to discrimination.

“The federal government has now sued 21 states for letting Dreamers who attended school in places like Arizona be able to afford a college education at our state’s community colleges and universities,” said Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes in a statement. “Fundamentally, this is about state’s rights and I will vigorously defend Arizona’s right to set its own rules, especially ones that are passed by voters themselves.” In Arizona, Proposition 308, which was approved by voters, ties a student’s eligibility to where they attended and graduated from high school, rather than to their place of residence.

The Trump administration argues that states that have adopted similar policies give foreign nationals access to public benefits at the expense of U.S. citizens. “As of today, we have now sued 21 states who we allege were thwarting Congress’s clear prohibition on placing aliens over citizens. Our efforts will not cease until President Trump’s promise is fulfilled: illegal aliens will not receive benefits denied to American citizens,” Associate Deputy Attorney General Stanley E. title: ICE, other federal agencies had access to Idaho city's license plate readers
description:
Shepard said only Idaho-based federal agents had access, not the entirety of the federal agencies.
“We had questions about it, so we felt it was safer to shut it down…keep it in the state of Idaho,” Shepard said in a phone interview.
But cutting off the federal agencies wasn’t all.
Some Idaho agencies, however, still have access, Shepard said, including Ada County, Boise Police, Caldwell Police, Lewiston Police and Meridian Police.
In Nampa, federal agents had the ability to log in and do the searches they wanted, according to Shepard.
text:
On June 15, ICE employee Garrett Rutherford logged into Nampa Police Department’s automated license plate reader system (similar to Flock but a different brand) late at night, according to data obtained via a records request. Rutherford ran five searches on the technology and viewed three plates, though portions of the document were redacted by Nampa’s records staff.

The next day, Rutherford was back around 7 a.m. searching for and viewing plates, part of over 100 searches run by Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Drug Enforcement Administration between June 1 and July 31 using a controversial technology that critics have said is an unacceptable level of mass surveillance.

The technology, called automated license plate readers, uses cameras to capture pictures of license plates and store the associated information in a database, according to the American Civil Liberties Union. Police typically use that information to “track cars in real time and to track the past locations of cars,” the ACLU said. Nampa keeps its data for 60 days, according to its records division.

ICE, which entered into its agreement with Nampa on Oct. 9, 2025, wasn’t the only federal agency with access, Nampa Police Lt. Chad Shepard told the Statesman. Nampa Police in 2023 authorized local agents of the Drug Enforcement Administration and the U.S. Marshals Service to use the system, Shepard said. The most recent addition, the FBI, signed up on July 30. Shepard said only Idaho-based federal agents had access, not the entirety of the federal agencies.

But by Aug. 20, Shepard said Nampa Police had terminated those agreements after seeing public furor over the technology and reviewing Idaho code, which says only an agency’s authorized personnel should have access to the data. The code defines an agency as the state of Idaho, any political subdivision of the state or any agency thereof. Nampa Police also cut off the Oregon State Police, Shepard said.

“We had questions about it, so we felt it was safer to shut it down…keep it in the state of Idaho,” Shepard said in a phone interview. “...We are doing our best to ease any concerns and stay in compliance with state code.”

Idaho code also says that agencies using the readers have to follow certain rules, including that the device and its data can’t be used for any purposes other than investigating felony or misdemeanor crimes, traffic accidents or searching for missing or endangered people.

But the question of immigration status is a civil matter, said Neal Dougherty, one of the founding partners at Boise-based Burnett & Dougherty. Not every plate searched for and viewed by ICE may have belonged to a target of immigration authorities.

“They are using these tools that are supposed to exist for enforcement of criminal violations and infractions,” Dougherty said in a phone interview. “That seems like a significant waste of resources, overreach and a violation of our privacy rights.”

Asked about that code section, Shepard referred the Statesman to ICE.

But cutting off the federal agencies wasn’t all. A day or two later, Nampa Police shut down more than 500 agreements with police departments nationwide, Shepard said, that allowed those other departments to search a plate and receive a notification if there’s a hit in Nampa.

Sandra Barker, a spokesperson for the FBI, declined to comment. In a statement, an ICE spokesperson said information sharing “is essential to identify who is in our country, including violent criminals, and determine what public safety and terror threats may exist.”

“Like other law enforcement agencies, ICE employs various forms of technology to investigate criminal activity and support law enforcement efforts while respecting civil liberties and privacy interests,” the spokesperson said.

Some Idaho agencies, however, still have access, Shepard said, including Ada County, Boise Police, Caldwell Police, Lewiston Police and Meridian Police.

This all began when Nampa Police started testing a brand of plate readers called Rekor in 2021, Shepard said, and initially installed the devices in 2022. The Police Department originally bought 25 devices for $30,000 and an ongoing annual subscription of more than $24,000, Shepard said.

In May 2025, the department implemented eight Motorola devices, purchased for more than $46,000 with around $7,000 in ongoing annual cost, according to Shepard.

As of now, 27 intersections in Nampa have automated license plate readers.

But these plate readers offer an opportunity for abuse. In Jerome County, a sheriff had used the Flock cameras to search for his wife’s car hundreds of times, according to KMVT. The sheriff ultimately retired, according to the outlet.

However, Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador said his office couldn’t prove a crime and didn’t have the authority to prosecute that sheriff, according to the Washington Post.

Flock cameras, in particular, have been under increasing scrutiny in recent months, prompting the company to make changes to its platform. Its CEO, Garrett Langley, in a recent interview on Fox News, called for “compromise” between privacy and safety.

In the Gem State, the group DeFlock Idaho has been leading the crusade against the technology. A co-founder, Tyler Cain, has filed tort claims over the tech in Wilder and Caldwell and collected signatures to force Wilder’s City Council to vote on removing the cameras. Nampa does not use the Flock brand.

In Nampa, federal agents had the ability to log in and do the searches they wanted, according to Shepard. Nampa Police conducted audits and spot checks of the federal agencies’ searches, Shepard said

Asked if the agency ever turned up anything problematic, Shepard said “not from where we can see, no.”

Down south in Twin Falls, anti-Flock advocates discovered immigration searches. A month after the searches, the police department changed its policy to prevent outside agencies from using the system, according to the Idaho Capital Sun.

But many remain skeptical.

Rebecca De León, spokesperson for the ACLU of Idaho, said evidence around the country of ongoing privacy violations related to police use of the technology, including law enforcement sharing data with ICE, “should be deeply troubling to absolutely everyone.”

“We at the ACLU believe there are no changes that can be made to a dangerous mass surveillance system that would turn it into a system that is fully protective of civil rights and civil liberties,” De León said.

Politicians around the country are jumping on the anti-license plate reader bandwagon and Idaho is no exception. On Monday, U.S. Rep. Russ Fulcher, R-Idaho, announced he was cosponsoring a bill to limit federal law enforcement agencies’ use and storage of data from technology like license plate readers.

“It’s simple: if the federal government wants to access state and local systems’ data on citizens, they need to get a warrant,” Fulcher said in a news release.

Shepard, with the Nampa Police Department, said the people attacking automated license plate readers are “very vocal,” but their claims of mass surveillance and Fourth Amendment violations aren’t true.

“Law enforcement’s objective is, and always has been, to serve our community and victims to the best of our ability,” Shepard wrote in a follow-up email. “The tools we use may change with the times, but so does crime, and we are struggling to keep up. If the community chooses to erode our capabilities, we will eventually lose the fight to protect them.”

He turned himself in on March 7, according to police. Additional victims came forward after his arrest.

In ICE custody

According to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), Ortiz entered the U.S. illegally in 2024. The agency issued a detainer for Ortiz after his arrest in April.

ICE has been incredibly vocal about this case, saying they want Ortiz out of the country and calling out Virginia's immigration policies.

"This 18-year-old criminal illegal alien should NOT have been attending a Virginia high school and allowed to prey on innocent teenage girls," DHS Deputy Assistant Secretary Lauren Bis said in a March statement.

"Heartening to see that the sheriff's department actively cooperated with ICE and observed they needed to transfer custody," said Sean Kennedy with Virginias 4 Safe Communities. title: Shifting strategy seen as ICE arrests surge across upstate NY - WXXI News
description:

And it comes as plans move forward to erect a 100-bed "temporary detention structure” at the Buffalo Service Processing Center in Batavia — expanding the only ICE detention facility upstate.
Those who are detained upstate increasingly are still pursuing legal status, and are not under a final order of removal, according to the data processed by the Deportation Data Project and analyzed by WXXI News.

text:
ICE arrests across upstate New York have doubled in recent months, records show — and four of every five cases now involve people with no criminal history.

Total arrests across upstate topped 600 in July, the most recent full month of data available, adding to what was a record 1,500 arrests by Immigration and Customs Enforcement across all of New York state.

The upswing — detailed in government data that ICE provided to the Deportation Data Project based at U.C. Berkeley and UCLA — shows the administration getting closer to its target of 2,000 daily arrests. The increase coincides with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin taking the reins in March and promising a quieter but more effective approach.

And it comes as plans move forward to erect a 100-bed "temporary detention structure” at the Buffalo Service Processing Center in Batavia — expanding the only ICE detention facility upstate. Homeland Security filed notice last week that it plans to award a sole source or no-bid contract for the project to Akima Infrastructure Protection, LLC, a U.S. contractor tied to human rights abuses at Guantanamo Bay.

Regional and statewide numbers mirror national trends as ICE target people accused of civil immigration violations but not charged with or convicted of any crimes, records show. ICE recorded nearly 50,000 arrests nationwide in July.

“We have seen patterns,” said Melina Ivanchikova, a founding member of the Finger Lakes Rapid Response Network, which assists families of undocumented immigrants. “For example, the 104 corridor from Williamson to Rochester is heavily surveilled. There's constant reports of ICE activity. And the pattern seems to be like an intense period of two or three weeks, and then a lull."

Not all arrests result in detention. Those who are detained upstate increasingly are still pursuing legal status, and are not under a final order of removal, according to the data processed by the Deportation Data Project and analyzed by WXXI News. That marks a stark departure from past practice.

ICE historically has focused on those already ordered removed by a judge. Data show that was true in 85% of all upstate arrests when President Donald Trump returned to office — but in just 25% this past July.

As Ivanchikova noted, the number of arrests has risen in waves during Trump’s second term, hitting peaks upstate in July 2025, again in December, and now July. Calls to Ivanchikova's group seemed to decrease in August, she said. The group covers Yates, Ontario, Wayne, Seneca and Cayuga counties.

“In July, we had the most intense period in the existence of our network, with the most number of calls and support needs,” Ivanchikova said. “In all those cases, men were taken but not women, and women and children were left behind. In some cases, women who weren't working.

"And so there's sort of this, I think, underreported social dimension of what it looks like when families are fractured, and when children have parents who've been plucked away suddenly.”

In a statement, a DHS spokesperson said the agency could not comment on the “source, accuracy, or completeness" of the data, nor the analysis, adding: “The bottom line is that the Deportation Data Project is not accurate.”

“Since Day One of the Trump Administration, DHS law enforcement has been delivering on President Trump’s promise to the American people to arrest and deport criminal illegal aliens including murderers, rapists, child predators, gang members, and terrorists,” the statement reads.

The statement claims that the majority of those arrested are people charged or convicted of a crime. The data shows the opposite, with convicted violent offenders accounting for less than 5% of arrests locally and nationally in July.

WXXI News had requested supporting data from the government if it disputed the numbers. No such data was provided.

“More than 3 million illegal aliens are out of the country and counting,” the DHS statement concluded. “Our message is clear: if you come to our country illegally, we will find you, we will arrest you, and we will deport you.”

Ivanchikova sees it differently.

“What I imagine is that our society is kind of like a healthy fabric,” she said, “and then as you pluck people out, you have a moth-eaten blanket that eventually will fall apart.”

text:
In a wide-ranging report published last week on children in England in the social care system, Parliament's Joint Committee on Human Rights expressed extreme concern over the fate of 40 unaccompanied asylum-seeking children who went missing from asylum hotels and who still remain missing.

The children were among 400 asylum-seeking children went missing from asylum hotels in 2023. Under the previous Conservative government, seven hotels were used to accommodate unaccompanied asylum-seeking children. They were closed in 2024 after the High Court held that their use for permanent or long-term housing was unlawful.

According to evidence given to the Committee in June of this year by Helen Waite, the Director of Children's Social Care at the Department for Education, 472 children went missing during the period in which hotels were used. Of these, 432 had since been located, leaving 40 unlocated. Two of those are still aged under 18, she said.

The Committee welcomed the fact that most of the missing children had been found but said it remained "extremely concerned" about those still missing.

It recommended that the Government regularly publish information about the missing children until all have been found and explain what action is being taken to locate them. The report also called for the Home Office to provide the Committee with updates every three months.

The Committee's report stressed: "The duty on local authorities to provide support and accommodation to children in need in their area, imposed by the Children Act 1989, extends to asylum-seeking children, and requires that children be provided with accommodation that suits their needs. Hotels must not be used to house unaccompanied asylum-seeking children, and we welcome the government's commitment to not place children in such accommodation."

Last November, the child rights organisation ECPAT UK published a 24-page report on trafficked and unaccompanied children going missing from care in the UK. It noted that around 9% of all children in care in England are unaccompanied asylum-seeking children, with many more affected by immigration issues.

ECPAT UK's research found that unaccompanied asylum-seeking children and trafficked children "are at very high risk of going missing from care". It noted: "This research revealed that an alarmingly high number of these children were going missing from care, with some never found. Data from 2014 to 2020 found that over one in four trafficked children and one in ten unaccompanied children go missing from care, highlighting continuing risks and systemic failures in protecting these children."

According to ECPAT UK , more than 2,000 trafficked and/or unaccompanied children went missing from care in the UK in 2024.

Laura Duran, Head of Policy of ECPAT UK, commented: "These children are not just statistics—they are individuals who have already endured unimaginable trauma. When they go missing from care, they are at extreme risk of further exploitation. The UK Government must ensure that the policies they are proposing do not exacerbate these risks and should instead focus on bringing effective safeguarding measures to protect children for harm."

text:
Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita and Monroe County Sheriff Ruben Marté reached a partial settlement in a dispute over immigration policies.

A central dispute over whether the sheriff must honor immigration detainer requests remains unresolved and is still in litigation.

Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita has claimed a “major victory” in his fight with Monroe County Sheriff Ruben Marté, but the central dispute in their clash over immigration remains unresolved.

Rokita and Marté have reached a consent decree — a negotiated settlement that carries the force of a court order — that addresses some of the dispute that began when Rokita sued Marté in July 2024.

Rokita won significant policy changes requiring Monroe County to remove several restrictions on immigration-related cooperation with federal authorities. However, the consent decree leaves unresolved the central dispute over immigration detainer requests and explicitly allows Marté to continue his current detainer policy while that issue remains in litigation.

In the 2024 lawsuit, Rokita alleged that parts of the sheriff's office immigration policy violated Indiana law by restricting deputies' ability to cooperate with federal immigration authorities, check immigration status and participate in certain immigration-enforcement activities. During the litigation, the Indiana General Assembly amended the state's immigration-cooperation statute, and Marté's office later revised its policy.

The consent decree follows a Monroe County court ruling from June 30 that blocked part of Indiana's new immigration law from being enforced against Marté and the Monroe County Sheriff's Office. The court's preliminary injunction — a temporary order that bars the state from enforcing the law against Marté while the lawsuit proceeds — prevented enforcement of a provision dealing with immigration detainer requests, and the sheriff's current policy continues to state that deputies will not hold someone beyond a scheduled release date solely because of an administrative immigration detainer.

A judge had said the new state law placed Marté in an "impossible" position: either comply with the state law and risk violating detainees' constitutional rights or refuse to comply and face state penalties.

In a news release, Rokita called the consent decree a “resounding success” that would “echo throughout the rest of the state as well, serving notice that we mean business when it comes to exercising our statutory authority to enforce these immigration laws and help the Trump administration detain and deport illegal aliens.”

Marté’s office did not immediately respond to an emailed inquiry.

Although Rokita and Marté settled part of their dispute over the sheriff's immigration policies, the central question of whether Monroe County must comply with ICE detainer requests remains unresolved and will continue to be litigated.

text:
The Constitutional Court, with judgment number 120 of 3 July 2026, stated that the penalties provided for the crime of death or injury as a consequence of crimes relating to illegal immigration, introduced by article 12-bis of the Consolidated Law on Immigration, following the so-called "Cutro Decree" ( Decree-Law 20/2023), do not infringe the Italian Constitution. The Court's ruling resolved the constitutional legitimacy issues raised by the preliminary hearing judge of the Syracuse Court in a criminal proceeding concerning a sea transport of 34 migrants, which tragically ended with the death of three people and the injury of ten others due to a collision with a rescue vessel.

At the heart of the constitutionality question were the severe statutory penalties provided for by the law, which punishes the offence with 20 to 30 years of imprisonment in the event of the death of multiple people or death and serious/great bodily injury. The referring judge considered the treatment to be disproportionate and detrimental to the rehabilitative function of penalties, thus breaching Articles 3 and 27 of the Constitution. According to the Syracuse Court, such a high minimum statutory penalty unreasonably equates penalties for the leaders of organised human trafficking with those for the so-called “scafisti”, that is, individual migrants, unrelated to criminal organisations, often themselves victims of the criminal system and coerced to drive the boats with trafficked or smuggled people, or who only occasionally operate them.

The Constitutional Court, still recognising that the new legislation constituted an "exceptionally harsh" punitive response, ruled that it was not manifestly disproportionate to the seriousness of the offences. The decision emphasises that the provision exclusively targets extremely serious conduct that endangers the lives and health of migrants, primarily protecting the physical integrity of the individuals involved and not targeting the management of migration flows. The severity of the penalty, therefore, signals the significant criminal nature of the conduct.

Focusing on the mere “scafista”, as opposed to the trafficker in human beings, the Constitutional Court clarified that the criminal system offers adequate tools to modulate their individual responsibility. When a migrant is forced to drive the vessel due to violence, threats, or necessity during the crossing, such defences apply and can exclude criminal responsibility. In other cases, general mitigating circumstances, such as the minimal importance of the contribution made or psychological subjugation to the traffickers, allow the judge to assess the conduct and alleviate the punishment based on the actual negative value of the act. The Court also rejected the comparison with murder, specifying that the relevant comparison should be made with multiple murder or homicide involving injury.

One company is bearing the brunt of the backlash: Flock Safety.

text:
AI cameras, drones, licence plate readers, sound detection, Flock - the United States is monitored through a growing, high-tech, and increasingly interconnected surveillance network. In some cities, like Houston, Texas, the true extent of this system is a secret. Law enforcement says this is all for public safety - to prevent crime and assist investigations. Critics think it is an invasion of privacy, open to misuse, and a sneaky tool aiding ICE in President Trump’s deportation drive. One company is bearing the brunt of the backlash: Flock Safety. Its network of AI-powered licence plate readers spans over 6000 communities, generating 20 billion vehicle scans a month. Vigilantes have been cutting down Flock devices. Social media is full of tips on how to obstruct or disable the cameras. Ellie House is in Houston, Texas, to investigate the surveillance network authorities do not want you to know about. She sees how Flock has been used by police to fight crime, gets inside the anti-surveillance techlash, and she sits down with Flock CEO Garrett Langley in his Atlanta HQ.

This episode of The Documentary, comes to you from Assignment.

title: Report: DHS Plans to Launch Voter Fraud Investigation Surge Tuesday | Chicago News
description:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has accelerated efforts to make the department a central force in President Donald Trump’s hunt for purported widespread election fraud.
Experts say there is no evidence that widespread voter fraud has occurred in recent elections.
Starting Tuesday, HSI is launching a “coordinated criminal voter fraud surge initiative to pursue investigative leads, conduct field interviews, and support timely prosecutorial review,” the guidance says.
Another memo directed HSI agents to coordinate with US Citizenship and Immigration Services to begin removal proceedings when a noncitizen is suspected of or linked to voter fraud.
Still, the administration has touted alleged election fraud arrests.
text:
CNN | August 31, 2026, 1:47 pm

(CNN) — The Department of Homeland Security is planning a surge in its efforts to investigate voter fraud in select states starting Tuesday, according to internal federal guidance reviewed by CNN.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has accelerated efforts to make the department a central force in President Donald Trump’s hunt for purported widespread election fraud. DHS has pushed states to share their voter rolls for audit and has vowed to withhold grant funding from those that refuse to adopt a broader set of election reforms.

The department has leaned for investigative work on one of its agencies — Homeland Security Investigations — an arm of Immigration and Customs Enforcement that typically tackles major crimes like human trafficking, drug smuggling and child exploitation. The agency has already surged an unprecedented number of agents to work on cases, including chasing down voter histories of people believed to be noncitizens who may have illegally voted or registered to vote.

Experts say there is no evidence that widespread voter fraud has occurred in recent elections.

Starting Tuesday, HSI is launching a “coordinated criminal voter fraud surge initiative to pursue investigative leads, conduct field interviews, and support timely prosecutorial review,” the guidance says.

Offices in nine states are expected to take investigative action from early September to mid-October, according to the guidance. Those states include Washington, Wisconsin, Missouri, Georgia, California, Pennsylvania, Nevada, New York and Connecticut.

The guidance’s reference to investigative steps is notable given the push comes as midterm elections get underway. Such “overt” investigatory actions while elections were approaching have historically been discouraged, under long-standing Justice Department policy limiting investigative actions could influence elections.

“Doing otherwise runs the risk of chilling legitimate voting and campaign activities and of interjecting the investigation itself into ongoing campaigns and the adjudication of any ensuing election contest,” the Justice Department manual says. “It may, however, often be appropriate, in consultation with the Public Integrity Section, to share information and allegations involving such matters with state or local authorities where an immediate need for overt measures exists.”

The DOJ formally rescinded the policy under the first Trump administration but still mostly abided by it, and it was reinstated under President Joe Biden.

But DHS, as a separate department, is not obligated to follow the policy, and the new guidance makes no reference to those timing concerns.

CNN reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment.

Under the Trump administration, agents have, for example, been assigned to investigate whether naturalized U.S. citizens registered or voted before becoming citizens, CNN previously reported. Another memo directed HSI agents to coordinate with US Citizenship and Immigration Services to begin removal proceedings when a noncitizen is suspected of or linked to voter fraud.

Despite the dramatic shift of resources toward investigating election fraud, the administration has brought only a handful of prosecutions — mostly targeting cases of noncitizens voting or being unlawfully registered to vote.

Still, the administration has touted alleged election fraud arrests. Last week, the Justice Department announced that a Honduran national who was legally living in the United States had been arrested and charged with fraudulently registering to vote and falsely claiming to be a U.S. citizen.

“Today’s arrest is the first of many to come,” First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli said in a statement.

Mullin, meanwhile, has positioned himself as a leading enforcer of Trump’s voter-fraud crackdown. Earlier this summer, his department announced an audit of public voter rolls had identified more than 250,000 registered noncitizens in just four states: California, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Nevada.

“One thing that I love about numbers, and I love about facts, is they don’t lie,” Mullin told reporters at the time, warning that election officials who fail to secure the midterms could face fines or even jail time.

But the numbers have, thus far, proved far less definitive than DHS initially suggested. The department publicly claimed it had found nearly 16,000 noncitizens on Nevada’s voter rolls. But behind closed doors, the department acknowledged to the state’s top election officials that it had “confirmed” just 185 of them, according to internal records reviewed by CNN. Another 6,200 were labeled “higher confidence matches” — but still required further vetting.

description:

Federal officials have also complicated his recovery with sporadic mealtimes while in custody, his daughter alleged.
The group is also calling on Philippine consulate officials in Seattle to immediately intervene on Javar's behalf and advocate for his release.

text:
A 76-year-old man with advanced prostate cancer has been detained by federal immigration officials for more than two months, causing him to miss several critical treatments, relatives and advocates said Monday.

Loreto Javar, of Fife, Washington, has been held at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma since he was taken into custody on June 23 during an interview for his U.S. citizenship application in Tukwila. The green card holder originally from the Philippines was detained despite several serious ailments, including stage 4 prostate cancer and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, according to his daughter, Daisy Javar.

Read More on News

"I want him out today," Javar, 52, told Newsweek following a hearing Monday during which an immigration judge granted an extension in her father's case to September 20.

But the delay will cause Javar to miss another appointment for his ongoing cancer treatment. Federal officials have also complicated his recovery with sporadic mealtimes while in custody, his daughter alleged.

"It's always late," she said. "He's getting medication and he needs to be eating on time. But the medications have been given on time, luckily."

Javar said federal immigration officials detained her father during what had been expected to be a routine citizenship interview, alleging that he had been entrapped prior to his arrest.

"I think so, I really think so," she said. "They know already that he's coming ... it's true, now I'm thinking about that."

Javar declined to discuss further details of what led to her father's ongoing detention, but court documents cited Monday by the Seattle Times indicate federal officials allege he was involved in an altercation in the 1970s in the Philippines that left one person dead. He told immigration officials during his arrest that he had served roughly three years in jail in the Philippines before being released on parole, the outlet reported.

"I just want them to treat people humanely," Javar told Newsweek. "It's inhumane how they treat people when they just grab them everywhere."

Moe Cinco, an organizer for the Tanggol Migrante Movement, a grassroots organization advocating for Javar's immediate release, said the ailing elderly man will miss his third oncology appointment following Monday's extension.

"He's been languishing in the detention center and separated from his cancer treatment," Cinco told Newsweek. "And his next one is September 4, so we're really trying to get him released by then."

The group is also calling on Philippine consulate officials in Seattle to immediately intervene on Javar's behalf and advocate for his release. Consulate officials have not responded to repeated requests for help by Javar's family, Cinco said.

"The consulate has a duty to protect their national," he said. "But they are not following through on that thus far."

A petition created by Tanggol Migrante officials calling for consulate intervention had garnered more than 150 signatures as of late Monday.

"No national should have to beg their own government to defend them," the petition reads. "We refuse to accept a Philippine government that depends on the labor and remittances of overseas Filipinos while failing to protect those same Filipinos when they are subjected to repression abroad."

Loreto, a retired hotel employee and married father of two, has lived in the United States since 1995, according to his daughter and advocates.

"For nearly three decades, he worked, raised his family, and contributed to the community," the petition continued. "He was detained by ICE while attending his U.S. citizenship interview—a process he pursued in good faith."

Multiple inquiries sent to the Philippine Consulate General in Seattle and Department of Homeland Security officials were not returned Monday.

Javar had been arrested in late June because he failed to disclose a criminal conviction in the Philippines when he applied for a visa to move to the United States in 1995 to join his father, ICE officials told the Seattle Times.

The disclosure would have made him ineligible at the time of his original application, ICE spokesperson Jason Chudy told the outlet.

"He is therefore ineligible to remain in the United States now," Chudy told the Times in an email without elaborating.

Javar, meanwhile, remains optimistic that her father will ultimately be released on compassionate grounds by federal immigration officials.

text:
The American Civil Liberties Union, New York Civil Liberties Union, MacArthur Justice Center, and Hecker Fink LLP are co-counsel in Genalo v. G.M. a case addressing unreasonably prolonged detention of immigrants and lack of due process.

In 2024, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit ruled that Keisy G.M., a lawful permanent resident who had been subjected to mandatory detention for 21 months, could not be detained any longer without a hearing on whether he poses a flight risk or danger. That decision was consistent with the vast majority of federal court rulings on the government’s practice of detaining people for prolonged periods of time without any individual hearings.

The Trump administration appealed the ruling in January 2026 and on June 15 the Supreme Court agreed to hear the case, setting oral argument for Oct. 13, 2026.

The Trump administration is taking a radical position the government has not taken in the 30 years since this mandatory detention statute, 8 U.S.C. 1226(c), was enacted by Congress. It says immigrants like Mr. G.M. do not have a protected liberty interest in not being locked up without a hearing — at a time when the administration is pushing hard to detain and deport as many immigrants as possible, often locking people away in inhumane ICE detention centers, where deaths are already at record levels.

On the government’s theory, it can lock up people under this mandatory detention statute for months, years, or even decades, without a hearing — as long as the removal case is still ongoing.

The government’s novel theory is contrary to our Constitution’s fundamental promise that the government cannot lock people up without due process. It is yet another example of the Trump administration’s ongoing campaign to demonize immigrants and expand the abusive ICE detention machine, including by stripping people of their rights. Whether that’s detaining record numbers of people, building new facilities out of converted warehouses, or racking up thousands of losses in court for cutting people off from bond hearings altogether.

The federal appeals court already got this right. In 2024, the Second Circuit ruled that once detention becomes “unreasonably prolonged,” the government has to come before a judge and show “clear and convincing evidence” that the immigrant would be a flight risk or a danger to the community if released, because no one in this country should be held indefinitely on the government's word alone.

text:
McALLEN, Texas (Border Report) — A coalition of immigrant rights organizations last week testified before the United Nations in Geneva, Switzerland, alleging escalating cases of abuse against non-citizens who are being held in the United States and deported to third countries.

Representatives with the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, along with the Center for Constitutional Rights told the U.N. Human Rights Council that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents are using aggressive and discriminatory arrest practices in the United States.

“In the face of one of its most deplorable immigrant rights records in modern history, the U.S. seeks to opt out of international accountability. Today, over 70,000 people are incarcerated in an immigration detention regime that subjects people to indefinite detention, deadly medical neglect,” said Sarah Decker, senior staff attorney at the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center.

The testimony came as the U.S. plans to have its Universal Periodic Review (UPR) in a couple months. These are formal peer reviews conducted by every member state every four and a half years.

The U.S. was supposed to have been reviewed in November 2025, but decided to boycott its own review and it was rescheduled for this November.

“The UPR process is a critical moment to acknowledge the endemic scale of human rights abuses in the U.S. immigration system. And we cannot afford to let this moment pass,” Decker said.

Migrant advocates alleged before the UN Human Rights Council that ICE detention facilities lack proper medical care facilities.

They also said some people have been sent to third countries or disappeared at military facilities such as Guantánamo Bay Naval Base in Cuba.

“Immigration is treated as a purely internal matter where states enjoy the broadest discretion. The scale of what is happening in the United States removes that argument. Indefinite detention in inhumane conditions, lack of due process and independent oversight, deaths in custody, transfers to third countries and overseas facilities are not policy choices within a margin of discretion, but violations of human rights obligations, and not of one state alone. Every government that accepts people transferred out of U.S. custody takes on its own,” said Laroslavna Kondrashova, a representative of the Global Rights Advocacy.

“We need U.N. bodies, member states, and civil society to join us in boldly holding the U.S. to account for these gross abuses,” said C.J. Sandley, senior staff attorney for the Center for Constitutional Rights.

During the UPR, the United States will have the opportunity to present a written report detailing its human rights progresses and challenges.

Sandra Sanchez can be reached at SSanchez@BorderReport.com.

text:
Photo: Alexcia Negrete / Daily Titan

The California chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR-CA) today welcomed the California State Legislature’s passage of Assembly Bill (AB) 2551. The bill will now advance to Governor Gavin Newsom’s desk for his signature.

Authored by Assemblymember Sade Elhawary and co-sponsored by CAIR-CA, this legislation represents a critical step toward ensuring that Time, Place, and Manner (TPM) restrictions are equally enforced across the California State University (CSU) system, including regulations such as limiting noise levels, restricting signs on government property, or dictating protest times.

Following campus protests over the past two and a half years, CSU administrations implemented systemwide expansions of TPM policies without consulting student government or faculty associations. AB 2551 would prevent the selective enforcement of TPM regulations by requiring that they be applied equally to all students, regardless of the content of their speech.

AB 2551 would also require that CSU include demographic data on students penalized for code of conduct violations in their annual reports, and it would require campuses to hold hearings to allow students subjected to TPM restrictions to provide input on the fairness and enforcement of those policies.

In a statement, CAIR-CA Legislative & Government Affairs Director Oussama Mokeddem said:

“AB 2551 is an important step toward ensuring that California’s public universities uphold the constitutional rights of the students they serve. We have seen how supposedly neutral campus policies can be applied selectively, particularly against students advocating for Palestinian human rights or other viewpoints the schools’ leadership find inconvenient. Transparency and accountability are essential to preventing unequal enforcement—we cannot allow ‘neutrality’ to be used as a smokescreen for discrimination.

“AB 2551 passing through the legislature and moving to the Governor’s desk is an incredible success amid strong contention from some elected officials. We urge the Governor to sign this bill and commit to future efforts that safeguard the civil liberties of students in our state’s university systems.”

CAIR-CA is the California chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR), the nation’s largest Muslim civil liberties and advocacy organization. Its mission is to enhance the understanding of Islam, protect civil rights, promote justice, and empower American Muslims.

description:

Over the same period, removal orders for unaccompanied children nearly tripled, from 390 to 1,112 per month, according to a review of federal government data by California-based nonprofit Mobile Pathways and shared with Bloomberg Law.
Immigration lawyers and former judges have voiced concern over the speedy timeline, which they say doesn’t give children a fair chance to find attorneys or prepare their cases.

text:
Unaccompanied children who appear before immigration judges have less than a 2% chance of getting their asylum claim approved, according to preliminary analysis of court data since President Donald Trump returned to office.

Asylum applications from migrant kids who entered the US without a parent or guardian were approved in roughly 1.5% of cases in July 2026, a drop from the 11% approval rate in January 2025. Over the same period, removal orders for unaccompanied children nearly tripled, from 390 to 1,112 per month, according to a review of federal government data by California-based nonprofit Mobile Pathways and shared with Bloomberg Law.

The analysis indicates potential ramifications of the Justice Department’s recent instructions to immigration judges to quickly advance unaccompanied children’s removal proceedings, giving migrant kids three weeks or less to find attorneys before deciding to move forward.

Immigration lawyers and former judges have voiced concern over the speedy timeline, which they say doesn’t give children a fair chance to find attorneys or prepare their cases. That’s left many to face potential deportation without legal representation.

Asylum grant rates have dropped sharply since January 2025 as DOJ’s Executive Office for Immigration Review under the second Trump administration has transformed the immigration courts to focus on case closures and deportations. The administration has fired more than 100 immigration judges, including many installed during the Biden administration, while bringing in more than 300 military lawyers, former ICE attorneys, and others to serve as temporary and permanent judges , according to a Bloomberg Law analysis.

The administration’s emphasis on lowering the immigration court case backlog has drawn particular concern for unaccompanied children, who are entitled to certain federal statutory protections, including access to pro bono legal counsel to “the greatest extent practicable,” and relief eligibility for young victims of abuse, neglect, or abandonment.

While removal orders have increased overall since January 2025, unaccompanied children have seen the steepest increase, according to the Mobile Pathways analysis. For accompanied children, removal orders increased from roughly 1,000 to 1,500 per month, while orders among adults more than doubled from about 31,000 to 80,000 per month.

Unaccompanied children, who in the past have been given three- to six-month delays to complete an asylum application or find an attorney, are being forced to appear before judges as they also face prolonged periods in government custody. At the same time, organizations providing legal services to these kids have seen their funding from Health and Human Services’ Office of Refugee Resettlement halted.

Executive Office for Immigration Review spokesperson Kathryn Mattingly previously told Bloomberg Law that the office “prioritizes the timely completion of all cases and makes scheduling adjustments as needed to ensure cases do not languish.”

text:
[Cliquez ici pour le français]

On August 12, Calgary Police called the Canada Border Services Agency to a protest by international graduates. CBSA officers demanded identification, checked protesters’ immigration status and issued exclusion orders to people who had come into the streets to take action for their rights.

This is a dangerous escalation. Migrants must be able to protest, organize, join a picket line and participate in public life without risking immigration enforcement as a result. If this is allowed to stand, it will send a chilling message to millions of migrants across the country.

We need organizations across Canada to stand together now and make clear that immigration enforcement must never be used to target protests. Add your organization’s name to the statement already endorsed by many of Canada's leading civil society organizations.

DEADLINE: End of day, Monday, August 31, 2026.

Only your organization will be listed in the letter when sent.

Do not post over social media or distribute widely, but please do share with organizations and encourage them to sign on.

Migrants Have the Right to Protest Without Fear

To: Prime Minister Mark Carney; Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree; Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab; Alberta Premier Danielle Smith

We, the undersigned civil society organizations, are deeply alarmed by the actions of Calgary Police and the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) at a protest by international graduates in Calgary on August 12, 2026.

Freedom of expression and peaceful assembly are fundamental Charter-protected rights. They do not belong only to Canadian citizens or permanent residents. Migrants must be able to speak out, organize and protest without those activities becoming a pathway to immigration enforcement.

A migrant worker standing on a picket line must be able to speak out against their employer. An international student must be able to protest government policy. Refugees and undocumented people must be able to attend rallies, organize in their communities and criticize those in power. Immigration enforcement cannot be the price of participating in public life.

At least 1,500 Portage College students completed programs that were eligible for post graduate work permits when they enrolled. After they had completed their studies, in June 2026, Immigration Canada introduced a new rule excluding so-called “non-credit” programs to deny their applications. As a result, they began a round-the-clock protest on July 17 in Calgary and Edmonton.

On August 12, Calgary Police entered the protest site reportedly over access to a sidewalk. Police then asked CBSA to verify the immigration status of four people. CBSA subsequently arrived, checked 20 protesters and referred 12 for further investigation. Ten of them have since received exclusion orders and face deportation. These students also have Federal Court challenges underway and are pursuing available legal processes to restore their status and obtain new study permits.

When police and immigration enforcement collect information from people exercising their democratic rights and use it for immigration enforcement, it creates a chilling effect far beyond the individuals involved. These actions are happening amid already growing fear in immigrant communities, with deportations at their highest level in more than a decade and new powers under Bill C-12 allowing the government to cancel or suspend immigration documents and application processing. Migrants across the country are being told that joining the next protest, picket line or public meeting could put their ability to remain in Canada at risk.

We have all watched in horror as immigration enforcement in the United States has been used against immigrants engaged in political expression. Canada must not go down that road. The events of August 12 must never be repeated.

We call on the federal government and the government of Alberta to take immediate action including:

1. Clear public policies ensuring that participation in peaceful protests, picket lines and other protected political activity does not result in immigration enforcement.

2. An independent investigation into Calgary Police and CBSA's actions on August 12, with public findings and accountability for any wrongdoing.

3. Immediate suspension of the exclusion orders and any removal action arising from the August 12 enforcement while these events are investigated.

4. Resolution to the fundamental injustice that brought these students into the streets by exempting them from the retroactive application of the new PGWP eligibility rules and assessing them under the rules in place when they enrolled.

text:
Harford County Sheriff Jeffrey Gahler is set to testify before Congress Tuesday as lawmakers examine sanctuary policies and their impact on public safety.

Gahler, who has been outspoken about immigration enforcement for years, says he plans to bring two Maryland murder cases to the center of his testimony: the killings of Rachel Morin and Kayla Hamilton.

“I want them to understand the harm that comes, the public safety that's undermined, by allowing ultra-sanctuary immigration policies to take hold,” Gahler told FOX45 News.

ALSO READ | Trump administration expands immigration crackdown with worldwide visa pause

In 2023, 37-year-old Rachel Morin was murdered while out on the Ma and Pa Trail in Harford County. Victor Martinez-Hernandez, who was in the country illegally, was later convicted in her killing.

A year earlier, 20-year-old Kayla Hamilton was murdered in Aberdeen. Walter Javier Martinez, who was also in the country illegally, was convicted in that case.

What I want them to remember when I testify, these are two stories that our community can tell, but there are communities like ours from one corner of this country to the other,” Gahler said.

The two cases have become part of a larger debate in Maryland over cooperation between local law enforcement agencies and federal immigration authorities.

Gahler has repeatedly called for greater cooperation, arguing that restrictions on immigration enforcement can undermine public safety.

Supporters of policies such as Maryland’s Community Trust Act have argued that limiting certain cooperation with federal immigration authorities helps build trust between immigrant communities and local law enforcement.

Supporters have also argued that the policies help ensure immigrants receive due process and place limits on how federal immigration officers operate in Maryland.

Gahler said his testimony before the House Judiciary subcommittee will focus on what he sees as the public safety consequences of sanctuary policies.

“That is not public safety. That's stupidity,” Gahler said.

Still, he said he hopes lawmakers on both sides of the aisle can find common ground on immigration policy.

“Hopefully Democrats and Republicans alike can put their heads together and actually get something done for the American people,” Gahler said.

As lawmakers continue debating immigration policy in Washington, Gahler said he wants them to remember the two Maryland women whose cases will be central to his testimony: Rachel Morin and Kayla Hamilton.

text:
McALLEN, Texas (Border Report) — A coalition of immigrant rights organizations last week testified before the United Nations in Geneva, Switzerland, alleging escalating cases of abuse against non-citizens who are being held in the United States and deported to third countries.

Representatives with the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, along with the Center for Constitutional Rights told the U.N. Human Rights Council that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents are using aggressive and discriminatory arrest practices in the United States.

“In the face of one of its most deplorable immigrant rights records in modern history, the U.S. seeks to opt out of international accountability. Today, over 70,000 people are incarcerated in an immigration detention regime that subjects people to indefinite detention, deadly medical neglect,” said Sarah Decker, senior staff attorney at the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center.

The testimony came as the U.S. plans to have its Universal Periodic Review (UPR) in a couple months. These are formal peer reviews conducted by every member state every four and a half years.

The U.S. was supposed to have been reviewed in November 2025, but decided to boycott its own review and it was rescheduled for this November.

“The UPR process is a critical moment to acknowledge the endemic scale of human rights abuses in the U.S. immigration system. And we cannot afford to let this moment pass,” Decker said.

Migrant advocates alleged before the UN Human Rights Council that ICE detention facilities lack proper medical care facilities.

They also said some people have been sent to third countries or disappeared at military facilities such as Guantánamo Bay Naval Base in Cuba.

“Immigration is treated as a purely internal matter where states enjoy the broadest discretion. The scale of what is happening in the United States removes that argument. Indefinite detention in inhumane conditions, lack of due process and independent oversight, deaths in custody, transfers to third countries and overseas facilities are not policy choices within a margin of discretion, but violations of human rights obligations, and not of one state alone. Every government that accepts people transferred out of U.S. custody takes on its own,” said Laroslavna Kondrashova, a representative of the Global Rights Advocacy.

“We need U.N. bodies, member states, and civil society to join us in boldly holding the U.S. to account for these gross abuses,” said C.J. Sandley, senior staff attorney for the Center for Constitutional Rights.

During the UPR, the United States will have the opportunity to present a written report detailing its human rights progresses and challenges.

Sandra Sanchez can be reached at SSanchez@BorderReport.com.

text:
Article Insights

Recent legislative, regulatory, and litigation developments have affected Temporary Protected Status (TPS)-related employment authorization, with implications for ongoing work authorization.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed into law July 4, 2025, includes a provision limiting TPS-based employment authorization documents (EADs) to a maximum validity period of one year, or the duration of an individual’s TPS status, whichever is shorter. The OBBBA also directly curtails the previously available 540-day automatic extensions that many TPS holders relied upon. An interim final rule from the Department of Homeland Security issued Oct. 30, 2025, eliminated the regulatory basis for those 540-day automatic extensions going forward.

The Deadline for TPS EAD Extensions

For TPS beneficiaries who filed EAD renewal applications before July 22, 2025, and whose applications remained pending, automatic work authorization extensions expired on July 22, 2026, regardless of any later expiration date reflected on a Form I-797C receipt notice. This affected TPS holders from El Salvador, Sudan, Ukraine, and other designated countries that had been counting on extension end dates as late as October 2026.

The Court’s Decision Upholding the 1-Year EAD Cap

Litigation over these policies has produced mixed results. On July 21, 2026, a federal court in Massachusetts temporarily stayed certain United States Citizenship and Immigration Services policies, briefly preserving prior extension expiration dates. However, on Aug. 5, 2026, that same court largely sided with the government, upholding the one-year cap policy and rejecting arguments that it was procedurally flawed or impermissibly retroactive. The court confirmed that TPS beneficiaries from El Salvador, Sudan, and Ukraine are subject to the July 22, 2026, expiration of their 540-day extensions.

The court did grant limited relief on an unrelated policy involving consequences for asylum applicants who failed to pay the annual asylum fee, staying that provision pending further proceedings.

Employer Considerations: I-9 Reverification and E-Verify Compliance

Employers with TPS workers on their payroll may wish to take the following steps:

Audit I-9 records to identify EADs tied to TPS categories A12 or C19.

Verify whether those EADs were subject to a 540-day automatic extension that has now been cut short.

Complete I-9 reverification for any affected employees.

Monitor E-Verify for status updates reflecting the revised expiration dates.

A Note on Ongoing TPS Litigation for Other Designated Countries

Work authorization for TPS beneficiaries from certain other countries, including Burma (Myanmar), Ethiopia, Haiti, Somalia, South Sudan, Syria, and Yemen, may still be protected by separate court orders and pending litigation.

The content of this article is intended to provide a general guide to the subject matter. Specialist advice should be sought about your specific circumstances.

text:
A 17-year-old Gainesville High School student-athlete, Sebastian Jimenez, was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Jimenez and his family were taken from their apartment on August 22, according to his football coach.

Jimenez and his mother are being held at a facility in Texas pending a bond hearing.

The community, including his football team and coach, has rallied to show support and seek legal help.

A Gainesville High School student-athlete has been detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, according to Gainesville High football coach Ashour Peera and athletic director Phillip Knight.

Sebastian Jimenez, a 17-year-old senior, was detained by ICE agents Aug. 22, along with his mother, stepfather and 28-year-old sister from their Gainesville apartment, according to Peera.

The Sun searched ICE’s “Online Detainee Locator System” for Jimenez but found no records. The website states that individuals under 18 cannot be searched in the database.

His mother – Anmary Mayela-Peroza – also did not appear in the website’s records. A call on Monday, Aug. 31, to the Miramar Sub Office, which handles ICE detentions in Florida, has not yet been returned.

Who is Sebastian Jimenez?

Jimenez plays football, soccer and baseball at Gainesville High. He was the kicker and punter for the Hurricanes in their season-opening game vs. Belleview on Aug. 21.

Peera is in his first season as GHS coach, but his son, Tyler, knew Jimenez, and Peera said Jimenez had been to his house before.

“He was the only player I knew at GHS when I arrived,” Peera said Aug. 28.

Since Jimenez’s detainment, GHS students are showing their support. Ahead of the Hurricanes’ Aug. 28 rivalry game against Buchholz at Citizens Field, the football team ran through a banner that had words of support for Jimenez.

The student section at the game also held a Venezuelan flag with Jimenez’s No. 17 jersey number on it. Peera said he considered wearing a shirt with Jimenez’s face on it during the contest.

Postgame, Peera spoke little of the game itself. Instead, he called attention to Jimenez.

“It’s not about football right now for us. It’s about getting him back safely and us doing him proud and giving the effort that he would want us to have,” Peera said.

How were Sebastian Jimenez and his family detained by ICE

A friend didn’t hear from Jimenez and his family on Aug. 22, the day after the opening football game, and that friend then emailed Peera.

On Aug. 23, Peera went to the family’s apartment and, as he arrived, Jimenez called him. Since then, Peera and Jimenez have spoken seven times on the phone, thanks to commissary funds Peera has provided.

Peera said the four family members were taken to an ICE detention facility in Jacksonville. Then, Jimenez and his mother were sent to the South Texas Family Residential Center in Dilley, Texas.

The current location of his sister and stepfather is unknown.

According to Peera, Jimenez, his mother and sister are Venezuelan. His stepfather is Brazilian.

The coach said the family moved to the U.S. when Jimenez was 7 years old. This came after his mother and sister had been kidnapped in Venezuela. The U.S. government began to allow asylum for Venezuelan citizens in 1998 when Hugo Chavez was elected, and Jimenez’s family had applied for it when their visa expired.

What’s next for Sebastian Jimenez and his family?

Jimenez and his mother are scheduled to have a hearing Sept. 8 at the Texas facility to determine their future, which could include a release on bond and a return to Gainesville.

Peera said that Jimenez sounded strong on the phone, but he could still sense fear in his voice.

Peera has reached out to several attorneys for help and to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s office. Peera coached Rubio’s son – Anthony – at the University of Florida from 2023-25.

“We don’t understand why this would happen to a kid that’s been here over a decade, that’s such a good member of his community, plays three sports, is a member of clubs, and a great friend and teammate, why he would be taken from his home,” Peera said. “We’d really like to see if there is anyone who can help us in this situation to provide guidance, tell us how to approach it and figure out what options do we have?”

text:
At least six people in California have died in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody during President Donald Trump’s second term — the highest number of deaths under a presidential administration in nearly two decades.

The data, sourced from government records and compiled by an immigration data analysis firm called Relevant Research, found that 56 people had died in ICE custody since the start of the current administration. That is roughly one person every 11 days.

In California, all six of the deaths occurred at hospitals and shortly after people had been at federal detention centers. Four of the deaths were of people held at the Adelanto ICE Processing Center in San Bernardino County. Two other people died after detainment at the Imperial Regional Detention Facility near the U.S. and Mexico border.

“Being in ICE custody is much broader than whether or not someone’s actually just physically inside of an immigrant detention facility,” said Austin Kocher, president of Relevant Research, at a Monday afternoon virtual news conference about the data.

Families of the deceased in five of the cases have alleged the facility or ICE failed to provide adequate medical care, according to media reports and an investigation by the California Department of Justice published in May.

The state DOJ investigation found that detention conditions had largely worsened as the federal administration’s mass deportation campaign led to “overcrowding and strained resources.” Dozens of news outlets have reported similar worsening conditions at detention facilities across the country.

“In a way, the complications of detention centers are bleeding out, to use unfortunately a very graphic and accurate metaphor, into all of these other medical facilities,” Kocher said.

Kocher, who is also a research fellow at American University’s Center for Latin American and Latino Studies, launched the “Detention Mortality Dashboard” earlier this month. The dashboard, using ICE records, shows that 289 people have died in ICE custody since October 2003. The data does not include deaths of people who were released from custody and later died from complications.

California accounts for 40 of the total deaths, which is second most in the nation after Texas. The two states are among the highest in total number of ICE detainees. In 2006, six people in California died in ICE custody — the most in any reported year for the state.

“This is not a problem that started with the Trump administration,” Kocher said.

As of this year, California has about 9,200 beds across eight U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facilities. All are operated by private companies and located in the southern half of the state.

Kocher said the data does not seek to answer why someone died in custody, noting that ICE announcements for deaths may be incomplete, inaccurate or framed to criminalize the person. He is also unable to evaluate the medical claims.

Following a death of a person in custody, ICE must issue an initial news release announcing the death. The agency then must publicize a more detailed report within 90 days. These reports have become shorter, less detailed and more dehumanizing under Trump’s second term, Kocher said.

“We’re not necessarily going to repeat those kinds of claims or repeat that kind of language, especially because we can’t verify it,” Kocher said.

The six people that died under Trump’s second term are Jose Guadalupe Ramos-Solano, Alberto Gutierrez-Reyes, Luis Yanez Cruz, Gabriel Garcia Aviles, Huabing Xie and Ismael Ayala-Uribe. All except Xie, of China, and Yanez Cruz, of Honduras, originated from Mexico.

This week, the California Legislature has advanced several detention-related bills to Gov. Gavin Newsom’s desk. Among the legislation are efforts to impose a 25% tax on the gross income of for-profit corporations that operate immigration detention facilities, prohibit the use of state-owned property for immigration enforcement and deny businesses involved with detention facilities from receiving state grants or loans.

Newsom has until Sept. 30 to sign or veto the bills.

text:
(Texas Tribune) — The third eyewitness to the fatal shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston by an immigration officer last month has been released from federal detention.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials released Victor Salgado Araujo, who is Lorenzo’s brother, from custody Sunday morning, after his attorney filed several legal petitions including a federal suit claiming he is wrongfully being detained. The government also indicated it would likely approve his application for a temporary legal status since he is a witness to a potential crime.

He had been held in the Montgomery ICE Processing Center, which is north of Houston, since the July 7 shooting.

That morning, Victor Salgado Araujo sat in the front seat of his brother’s van as they picked up two fellow workers for a construction job, when ICE officers started following them in unmarked vehicles.

ICE initially said Lorenzo Salgado Araujo rammed their vehicles as he tried to flee and an officer shot him in self-defense. But Victor Salgado Araujo and the two other passengers disputed that account.

Victor Salgado Araujo’s release comes just days after Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare publicly said he plans to bring the case to a grand jury in the “next few weeks,” partly to force the release of more evidence. And because there is no body camera or dash camera footage of the shooting, his testimony as one of just three eyewitnesses is even more crucial to the understanding of what happened.

The other two eyewitnesses, Daniel Tirado Pantoja and Jose Trinidad Rojas Pliego, have already been released from ICE custody.

“Victor’s release is an important moment, but it is not the end of this fight,” his attorney, Ruby Powers, said in a statement. “The pursuit of truth, accountability, and justice for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo continues, and we remain steadfast in protecting Victor’s immigration rights and standing alongside him and his family.”

Ronaldo Salgado, Lorenzo’s son, similarly called his uncle’s release “a key step” in getting justice for his father.

“His first meal was chilaquiles from his favorite restaurant, just as his usual Sunday routine called for,” he added in a Facebook post. “He is now with family, finally able to process the tragic loss he witnessed and the nearly two months spent in detention.

text:
A small but committed group of protesters opposed to the Trump administration have become a familiar site on Saturdays at the intersection of East Putnam Ave and Indian Field Rd in Cos Cob.

While Indivisible Greenwich’s No Kings rallies have drawn over 1,000 people to the Havemeyer lawn, with officials including Governor Lamont and Attorney General Tong speaking, the grassroots demonstrators in Cos Cob stand out for their persistence.

For more than a year, and in all types of weather, the small group has appeared with handmade signs at the highly visible intersection for an hour every Saturday.

They count their support in honks.

Dan Edelstein from Old Greenwich said no permit was required for the weekly protests. Greenwich Police had stopped by to say the only rules were not to go in the street, not to impede traffic, and to always cross with the light.

“Everybody makes their own signs, but I bring extras,” Edelsein said amid honking horns while Bob Marley’s “Get Up, Stand Up,” played from the speaker he totes to Cos Cob on Saturdays.

“We feel like we should be here as a conscience – to let our neighbors know, especially our moderate neighbors, know that we are not okay with what’s going on in Washington, DC,” Edelstein said. “We are not okay with the threatened end to democracy. We are not okay with the President acting like a king. We are not okay with the actions of ICE.”

Cos Cob resident, Chris Day, explained his participation. “I can’t just do nothing. I can vote, but I can’t wait until November.”

“Every hour something different that’s crazy comes out, which just waters down all the other crazy, and then everyone just gets used to crazy,” Mr. Day said.

“I don’t want to be out here doing this,” he added. “But that’s how they win.”

Mr. Day, who waived a large American flag, said there were more honks of support than a year ago, which he said was heartening.

But he and Edelstein were particularly unhappy with ICE tactics in Fairfield County.

As Edelstein’s playlist moved on to The Who’s “Won’t Get Fooled Again,” Mr. Day criticized the President.

“He didn’t win the presidential election. He was caught in Florida with the documents. In Georgia tried to fix the vote,” he said. “If he loses ground in November, different versions of the same ridiculousness will be back because he’s given us, virtually every day, doing something illegal. He’s a felon. He’s a rapist.”

A few feet away, Pat Ferris pointed out that the drivers honking weren’t just workers in trucks and vans, but Porsche and BMW drivers beeping and giving the thumbs-up gesture.

“Once it’s near you, it makes a difference,” Ferris said of the ICE activity in Connecticut last week.

“What I notice is I’m not getting any negativity. In the past we were told to shut up. Last week we were called ‘retarded.’ They’ll give us the thumbs down or they’ll root for Trump. But, today it’s amazing. It’s so much beeping and thumbs up.”

As for ICE rounding up immigrants in Connecticut, and the refrain that ICE is only targeting people with criminal records, she exclaimed, “Don’t we all want the criminals gone!”

“It’s just such a cover up. They’re blanketing all immigrants. It’s just evil. Stephen Miller and his quotas, and hiring all these goons. It’s sinful.”

“The mass deportation policy is among all the terrible policies inflicted on the American people,” Edelstein said. “They’re sending them to these camps with terrible conditions, where they are denying people medication and treating them terribly. The conditions are miserable to the point that people are dying. It’s a completely cynical policy. No one in this administration actually believes that these people have anything to do with the downturn of our country. They are not criminals.”

“Statistically, average Americans are much more likely to commit crimes than these so-called felons. These are gardeners, teachers and people who work in kitchens. They are the foundation of America. They are not a threat to society.”

Last week ICE made arrests in Stamford, Bridgeport and Danbury.

“They kidnapped about 100 people,” Edelstein said. “I can guarantee you that almost none of them have any criminal record at all, and many of them have not been accused of, much less convicted of a crime.”

“These are all hard working people. On Monday at Home Depot in Stamford on Main Street, a mother of three kids – one of whom is disabled – was kidnapped in front of her family by ICE. If people think this happens elsewhere or only in Minnesota, they are wrong. This is happening here and now,” Edelstein said.

Edelstein said ICE was rounding up groups of people and using facial recognition software to scan faces.

“If they get a hit, there is absolutely no due process. They are quickly taking people to other states so they have less resources, and to make it harder to get an attorney,” he added.

At a press conference in Danbury on Wednesday, Governor Lamont decried ICE activity in Fairfield County coinciding with the start of the school year.

Approximately 50 members of the Danbury community were detained in the first three days of the week, with the effort starting on the first day of school.

Governor Lamont said people being picked up included those “doing it right” – those participating in the asylum process and those married to US citizens.

The Governor said he was outraged.

“We stand for due process, not the secret police. That’s what this country is about – the fifth and sixth amendment,” Lamont continued. “I was on the phone with Secretary Mullin, and I said, I’m outraged. This is the first day of school…and you have people patrolling around our courthouses and patrolling around schools. Stay away. Let our kids get to school safely.”

Mayor of Danbury, Roberto Alves, who appeared at the press conference with the chief and deputy chief of police, said the Danbury Police Dept does not partner with ICE. He said it was important that the immigrant community knows they can call police if they are victims of crime, victims of domestic abuse, or witness a crime being committed.

“This isn’t a targeted campaign on folks who have committed serious crimes. We are now seeing racial profiling,” Mayor Alves said.

A statement from ICE on Wednesday said, “Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin, if you break the law, you will face the consequences. Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the U.S.”

Lamont, Blumenthal, Himes Issue Statements on ICE Activity in Connecticut
