He notes this is a clear violation of human rights from all perspectives.
text:
A South African judge has barred deportations of undocumented foreign nationals, while the UN has called for vigilante groups in the country to be banned, and the African Union (AU) has formally been urged to act on the ongoing illegal immigrant sentiment in SA to preserve solidarity on the continent, notes Legalbrief. The Gauteng High Court (Johannesburg) has been inundated with urgent applications from undocumented foreign nationals challenging their deportations, a surge Judge Mandlenkosi Motha described as the 'aftershock' of March and March’s Abahambe (They must leave) campaign. GroundUp reports that between 17 and 21 August, nearly 60 matters were placed on Motha’s motion roll, with 21 proceeding. Most involved Ethiopian, Congolese and Nigerian nationals detained at Lindela Repatriation Centre who had not been interviewed by the Refugee Reception Office (RRO). In his judgment, Motha rejected the practice of releasing undocumented migrants back into society only to face re‑arrest, calling it 'the height of folly'. He said such 'catch and release' procedures were undignified, fostered corruption, and exposed vulnerable individuals to exploitation. 'The expression of an intention to apply for asylum is no reason to release an undocumented foreign national back into society under the hope that within 10 or 15 days they will present themselves to the RRO,' he said. The court barred the deportations and ordered Home Affairs to deploy immigration and refugee officials to Lindela or transport detainees to the nearest RRO for processing.

The ruling follows the Constitutional Court’s July decision that asylum seekers cannot be deported before accessing the asylum system. GroundUp reports the judgment struck down sections of the Refugees Act requiring transit visas, finding the provisions unconstitutional and inconsistent with the principle of non‑refoulement. Motha noted, however, that the apex court left lower courts in a 'Catch‑22' by failing to define what a 'merits‑based determination' entails. Motha also cautioned against courts becoming echo chambers dominated by well‑resourced NGOs, noting that grassroots organisations such as Operation Dudula and March and March were absent from the hearings despite representing significant public sentiment. 'To ignore the views of the impoverished and downtrodden members of society does not augur well for the future,' he warned. The respondents were ordered to pay the costs of all applications.

Full GroundUp report

A UN committee has called on SA to prohibit and dismantle organised racist vigilante groups, citing at least four migrant killings and the displacement of at least 50 000 migrants amid a wave of xenophobic violence since early 2026. According to the Mail & Guardian, the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) raised concerns about inadequate policing and insufficient accountability for attacks, unlawful evictions and home raids targeting migrants, refugees and asylum seekers. Its decision, adopted on 21 August and publicised on 27 August, adds international scrutiny to the government’s response after earlier warnings from African human rights authorities and a domestic court order requiring action against xenophobic conduct. CERD specifically named the Insizwa Nobunsizwa Development Foundation and March and March movement in expressing concern about racist hate speech and harmful stereotypes targeting migrants, particularly on the internet and social media. The committee called for measures to prevent the formation of organised vigilante groups responsible for racial discrimination, hate speech and hate crimes and to prohibit and dismantle such organisations. The committee highlighted reports of abductions, looting, destruction of migrants’ property and businesses, unlawful evictions by landlords, identity checks and home raids.

Full Mail & Guardian report

Nigeria's President has demanded urgent action to sustain Africa's solidarity and unity at yesterday’s 21st Extraordinary African Union (AU) Summit, reports Premium Times. President Bola Tinubu has formally reported the recurring xenophobic and Afrophobic attacks against Africans and other nationals in SA to the AU, warning that the incidents undermine the continent's solidarity, unity and peaceful coexistence. Specifically, he requested prompt collective action from the continent's leaders, including the placement of this matter on the agenda for the 40th Ordinary Session of the Assembly. The Nigerian leader made the nation's position known in a message delivered by his deputy, Vice-President Kashim Shettima, at the 21st Extraordinary Session of the Assembly of the AU in Luanda, Angola. The President urged African leaders to reaffirm their commitment to the safety, protection and dignity of all African nationals. ‘While recognising South Africa's sovereign right to enforce its immigration laws and acknowledging its contributions to the continent, Nigeria stresses that such attacks undermine African solidarity, unity and peaceful coexistence, and require urgent collective attention.’ ‘It is on this note that Nigeria calls on this august Assembly to place the matter on the agenda of the upcoming 40th Ordinary Session of the AU Assembly, scheduled for January 2027, for consideration and appropriate action,’ he declared. Tinubu called for stronger continental efforts to combat xenophobia and Afrophobia, stressing that dialogue, preventive diplomacy, and collective action remained essential to preserving African unity.

Full Premium Times report

The South African Government’s decision to apply immigration laws and close loopholes – long overdue in my opinion – has not gone down well with some governments on the continent. Some perceive this as Trumpian in nature, while Ghana’s government went a step further in petitioning the AU, observes journalist Fred Khumalo. ‘On the face of it, this might seem hostile, but Ghana’s petition is not merely justified – it’s a vital duty of Pan-African stewardship,’ Khumalo writes in News24. He notes at the heart of Ghana’s intervention is an urgent concern for human safety and continental solidarity. ‘Sporadic outbreaks of violence targeting African migrants endanger lives, threaten small businesses, and erode the mutual trust essential for projects like the African Continental Free Trade Area,’ Khumalo explains. He argues that by framing these flare-ups as an ‘urgent matter of continental interest’, Accra rightly underscores that the rights of African nationals cannot stop at national borders. Under the AU Constitutive Act and the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights, member states commit to safeguarding the dignity, liberty, and human rights of everyone residing within their jurisdiction. ‘When foreign nationals face physical danger simply because of their origin, it challenges the legal and moral obligations shared by all signatory states,’ Khumalo writes. He recalls when March and March announced undocumented foreign nationals should vacate the country by 30 July, hundreds of Malawians fled to the consulate for safety. On sporadic occasions, some of them have been taken in buses to Lindela, the transit camp where foreigners get stationed before they are sent to their home countries. However, two months later, Malawians are still squatting outside their consulate. He notes this is a clear violation of human rights from all perspectives.

Khumalo argues Malawian authorities have shirked their responsibility and the South African Government has not lived up to the letter and spirit of the AU’s African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights. Rather than pursuing contentious legal litigation, Ghana’s petition outlines a structured, diplomatic path focused on preventative continental governance,’ he explains. Ghana is asking the AU to place xenophobic violence on the agenda of AU Summits, to strengthen AU monitoring of member states’ human rights compliance, to deploy an official AU fact-finding mission to investigate root causes and to facilitate AU-led dialogue initiatives to foster pan-African unity. Khumalo believes these requested actions demonstrate a measured and constructive approach. He notes that Pretoria, through the Department of International Relations & Co-operation, has cautioned against isolating single nations. ‘South African authorities highlight that law enforcement has moved to condemn violence and arrest perpetrators, arguing tensions stem from broader, systemic issues – such as economic anxieties, high unemployment, and continental migration pressures – rather than state-sanctioned hostility,’ he writes in News24. SA advocates for a holistic continental discussion on the ‘push and pull factors of migration’. Khumalo argues Pretoria’s position underscores exactly why an AU-level dialogue is essential. ‘Addressing migration pressures, socio-economic strain, and border management requires shared responsibility across origin, transit, and destination states,’ he explains. He argues Ghana’s intervention is the spur Pretoria needs to review and properly implement and monitor its immigration programme. ‘Ghana’s request for formal AU involvement provides the exact multilateral platform needed to bridge these perspectives, to bring about shared responsibility across origin, transit and destination states. Elevating this issue to Addis Ababa doesn’t mean pointing fingers at SA. It means equipping the continent to solve a shared, systemic challenge together,’ Khumalo concludes.

Full News24 analysis

title: Federal probe closes in on 'Lawyer of Miracles' after 54,000 immigration cases left in limbo
description:
Agents from a specialized immigration fraud unit have started interviewing complainants as part of an investigation that could lead to criminal charges.
Unjust enrichment, racketeering, legal malpractice and breach of contract are among the claims raised in the lawsuits against Lozano.
According to the class-action complaints, she represented more than 80,000 clients, most of them undocumented Mexican immigrants, who paid between $10,000 and $25,000 per case.
When Lozano surrendered her law license in May, a move that shielded her from disciplinary proceedings before the Washington State Bar Association, she left nearly 54,000 immigration cases in limbo.
The “Lawyer of Miracles” told him that this made him eligible for a T visa, which is available to survivors of labor or sex trafficking.
text:
No one knows where Alexandra Lozano is. The self-styled “Lawyer of Miracles” is facing two class-action lawsuits accusing her of enriching herself at the expense of dozens of migrants who paid her thousands of dollars, believing she could help them obtain legal status in the United States. Some of those clients were ultimately deported to Mexico. While Lozano has remained silent, the federal government has begun scrutinizing her activities. Agents from a specialized immigration fraud unit have started interviewing complainants as part of an investigation that could lead to criminal charges.

The inquiry is being conducted by agents in Seattle, Washington, from the Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate (FDNS), a division of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), according to federal officials who spoke to EL PAÍS on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the press.

“They are speaking with witnesses,” one source said. “The goal is to present the case to a grand jury so that an indictment can be pursued in the Western District of Washington.”

FDNS, the agency that has Lozano on its radar, “safeguards the integrity of the nation’s lawful immigration system by leading USCIS’ efforts to combat fraud, [and] detect national security and public safety threats,” according to the USCIS website.

At this point, Lozano has not been charged with any crime. Attorneys from the law firm Angeli & Calfo, which has offices in Seattle and Portland, did not respond to requests for comment from EL PAÍS.

Days earlier, Angelo J. Calfo, Lozano’s lead attorney, rejected the allegations made against his client in the two class-action lawsuits. “Alexandra denies the claims brought by this small group among the thousands of people she has represented,” Calfo told Telemundo Noticias. “She will respond to these allegations in court.”

54,000 cases left in limbo

The downfall of the “Lawyer of Miracles” began as complaints mounted from clients who accused her of misleading them in applications for lawful permanent residency, or green cards, using false information, charging exorbitant fees and initiating immigration cases that she allegedly knew were unlikely to succeed. Former clients also alleged that staff members memorized scripts containing misleading promises and that the firm developed legal strategies based solely on software-generated assessments, without reviewing individual case files.

Many of the cases handled by Lozano relied on the Violence Against Women Act (VAWA), a 1994 law that allows victims of domestic abuse married to U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents to seek immigration relief independently of their abusers. According to the allegations, however, Lozano submitted false or exaggerated accounts to support some of those petitions, which were ultimately denied by immigration courts.

Unjust enrichment, racketeering, legal malpractice and breach of contract are among the claims raised in the lawsuits against Lozano. According to the class-action complaints, she represented more than 80,000 clients, most of them undocumented Mexican immigrants, who paid between $10,000 and $25,000 per case.

With part of those earnings, Lozano purchased a Bombardier Challenger 300 private jet valued at roughly $25 million, painted it pink and used it for both business and leisure travel. The lawsuits allege that her broader strategy was to build what they describe as a “multimillion-dollar domestic real estate portfolio.” Her assets allegedly included luxury condominiums in Seattle and Chicago worth more than $4 million, as well as two properties in Mexico. The most valuable was a mansion in Bosques de las Lomas, one of Mexico City’s most exclusive neighborhoods.

When Lozano surrendered her law license in May, a move that shielded her from disciplinary proceedings before the Washington State Bar Association, she left nearly 54,000 immigration cases in limbo.

“She’s in hiding, she won’t show her face,” said attorney Vicente Barraza, who represents the 34 plaintiffs. Barraza added that the situation has put thousands of people at risk at a time when immigrants are facing increasingly aggressive enforcement under the Trump administration. “It’s a different matter when a lawyer has her clients’ lives in her hands.”

From fake trafficking victim to deportee

With her trademark blonde hair and lightly accented Spanish, Lozano often filmed videos in front of an image of Our Lady of Guadalupe or wore clothing featuring designs reminiscent of the Sacred Heart of Jesus. It was part of an aggressive marketing strategy on Facebook and TikTok that projected an almost saintly image of her services.

“Lozano’s marketing materials created the impression that Ms. Lozano is capable of performing miracles because of her association with the Virgen de Guadalupe and the Catholic church, and that Lozano represents and follows the values associated with the Virgen de Guadalupe,” said one of the lawsuits, which was filed on behalf of 34 clients, at least six of whom have been deported to Mexico.

One of them is Severo López Contreras, a Mexican national who paid $17,500 in the hope of being protected from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) operations. According to the lawsuit, the opposite happened.

The complaint alleges that Lozano’s firm falsely tried to portray López Contreras as a victim of human trafficking on the grounds that his construction company had not been paid for a drywall installation job in 2016. The “Lawyer of Miracles” told him that this made him eligible for a T visa, which is available to survivors of labor or sex trafficking. He was promised a work permit within six months and a green card within two years.

That hope evaporated on Oct. 1, 2025, when López Contreras was detained during an ICE raid. While in ICE custody, he contacted Lozano, who informed him that, despite the substantial fees he had paid, her firm had never actually filed the T visa application.

According to the complaint, “showing neither contrition nor taking responsibility for the failure, Lozano demanded an additional payment of $20,000 after Mr. Lopez Contreras’s arrest to file an asylum claim for him while he remained in an immigration detention facility.”

Lozano never refunded him a cent. López Contreras ultimately accepted deportation to Jalisco, bringing to an end three decades of life in the United States.

title: Immigration advocates testify before UN regarding U.S. human rights violations against non-citizens
description:
Held regularly since 2008, the UN Human Rights Council conducts a UPR of each member state every four and a half years.
These formal peer reviews are a platform for international accountability, with civil society organizations and nonprofits submitting reports on relevant human rights issues and violations.
“The UPR process is a critical moment to acknowledge the endemic scale of human rights abuses in the U.S. immigration system.
The United States cannot claim to respect human rights while stripping hundreds of thousands of Haitians of protection and subjecting them to increasingly aggressive and discriminatory enforcement.
The full immigration coalition includes Amnesty International; The Advocates for Human Rights; AVAN Immigrant Services; Black Alliance for Just Immigration; Center for Constitutional Rights; Center for Human Rights and Constitutional Law; Community Justice Project; Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project; Global Rights Advocacy; Haitian Bridge Alliance; Hope Border Institute; Human Rights First; Immigration Services and Legal Advocacy; Immigrant Defenders Law Center; International Refugee Assistance Project; Muslim Advocates; National Immigration Project; Physicians for Human Rights; Public Council; Refugee Council USA; Refugees International; The Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center; Southern Border Communities Coalition; and United Stateless.
text:
Washington, D.C., August 31, 2026 – Last week, a coalition of immigrant rights organizations testified before the United Nations about the United States’ escalating abuse of non-citizens through inhumane practices such as mass immigration detention; third country removals; and increasingly aggressive, discriminatory ICE enforcement. Representatives from the coalition presented before the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, in preparation for the United States’ rescheduled Universal Periodic Review (UPR) in November 2026.

Held regularly since 2008, the UN Human Rights Council conducts a UPR of each member state every four and a half years. These formal peer reviews are a platform for international accountability, with civil society organizations and nonprofits submitting reports on relevant human rights issues and violations. Following the review, other UN member states make recommendations to the country under review based on civil society reports and interactions with government representatives.

In November 2025, the United States made the unprecedented decision to boycott its own review. In light of the U.S. government’s refusal to participate, the UPR was rescheduled for November 2026.

“In the face of one of its most deplorable immigrant rights records in modern history, the U.S. seeks to opt out of international accountability. Today, over 70,000 people are incarcerated in an immigration detention regime that subjects people to indefinite detention, deadly medical neglect, rampant sexual abuse, and retaliation through solitary confinement with virtually no oversight,” said Sarah Decker, senior staff attorney at the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center. “The UPR process is a critical moment to acknowledge the endemic scale of human rights abuses in the U.S. immigration system. And we cannot afford to let this moment pass.”

During their testimony, representatives from the coalition called out the United States’ recent human rights violations against immigrants and asylum seekers, including the deadly lack of adequate medical care within ICE facilities; the renewed use of family detention; enforced disappearances to third countries and military facilities such as the Guantánamo Bay Naval Base; and racially discriminatory ICE enforcement practices. Representatives also referenced additional abuses documented within the coalition’s April 2026 report, which was submitted as part of the formal UPR process.

“Immigration is treated as a purely internal matter where States enjoy the broadest discretion. The scale of what is happening in the United States removes that argument. Indefinite detention in inhumane conditions, lack of due process and independent oversight, deaths in custody, transfers to third countries and overseas facilities are not policy choices within a margin of discretion, but violations of human rights obligations, and not of one State alone. Every government that accepts people transferred out of US custody takes on its own. Despite the US’s absence from the UPR, the dialogue continues and civil society still has a platform to share its concerns,” said Iaroslavna Kondrashova, Representative of the Global Rights Advocacy.

“In the name of mass deportation – nearly half a million people deported in a single year, including about 23,000 to third countries – the U.S. has flouted domestic law and international treaty obligations such as the Convention Against Torture. We need UN bodies, member states, and civil society to join us in boldly holding the U.S. to account for these gross abuses,” said C.J. Sandley, senior staff attorney, Center for Constitutional Rights.

“This month, over 350,000 Haitians woke up undocumented as the US Supreme Court granted the Trump Administration permission to strip them of their legal status known as Temporary Protected Status (TPS), leaving families vulnerable to detention and deportation,” said Guerline Jozef, Executive Director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance. “We are now seeing Haitians and other Black immigrants being boxed in by ICE SUVs and kidnapped on the spot. The Haitian community is afraid to take their US children to school, let alone be separated from them. The United States cannot claim to respect human rights while stripping hundreds of thousands of Haitians of protection and subjecting them to increasingly aggressive and discriminatory enforcement. The Black immigrant communities continue to be the target of relentless harassment and abuse.”

Now that civil society testimony has concluded, the UN Human Rights Council will determine specific questions and areas of focus for the United States’ scheduled review in November.

The full immigration coalition includes Amnesty International; The Advocates for Human Rights; AVAN Immigrant Services; Black Alliance for Just Immigration; Center for Constitutional Rights; Center for Human Rights and Constitutional Law; Community Justice Project; Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project; Global Rights Advocacy; Haitian Bridge Alliance; Hope Border Institute; Human Rights First; Immigration Services and Legal Advocacy; Immigrant Defenders Law Center; International Refugee Assistance Project; Muslim Advocates; National Immigration Project; Physicians for Human Rights; Public Council; Refugee Council USA; Refugees International; The Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center; Southern Border Communities Coalition; and United Stateless.

title: Northern California ICE Arrests Surged This Summer - KQED
description:
In California, in ICE’s San Francisco “area of responsibility,” which includes all of the state north of Bakersfield, ICE made 890 arrests in July.
Despite the statewide increase, there are still far fewer immigration arrests here than in Texas and Florida.
And we’re not leading in terms of the number of ICE arrests.
“By contrast, when a state like Texas or Florida allows 287(g), that increases ICE arrests overall,” Chan said.
“If local law enforcement is engaged in immigration enforcement, that’s going to drive up ICE arrests.
text:
Immigration agents arrested more people in Northern California in July than at any point since President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025. That’s according to a KQED analysis of newly released data compiled by UC Berkeley’s Deportation Data Project.

Arrests by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement across California and nationally have likewise surged to new levels, the data shows, even as the Trump administration has backed off the high-profile raids it launched last year in cities from Los Angeles to Minneapolis, where ICE agents fatally shot two protesters.

Nationwide, ICE recorded nearly 50,000 arrests in July. Close to 4,300 of them were in California, making it the state with the third-highest number of arrests — though it was dwarfed by the scale of arrests in Texas and Florida, which together accounted for nearly 20,000 of the month’s immigration arrests.

In California, in ICE’s San Francisco “area of responsibility,” which includes all of the state north of Bakersfield, ICE made 890 arrests in July. That’s more than a 60% increase since February, the last month for which this data was previously available.

Bay Area immigration lawyers say they’ve seen the increase reflected in a jump in calls to rapid response hotlines this summer.

Most of the arrests are taking place at ICE check-in appointments, for which people are often summoned abruptly, they said. Typically, immigrants required to check in are people who lack a visa but have some type of provisional permission to remain in the country, including a pending asylum case.

Lourdes Martinez, an attorney at Centro Legal de la Raza in Oakland, said her nonprofit recommends that people who are called into an ICE office “out of the blue” contact their county’s rapid response network before they go.

“We started this year with a low number of arrests,” Martinez said. “But we heard with the big appropriations bill last year that they were hiring 10,000-plus new agents. And so we were expecting that things were going to pick up.”

The number of people arrested has risen sharply this spring across California, but it remains lower in the San Francisco area of responsibility than in ICE’s two other subdivisions in the state. The San Diego border region saw 1,955 arrests in July, and the Los Angeles office arrested 1,406 people.

Despite the statewide increase, there are still far fewer immigration arrests here than in Texas and Florida. That’s largely because of California laws passed during the first Trump administration that restrict the ability of local law enforcement to cooperate with ICE, according to Angela Chan, an assistant chief attorney at the San Francisco Public Defender’s Office.

“California has the highest number of immigrants compared to any other state. And we’re not leading in terms of the number of ICE arrests. That’s likely largely due to our sanctuary laws,” said Chan, who helped author the laws.

She said in 2018, after California barred participation in a federal program known by its code section, 287(g), that delegates police and sheriff’s deputies to take on some duties of ICE agents, immigration arrests dropped by nearly 25%.

“By contrast, when a state like Texas or Florida allows 287(g), that increases ICE arrests overall,” Chan said. “If local law enforcement is engaged in immigration enforcement, that’s going to drive up ICE arrests. Any contact with police can turn into an immigration enforcement action.”

The Deportation Data Project obtained the government data from ICE under a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit. The new numbers run from October 2022 through Aug. 6 of this year.

In a statement in response to questions from KQED, a U.S. Department of Homeland Security spokesperson who declined to be identified said the information released by the Deportation Data Project “relies on information releases that have not been reviewed, audited or given context,” and alleged that the organization had “cherry-picked” the data “to peddle a false narrative.”

But as enforcement increases, those arrested are less likely to be dangerous criminals and more apt to be people who lack a secure immigration status, Ruiz Soto said.

“We know that when there have been more arrests, the share of people who have no criminal conviction or charge aside from being in the country without status has continued to increase,” he said. “Most people who are being arrested are not the worst of the worst.”

California Newsroom data reporter Emily Zentner contributed to this report. The California Newsroom is a collaboration between NPR stations and nonprofit newsrooms throughout the state.

title: 'Springfield is under siege right now.' ICE agents in Ohio have detained 2 Haitian pastors.
description:
“Springfield is under siege right now,” said Carl Ruby, pastor of Springfield’s Central Christian Church.
Fellow Springfield pastor Gilbert Joubert Adrien was detained by ICE agents on Aug. 20 and advocates are calling for his release.
Many Haitians detained in Springfield by ICE are being sent to Butler County Jail in Hamilton, which had 1,103 total inmates as of Friday afternoon.
Haitians living in Springfield are being required to report to ICE offices in Blue Ash or Westerville and wear ankle monitors.
It is designed to humiliate, and we want it to stop right now.” The pastor recently helped a Haitian family relocate to Canada.
text:
More than 40 Haitians in Springfield have been detained by United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement after President Donald Trump revoked their legal status earlier this summer.

Faith leaders recently spoke out against the ICE activity that has been taking place in the Clark County city after a June decision by the U.S. Supreme Court allowed President Donald Trump to end temporary protected status for the 330,000 Haitians who’ve fled the violence in their home country. Legal protected status for Haitians officially ended on July 27.

Haitian Support Center Executive Director Viles Dorsainvil is a TPS holder with an asylum case pending.

“I am calling out this administration to tell them that we deserve to be treated with dignity,” he said. “We deserve to be treated as human beings. We are not animals.”

Dorsainvil is one of about 15,000 Haitians who live in Springfield, with a mixture of temporary protected status, citizenship, and other legal status.

“They are not a threat to the community,” Dorsainvil said.

First Baptist Church Pastor Adam Banks said Haitian people are not “political bargaining chips.”

“They are not threats to be monitored and removed,” he said. “They are care providers, co-workers, faith leaders, and family. … We demand an end to deportations that tear families and our community apart.”

ICE agents are detaining people in Springfield in shopping plazas, gas stations, and apartment complexes.

“Springfield is under siege right now,” said Carl Ruby, pastor of Springfield’s Central Christian Church.

Fellow Springfield pastor Gilbert Joubert Adrien was detained by ICE agents on Aug. 20 and advocates are calling for his release.

“We hope that will happen very, very soon,” Ruby said. “He needs to be out immediately. He is a good man with a congregation to serve, and they are without a pastor right now.”

A pastor from the First Haitian Evangelical Church of Springfield was detained last week when he was in Northwest Ohio and he might be out of the country already, according to Ruby.

Many Haitians detained in Springfield by ICE are being sent to Butler County Jail in Hamilton, which had 1,103 total inmates as of Friday afternoon.

The general housing capacity for Butler County Jail is 844, even though the Ohio Department of Rehabilitation and Correction recommends 756 as the housing capacity, according to a 2025 ODRC inspection report.

Haitians living in Springfield are being required to report to ICE offices in Blue Ash or Westerville and wear ankle monitors.

“Being outfitted with that monitor, it just symbolizes slavery,” Dorsainvil said.

He shared the story of a mother who came to the Haitian Support Center, having given birth a few weeks prior, but lost the baby.

“She could not even walk, but they put the shackle on her,” Dorsainvil said. “You cannot understand how hard it is to hear those people on a daily basis crying.”

Advocates are calling for an end to the ankle monitors.

“It is inhumane,” Ruby said. “It is an insult. It is designed to humiliate, and we want it to stop right now.”

The pastor recently helped a Haitian family relocate to Canada.

“Their children had survived kidnapping attempts when they were in Haiti,” he said. “Most families can’t go to Canada. It was only an option for this family because they had an immediate family member who was there.”

The U.S. Department of State currently has a Level 4 “Do Not Travel” advisory for Haiti “due to the risk of crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest, and limited healthcare,” according to the agency.

A top security official and chief of staff to the nation’s defense minister was kidnapped in June.

The federal government promised Haitians who self-deport a free airplane ticket and a $2,600 check to return to Haiti.

“They are not getting the money that our government has promised,” Ruby said.

He talked to a reporter in Haiti who shared that Haitians who are being deported are getting off the plane and running for their lives.

“It puts a target on them that says to the gangs, ‘come get this person.’ ”

text:
MEMPHIS, Tenn. — As we continue coverage of an ICE raid operation that took place at a Mexican bar in Berclair, we are also sharing that, for some families, the fear of immigration enforcement didn’t end at the bar on Macon Road, but it could have carried over into drop-off at campuses across the district.

In January, ICE raids impacted school attendance, and on Monday morning, one parent said they fear those concerns will rise again following the operation that may have detained more than 100 people.

“A lot of families are scared to come and drop their kids off at school. Like, some parents have to have other people drop their kids off, you know? Like, for my family, I know like my mom is scared to come out because my stepdad was deported last year,” said Esmeralda Moreno, a parent.

In a video shared with WREG from advocacy group Vecindarios 901, ICE agents patrolled the parking lot with a bus used to transport captives. The advocacy group says more than 100 people were detained.

“I’ve never seen nothing like that, and it’s really sad people can’t even go out and have a good time without people coming and taking them,” Moreno said. “All they did was come over for a better future for their family and themselves.”

In January, we previously reported on deportation fears impacting campus attendance across the city, where parents urged board members to do something or risk students missing critical learning time.

“People can’t even come and drop their kids off because maybe they think, “Oh, ICE is going to come get me today,” Moreno said.

At this time, it is unclear if this incident impacted school attendance today, but in a one-on-one interview with Superintendent Dr. Roderick Richmond early this year, he said the district hadn’t seen or heard ICE agents on any of the campuses.

Moreno says while she understands the fear families may experience right now, she’s doing her part to support those who need it.

“If they’re ever scared, they can always contact anybody that’s willing to help them. There are people willing to help them to come drop their kids off, like myself. If they ever need help, I don’t mind coming to help to drop their kids off,” Moreno said.

text:
The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York entered judgment revoking the naturalization of convicted rapist Gurmeet Singh.

“American citizenship is not a shield for criminals,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Gurmeet Singh, a convicted rapist from India, is no longer a U.S. citizen. He concealed a rape and kidnapping during the naturalization process, and a federal court has now revoked his citizenship. This Department took this case across the finish line, and we will continue to move expeditiously on denaturalization referrals. Fraudulently obtained citizenship will not protect criminals from justice.”

“Singh unlawfully obtained the privileges of U.S. citizenship by concealing horrible criminal acts,” said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. “The Department will continue to protect the integrity of the citizenship process and hold accountable those who defraud our immigration system.”

“The Court’s judgment, which requires the defendant to surrender his wrongfully obtained citizenship, sends a strong message to those who obtain citizenship through deceit, and demonstrates the Administration’s resolve to pursue denaturalization proceedings in all cases permitted by law and supported by the evidence,” said U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr for the Eastern District of New York.

A native of India, Singh entered the United States in February 1992 as a visitor for a temporary period not to exceed six months. He then remained in the United States without authorization for years until a family-based immigrant visa petition allowed him to become a permanent resident in June 2000.

In May 2011 — mere weeks before he filed his application to naturalize as a U.S. citizen — Singh, a taxicab driver at the time, drove a female passenger who fell asleep during her ride home to a location with no witnesses. When his passenger awoke, she found Singh on top of her with a knife against her throat. He threatened her, bound and gagged her, blindfolded her, removed her clothes, and raped her. Afterwards, the victim escaped from the cab and ran to someone in the streets at dawn for help.

Singh concealed these acts throughout his naturalization proceedings, leading to his becoming a U.S. citizen on Oct. 19, 2011. After naturalizing, Singh was convicted in New York of Rape in the First Degree and Kidnapping in the Second Degree as a Sexually Motivated Felony and sentenced to 20 years in prison.

The Aug. 26 order revoking Singh’s naturalization follows a complaint the Justice Department filed on Feb. 2.

This case was prosecuted by Trial Attorney Christopher Lyerla of the Civil Division’s Office of Immigration Litigation and Assistant U.S. Attorney Layaliza Soloveichik for the Eastern District of New York.

title: ILRC Submits Comment Opposing DHS Final Rule on Immigrant Registration
description:
The Immigrant Legal Resource Center (ILRC) submitted a comment strongly opposing the Department of Homeland Security’s Final Rule on “[Immigrant] Registration Form and Evidence of Registration.” The rule expands and formalizes a registration process that could expose millions of immigrants—and potentially U.S. citizens—to increased fear, confusion, racial profiling, and immigration enforcement.
In its comment, the ILRC provides that the Final Rule violates the Administrative Procedure Act and Paperwork Reduction Act, including by failing to provide meaningful notice and opportunity for public comment.
The ILRC further warns that registration systems have a long history of enabling discrimination and government abuses.
The current registration process threatens to similarly harm immigrant communities, particularly children, people with limited English proficiency or access to technology, people with disabilities, and survivors of domestic violence, crime, and human trafficking.
The ILRC urges DHS to rescind the Final Rule in its entirety and eliminate the registration requirement.

text:
The Trump administration deported a Nigerian man despite a standing order protecting him from being returned to the country where an immigration judge found he had previously been tortured by government officials, prompting a federal judge to order the government to explain what it is doing to bring him back to the United States.

Judge Michelle Williams Court of the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California on Thursday granted a temporary restraining order sought by Etinosa Osahon and ordered the government to disclose his current location, custodial status and any steps being taken to return him to the U.S.

Osahon, 49, came to the United States as a lawful permanent resident in May 2002, according to court filings reviewed by Newsweek. He was later convicted in a federal scheme involving stolen mail, bank fraud and aggravated identity theft, per the filings. Although an immigration judge found him removable, the court granted him protection under the Convention Against Torture in 2012 after determining he had previously been tortured in Nigeria and would likely face torture again if returned there.

Read More on News

The man is now hiding in Togo, has contracted malaria and is separated from his wife and three children in California, his attorneys say.

In a withering critique, judge Williams Court said that federal officials appeared to have acted "in flagrant violation of their own regulations and the Fifth Amendment's Due Process protections" by deporting Osahon without the procedural safeguards required by law.

Newsweek has contacted the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). the man's attorneys and Nigerian authorities for comment.

Tortured In Nigeria

According to the 2012 immigration court decision, which Judge Williams Court summarized in her ruling, Nigerian government officials tortured Osahon on two occasions. He was detained without trial, tied to a tree, forced to stare at the sun, beaten and hung from a ceiling while officials attempted to extract a confession.

Osahon remained in the United States under an order of supervision for the next 14 years. Court filings say he consistently reported to Immigration and Customs Enforcement appointments, never missed a check-in, and was never cited for violating the terms of his supervision. During that time, he married a U.S. citizen, and the couple had three children, all U.S. citizens.

The lawsuit alleges that after receiving an email directing him to report to ICE's Los Angeles field office on May 21, Osahon appeared believing it was a routine appointment. Instead, he was taken into custody and transported through a series of detention facilities before being flown to Ghana.

According to the complaint, Ghanaian authorities later informed him that his final destination was Nigeria. Osahon objected, saying he was protected from removal under the Convention Against Torture and could not be returned there. He ultimately ended up in neighboring Togo, where he remains in hiding, according to court filings.

The court said Osahon alleges he has contracted malaria, lacks legal immigration status in Togo, cannot legally work, and has limited access to medical care.

Government lawyers argued the case should be dismissed because Osahon had already been removed from the United States before filing his habeas petition. Judge Williams Court agreed that the habeas claims could not proceed because he was no longer in custody when the petition was filed, but converted the matter into a civil lawsuit and allowed his constitutional and statutory claims to move forward.

In her ruling, Williams Court found Osahon is likely to succeed on claims that ICE failed to follow regulations governing the revocation of his order of supervision and the termination of his Convention Against Torture protections. The judge noted that the government submitted no evidence showing it followed those procedures before removing him.

"The present case is, unfortunately, strikingly similar to Abrego Garcia v. Noem," Williams Court wrote, referring to the high-profile wrongful deportation case of the Salvadorian man who was sent to the notorious CECOT prison.

Judge Williams Court also said that Osahon is likely to prevail on his due process claims, finding there is no evidence that he received notice explaining why his supervision was being revoked or that he was allowed to challenge his removal.

What Happens Next?

The ruling bars the government from taking further steps to facilitate Osahon's transfer to Nigeria and requires officials to preserve records related to his detention, transfer, and removal.

The court ordered the government to file a declaration by September 3 addressing Osahon's whereabouts and detailing what actions, if any, are being taken to facilitate his return to the United States. A hearing is scheduled for September 4.

text:
Senate investigation revealed ICE has attempted to deport 282 veterans and their relatives; could be violating law that prevents the use of military against civilians

Washington, D.C. — Congresswomen Maggie Goodlander (D-N.H.), Chrissy Houlahan (D-Pa.), Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.), and Lizzie Fletcher (D-Texas), along with U.S. Senators Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) led dozens of their colleagues in a bicameral letter pressing the Trump administration on its efforts to coordinate the arrest, detention and deportation of hundreds of veterans and military families.

The letter follows an April 2025 move from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to rescind its long-standing policy that treated military service a “significant mitigating factor” when deciding whether to pursue immigration enforcement, replacing it with a new policy stating that military service alone “does not automatically exempt” non-citizens from enforcement actions.

You can read the full letter and list of signers here.

“These efforts imperil military readiness, weaken service members’ morale, and betray America’s promises to the people who put their lives on the line for our nation,” write the lawmakers.

Alarmingly, DoD has been reportedly targeting individuals at military installations, detaining them on military property, and turning them over to ICE — effectively converting military bases into “traps” for noncitizens. For example, a 22-year-old military wife was recently detained while attempting to obtain a military spouse I.D. Military officials allegedly called DHS and held her in a room until ICE agents arrived to take her to a detention center.

The lawmakers continue, “DoD’s participation in civil immigration enforcement activities raises both ethical and legal concerns, including potential violations of the Posse Comitatus Act, which prohibits using the armed forces of the military for civilian law enforcement.”

A 2025 investigation revealed that ICE has attempted to deport 282 veterans and their relatives. DHS refused to disclose the number of active-duty troops and their families who have been threatened by the administration’s policy. But new reports indicate that DoD and DHS appear to be coordinating to convert military bases into “traps” for individuals this administration deems deportable and has detained non-citizens during routine check-ins, visits, and drop-offs at or near military installations. At the same time, DoD has continued to recruit new service members with the promise of immigration protections.

Recent reporting by the Associated Press reveals that, since January 2025, more than 50 parents and spouses of active-duty service members have been detained, and at least six have been deported. ICE’s statistics show that the agency has arrested 16 non-citizen armed forces members since the beginning of Fiscal Year 2026. Some service members have reportedly needed to take leave or delay deployment because ICE detained their families.

The coalition warned that if service members were to be swept up in any of these enforcement actions, it could separately constitute a violation of the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, which provides protections to all members of the United States military on active duty, including non-citizens, from civil actions—such as immigration proceedings—that interfere with their military duties.

“Service members must have confidence that their sacrifices will be honored, not used against them or to target their loved ones,” wrote the lawmakers. “DoD’s new anti-immigrant practices risk deterring future recruits and damaging the credibility of military recruitment efforts—which promised to care for service members even after their time in uniform.”

The lawmakers requested that the agencies explain the enhanced coordination between DoD and DHS, restore long-standing immigration protections for family members of service members, and explain what steps they are taking to protect troops, veterans, and their families from unjust immigration enforcement by August 23, 2026.

The letter was endorsed by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), Immigration Defenders Law Center, the Seattle Clemency Project, Common Defense, Repatriate Our Patriots, and League of United Latin American Citizens.

“It is hard to imagine a more profound betrayal than targeting service members, veterans, and military families for deportation,” said Jennie Pasquarella, interim executive director of the Seattle Clemency Project. “This administration is abandoning decades of bipartisan policies that recognized a simple truth: protecting those who serve makes our military stronger and our nation safer. Targeting the very communities that have sacrificed for this country is not just morally indefensible, it is a direct attack on military readiness, recruitment, and trust.”

“This administration has made a conscious decision to abandon its promises to military families and fail those who put their lives on the line for our nation,” said Amanda Schuft, director of legal services at Immigrant Defenders Law Center. “We have seen the devastating human cost firsthand. Our client, the father of an active-duty Army service member, was detained by ICE despite suffering from terminal renal failure, forcing his son to take leave from military service to plead for his release and provide evidence of his grave medical condition. The government ignored those pleas. After his health deteriorated in detention, our client was eventually released, only to die within weeks.”

“Family readiness directly impacts mission readiness. Behind every military spouse or parent in detention is a servicemember who could deploy at any moment. Without a strong homefront, we cannot have a ready force. Our government must honor its commitments to those who serve,” said Danitza G. James, MSW, President, Repatriate Our Patriots.

text:
Two migrants have pleaded guilty to possessing counterfeit green cards after federal agents raided a home in Kansas City, Kansas, authorities said, marking the latest immigration fraud case pursued by the Trump administration.

The Justice Department said Santos Ramirez-Ramirez, 38, of Guatemala, and Yolanda Mendoza-Emiliano, 32, of Mexico, admitted to fraud and misuse of immigration documents after investigators found forged permanent resident cards and falsified Social Security cards during a search of a residence on South 16th Street.

Under the Trump administration's aggressive mass deportation policy, the government has also focused on cracking down on immigration fraud, pursuing cases involving counterfeit immigration documents, sham marriages, and other alleged schemes used to obtain legal status in the United States.

Read More on News

Fake Green Cards Found

Prosecutors said the counterfeit green cards displayed the defendants' names and photographs but were linked to alien registration numbers assigned to other people. An alien registration number, or A-number, is a unique identifier used by U.S. immigration authorities to maintain an individual's immigration file. Authorities said the Social Security cards also contained invalid numbers.

Federal agents executed the search warrant on May 28. Prosecutors said agents entered the home after occupants did not comply with instructions to leave the residence.

Prosecutors said a third defendant charged with possessing false immigration documents has not yet resolved the case. Several others arrested at the home were later indicted on separate immigration offenses, including unlawful reentry after deportation, according to the DOJ.

The Justice Department said Mendoza-Emiliano was apprehended four times in Arizona over 10 days in April 2024 for illegally entering the United States and was allowed to voluntarily return to Mexico after each encounter. Sentencing dates for Ramirez-Ramirez and Mendoza-Emiliano have not yet been announced.

The investigation was led by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the principal investigative division of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which handles cases involving immigration and document fraud, transnational criminal organizations, and other federal crimes.

“Counterfeit immigration documents are not harmless pieces of paper. They are tools used to undermine the integrity of our immigration system, conceal identities, and enable individuals to remain in the United States unlawfully,” HSI Kansas City Special Agent in Charge Rick Sabatini said in a press release on August 28. “HSI will aggressively investigate document fraud and work relentlessly with our federal partners to hold offenders accountable.”

Sham Marriage Crackdown

"Falsified federal documents often include information that belongs to an actual person,” U.S. Attorney Ryan A. Kriegshauser said in a press release. “Victims can have their lives turned upside down with the IRS, creditors, and other entities seeking money they don’t actually owe but are asked to pay because criminals are securing jobs, renting homes, and opening lines of credit using their information.”

Earlier this month, the Justice Department charged 11 people in what officials described as a decade-long scheme that allegedly helped hundreds of Chinese nationals obtain green cards through sham marriages to U.S. citizens. Prosecutors said the operation arranged more than 1,000 fraudulent marriages and generated millions of dollars in fees. Attorney General Todd Blanche said the alleged marriage-fraud network was among the largest ever prosecuted by federal authorities.

Authorities allege the defendants used word-of-mouth, social media and advertising to arrange fraudulent marriages for immigrants seeking permanent residency. Foreign nationals reportedly paid up to $100,000, while recruiters and facilitators received commissions for finding U.S. citizens willing to participate.

Prosecutors say some Americans were paid tens of thousands of dollars to enter marriages that existed only on paper. To make the relationships appear genuine, the network allegedly staged weddings, photo shoots and other events, submitting the images with immigration applications as evidence of bona fide marriages.

“Springfield is under siege right now,” said Carl Ruby, pastor of Springfield’s Central Christian Church.
Fellow Springfield pastor Gilbert Joubert Adrien was detained by ICE agents on Aug. 20and advocates are calling for his release.
Many Haitians detained in Springfield by ICE are being sent to Butler County Jail in Hamilton, which had 1,103 total inmates as of Friday afternoon.

text:
BY MEGAN HENRY

Ohio Capital Journal

More than 40 Haitians in Springfield have been detained by United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement after President Donald Trump revoked their legal status earlier this summer.

Faith leaders recently spoke out against the ICE activity that has been taking place in the Clark County city after a June decision by the U.S. Supreme Court allowed President Donald Trump to end temporary protected status for the 330,000 Haitians who’ve fled the violence in their home country. Legal protected status for Haitians officially ended on July 27.

Haitian Support Center Executive Director Viles Dorsainvil is a TPS holder with an asylum case pending.

“I am calling out this administration to tell them that we deserve to be treated with dignity,” he said. “We deserve to be treated as human beings. We are not animals.”

Dorsainvil is one of about 15,000 Haitians who live in Springfield, with a mixture of temporary protected status, citizenship, and other legal status.

“They are not a threat to the community,” Dorsainvil said.

First Baptist Church Pastor Adam Banks said Haitian people are not “political bargaining chips.”

“They are not threats to be monitored and removed,” he said. “They are care providers, co-workers, faith leaders, and family. … We demand an end to deportations that tear families and our community apart.”

ICE agents are detaining people in Springfield in shopping plazas, gas stations, and apartment complexes.

“Springfield is under siege right now,” said Carl Ruby, pastor of Springfield’s Central Christian Church.

Fellow Springfield pastor Gilbert Joubert Adrien was detained by ICE agents on Aug. 20and advocates are calling for his release.

“We hope that will happen very, very soon,” Ruby said. “He needs to be out immediately. He is a good man with a congregation to serve, and they are without a pastor right now.”

A pastor from the First Haitian Evangelical Church of Springfield was detained last week when he was in Northwest Ohio and he might be out of the country already, according to Ruby.

Many Haitians detained in Springfield by ICE are being sent to Butler County Jail in Hamilton, which had 1,103 total inmates as of Friday afternoon.

The general housing capacity for Butler County Jail is 844, even though the Ohio Department of Rehabilitation and Correction recommends 756 as the housing capacity, according to a 2025ODRC inspection report.

Haitians living in Springfield are being required to report to ICE offices in Blue Ash or Westerville and wear ankle monitors.

“Being outfitted with that monitor, it just symbolizes slavery,” Dorsainvil said.

He shared the story of a mother who came to the Haitian Support Center, having given birth a few weeks prior, but lost the baby.

“She could not even walk, but they put the shackle on her,” Dorsainvil said. “You cannot understand how hard it is to hear those people on a daily basis crying.”

Advocates are calling for an end to the ankle monitors.

“It is inhumane,” Ruby said. “It is an insult. It is designed to humiliate, and we want it to stop right now.”

The pastor recently helped a Haitian family relocate to Canada.

“Their children had survived kidnapping attempts when they were in Haiti,” he said. “Most families can’t go to Canada. It was only an option for this family because they had an immediate family member who was there.”

The U.S. Department of State currently has a Level 4 “Do Not Travel” advisory for Haiti“due to the risk of crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest, and limited healthcare,” according to the agency.

A top security official and chief of staff to the nation’s defense minister was kidnapped in June.

The federal government promised Haitians who self-deport a free airplane ticket and a $2,600 check to return to Haiti.

“They are not getting the money that our government has promised,” Ruby said.

He talked to a reporter in Haiti who shared that Haitians who are being deported are getting off the plane and running for their lives.

“It puts a target on them that says to the gangs, ‘come get this person.’ ”

text:
The Department of Homeland Security sent colleges and universities a memo last week limiting international students’ abilities to complete internships, The Wall Street Journal reported. International students have long been allowed to participate in internships through a program called curricular practical training, but now they can only do so if the employer has a partnership with their college and if all students in their program are required to complete an internship to graduate, the memo said.

DHS warned that institutions that do not comply with the new policy could lose authorization to enroll international students.

“Schools and employers should consider themselves on notice: under President Trump, abuse of this generous system will no longer be tolerated,” a spokesman for DHS told the Journal.

International education leaders said the policy change could make the United States a less attractive destination for international students. That’s on top of other Trump administration policy changes, including new regulations limiting how long international students can stay in the country, which experts say are encouraging international students to seek higher education elsewhere. In 2025, the number of new visas issued to international students dropped by 23 percent.

“The absence of the opportunity to engage in learning experiences through internships could cause students to reassess their plans to study in the United States,” said Ivor Emmanuel, director of the Berkeley International Office at the University of California, Berkeley. “International students are aware of the value that employers place in students gaining hands-on experience that is directly linked to the academic major.”

text:
The state of Florida has been dogged in its determination to become the death penalty capital of the nation. It allows non-unanimous juries to impose death sentences. It allows prosecutors to seek such sentences for people convicted of sexual battery against children under age 12. And in 2025, it passed a law making the death penalty mandatory for any illegal alien convicted of first-degree murder.

Last month, a prosecutor in Lake County became the first to use that law as the basis of a capital prosecution. State Attorney Bill Gladson is seeking the death penalty for Shahidul Islam, a Bangladeshi national. He is an illegal alien, who was deported but returned to the U.S. While here, he allegedly shot and killed his sister-in-law.

If Gladson succeeds in getting a death sentence, he will have pulled off a MAGA double-header, combining the movement’s embrace of capital punishment and its hostility toward people who enter the country illegally.

Recall that in October 2024, President Trump made that connection when he said, “I’m hereby calling for the death penalty for any migrant who kills an American citizen or a law enforcement officer.”

And on the first day of his second term, he issued an executive order directing the attorney general to “seek the death penalty regardless of other factors for every federal capital crime … committed by an alien illegally present in this country.” His order also encouraged states to adopt similar policies.

That is why you can be sure that Trump administration officials will be following Islam’s prosecution closely.

It is no coincidence that the law under which he is being charged is called the TRUMP Act, and that it cites several of the president’s anti-immigration initiatives in the law itself. In the words of the law, “the Legislature finds it necessary to rigorously implement both the letter and spirit of Trump’s plan to secure our border, protect our state and national sovereignty, support Florida law enforcement, and affirm the federal government’s responsibility over immigration.”

In addition, if Gladson succeeds in securing a mandatory death sentence for Shahidul Islam, it will tee up a challenge for the Supreme Court. Fifty years ago, the court held that the death penalty could never be made mandatory or imposed automatically.

The law’s supporters knew what they were doing. As one of them put it, “We have cho­sen to pass things that we knew were uncon­sti­tu­tion­al at the time we passed them, because we believed the Supreme Court would change their minds.” That is not how the Supreme Court has ever understood what the Constitution requires in capital cases. If the Islam case ever reaches the court, it should not change its stance.

In 1976, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down a statute that made the death penalty mandatory for specified crimes. Writing for the majority, Justice Potter Stewart explained: “In capital cases the fundamental respect for humanity underlying the Eighth Amendment requires consideration of the character and record of the individual offender and the circumstances of the particular offense as a constitutionally indispensable part of the process of inflicting the penalty of death.”

He added that manda­to­ry death sentences treat defendants as “a faceless, undifferentiated mass.”

That is exactly what Gladson is trying to do with Islam. He made that clear during a press conference announcing the prosecution, calling the crime “completely preventable” and laying the blame on the Biden administration’s open border policy.

Gladson praised the state’s illegal alien law and its mandatory death penalty provision. He said that it gives notice to people who are in this country illegally that if they commit a capital crime, they will not be deported. Instead, he said, “they will face the trial of their life.”

The state attorney and his colleagues made clear that they care little about why Islam may have committed the crime with which he is charged, or about the circumstances that may have contributed to it. For them, he is a stand-in for, and symbol of, a nation allegedly overrun by illegal immigrants.

It seems not to matter to them that, in fact, illegal immigrants are less likely to commit violent crimes and homicides than people born in the U.S. And it is ironic that in a state so devoted to enforcing the law, Islam is being prosecuted under a law that is itself of questionable legality.
