description:
Today, I do four things for a living: publish this newsletter, write a Bloomberg Law column, host a podcast, and do some paid speaking.
Lawyer of the Week: Beth Wilkinson.
And if I drew up a short list of the litigators I’d want to work for, it would include Beth Wilkinson of Wilkinson Stekloff, trial lawyer extraordinaire.
She has won about 60 cases and lost four jury verdicts, two of which were set aside and one settled.
Wilkinson Stekloff was trial counsel for Meta, alongside Covington & Burling and Davis Polk—but Wilkinson wasn’t her firm’s main courtroom lawyer.
text:
Twenty years ago today, on August 30, 2006, I launched Above the Law. This anniversary led me to reflect on how the world of legal media has changed dramatically over the past two decades—ATL included.

If you look back at my inaugural post on Above the Law, you’ll see my initial vision for the outlet was focused heavily on gossip and humor. And while there are still traces of that DNA at ATL—hello, Biglaw Biter—it’s fair to say the Above the Law of 2026 is a more serious and substantive publication than the self-described “legal tabloid” of 2006. For instance, I doubt the original ATL would have been the subject of a 1,600-word feature by Elizabeth Williamson of The New York Times (gift link).

As for me, I left ATL in 2019, tried out legal recruiting, and almost died of COVID. That near-death experience made me realize I wanted to return to full-time writing—which I did in May 2021, by activating paid subscriptions here at Original Jurisdiction.

When I launched OJ, I felt the same anxiety I did when I started ATL: Will this flop? Fortunately, like ATL, OJ thrived—and I owe it all to you, my subscribers and sponsors.

Today, I do four things for a living: publish this newsletter, write a Bloomberg Law column, host a podcast, and do some paid speaking. I’m professionally happier than I’ve ever been, and for the first time, I’m not looking for “the next big thing.” My current plan is to keep doing exactly what I’m doing—until I retire, die, or get replaced by AI. To my readers, listeners, and sponsors, I have just two words: thank you.

A programming note: the next OJ podcast episode will air on September 9, instead of September 2 (because of having to schedule the recording around the crazy schedule of my next guest, one of the busiest lawyers in America). But I’ll still have plenty of content for you, possibly including a Supreme Court clerk hiring post; if you’re aware of any hires not included in my last report, please drop me a line.

Now, on to the news—ridiculously busy for the last full week of August.

Lawyer of the Week: Beth Wilkinson.

In a podcast interview I recorded last week with Jacob Robinson for Law of Code (teaser here), he asked me if I’d ever return to practicing law. Although I keep my New York law license active—mostly to keep my mother honest when she tells people, “My son is a lawyer”—I no longer practice, and I have no desire to return to practice.

There are, however, two things I’d be willing to return for, on a temporary basis: to argue before the U.S. Supreme Court, or—more realistically—to try a case to a jury, all the way to verdict (even a boring case, and even as the most junior person on the trial team). And if I drew up a short list of the litigators I’d want to work for, it would include Beth Wilkinson of Wilkinson Stekloff, trial lawyer extraordinaire.

Oh, you want to work with Beth Wilkinson? Take a number. Right now she’s handling three of the biggest litigations in the country, as noted in Jessica Toonkel’s recent profile of Wilkinson in The Wall Street Journal (gift link):

Wilkinson has successfully defended the National Football League and pharmaceutical giant Pfizer, as well as Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh against accusations of sexual assault in his confirmation hearings, making her a go-to trial lawyer in high-stakes cases. She has won about 60 cases and lost four jury verdicts, two of which were set aside and one settled. She has never had a client pay a judgment.

She is now in the middle of the three most high-stakes media battles in years…. In addition to working for Paramount [in its litigation against state attorneys general trying to block its $81 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery], Wilkinson is also representing TV station operator Nexstar Media Group in defending its $6.2 billion acquisition of competitor Tegna, a deal state attorneys general have also sued to block, and Walt Disney Co. ABC in its fight with the Federal Communications Commission over the network’s broadcast licenses.

If ABC v. FCC rings a bell, it should: filed by Wilkinson and leading Supreme Court litigator Paul Clement, it was last week’s Litigation of the Week.

Given the many famous cases she has handled over her long career, some of which we discussed in our podcast interview—including, of course, her successful prosecution of the Oklahoma City bombers—Wilkinson has many individual wins to celebrate. But as she told me in our conversation (and later wrote in a Bloomberg Law piece), what excites her most at this point in her career is mentoring and developing younger colleagues, then sitting back and watching them thrive.

In that sense, one of the biggest signs of Wilkinson’s success is a fourth case in the headlines, People of the State of California v. Meta Platforms Inc. This litigation settled in the middle of trial, for $17 billion—which many analysts see as an excellent outcome for the defense (for reasons discussed below, under Litigation of the Week).

Wilkinson Stekloff was trial counsel for Meta, alongside Covington & Burling and Davis Polk—but Wilkinson wasn’t her firm’s main courtroom lawyer. Instead, if you look at Meta’s written filings and news stories about key cross-examinations, you’ll see mention of colleagues like Brian Stekloff and Moira Penza. And that is, in my view, a testament to the team that Beth Wilkinson has helped build at Wilkinson Stekloff: a firm so formidable that clients like Meta will trust it with matters of existential importance—whether or not Beth Wilkinson herself is personally involved.

Other lawyers in the news:

Speaking of legendary litigators who have appeared on my podcast, David Boies, still going strong at 85, had a good week:

On Thursday, Judge Jed Rakoff (S.D.N.Y.) approved Bank of America’s $72.5 million settlement with Jeffrey Epstein victims who alleged that B of A aided in Epstein’s sex trafficking. Judge Rakoff also signed off on a 30% fee request for the lawyers—including Boies, Sigrid McCawley, and Andrew Villacastin, of Boies Schiller Flexner, and Brad Edwards, of Edwards Henderson.

On Friday, Judge Richard Seeborg (N.D. Cal.) awarded almost $147 million in attorneys’ fees to Boies and his co-counsel in a privacy class action against Google that covered 98 million people and resulted in a $425 million jury verdict. Judge Seeborg said the one-third fee was high but justified, given counsel’s “exemplary performance.” The lawyers included David Boies, Alexander Boies, and Mark Mao of BSF; Bill Carmody, Amanda Bonn, and Shawn Rabin of Susman Godfrey; and Ryan McGee of Morgan & Morgan.

Will Scharf, who will assume the role of White House counsel on September 1, was profiled by Luke Broadwater for The New York Times (gift link via Howard Bashman’s How Appealing). The article struck me as neutral to positive, maybe 6/10; ChatGPT agreed (6.5/10), while Claude dissented (4/10).

Who’s replacing Will Scharf in the influential role of White House staff secretary? A fellow lawyer: current deputy staff secretary Benjamin “Ben” Moss, who graduated from the University of Chicago Law School and previously served as general counsel to then-senator JD Vance (R-Ohio).

Speaking of job changes, Kerry Abrams will step down as dean of Duke Law after more than eight years in the role. Query whether she can resolve the DOJ investigation into alleged racial discrimination in Duke’s admissions before she departs at the end of the 2026-27 academic year.

Abrams is leaving the deanship voluntarily, while staying on at Duke as a member of the faculty. In contrast, Nathaniel Cullerton—the Wachtell Lipton partner caught making out with an associate in Central Park, in a viral video—“is being forced out by the elite law firm,” per The New York Post.

In the August 23 edition of Judicial Notice, I discussed Department of Homeland Security General Counsel James Percival, his thread on X criticizing four judges who ruled against DHS, and an ethics complaint filed against Percival by 128 retired judges, including Nancy Gertner and J. Michael Luttig. In a reader poll that drew almost 600 votes, 65% of you expressed support for the complaint. For additional views, see (or hear) Sarah Isgur of Advisory Opinions, who criticized the complaint as “barfare” (weaponization of the attorney ethics process), or Professor Steve Vladeck of One First, who argued that the real issue isn’t the ethics complaint, but the “abominable” nature of Percival’s conduct.

In memoriam: assistant U.S. attorney Andrew Haden (S.D. Cal.) passed away on August 19, at 48. Initial reports didn’t specify the cause of death, but last week, the San Diego County Medical Examiner’s Office confirmed that he died by suicide. If you or someone you know is experiencing a mental-health crisis, please call the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline (988) or contact a lawyer assistance program in your state. As someone who is all too familiar with the devastating toll of suicide, I encourage you to donate to the American Foundation for Suicide Prevention or a similar charity focused on suicide prevention.

Judges of the Week: Judges Rita Lin and Noël Wise.

Last week, I wrote that the Northern District of California is one of the five most important district courts in the country right now, thanks to its popularity as a venue for (1) big-ticket cases involving Big Tech and (2) challenges to Trump administration policies. I picked Chief Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers (N.D. Cal.) as the most recent Judge of the Week based on her handling of a major tech case, People of the State of California v. Meta Platforms Inc. (discussed below). And now I’m bestowing Judge of the Week honors on two of her colleagues, Judges Rita Lin and Noël Wise, based on their benchslaps of the Trump administration: In the span of roughly 24 hours, these two relatively new Biden appointees ruled against the federal government in a pair of high-profile cases, both based on the First Amendment.

On Thursday, in Anthropic PBC v. U.S. Department of War, Judge Lin blocked the Pentagon’s blacklisting of Anthropic. After the AI giant refused to allow its Claude AI models ​to be used by the U.S. military for surveillance or autonomous weapons and publicly criticized the government’s views on AI safety, the government took action against Anthropic—including designating the company “a supply chain risk.” Represented by WilmerHale, Anthropic sued, alleging it was retaliated against for its speech in violation of the First Amendment. In a 59-page opinion, Judge Lin agreed, declaring that the Trump administration’s actions were “illegal and baseless.” In one of the opinion’s most widely quoted lines, she wrote, “The empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics.”

On Friday, in Stanford Daily Publishing Corporation v. Rubio, Judge Wise ruled that the Trump administration violated the First Amendment by arresting, detaining, and deporting noncitizen students for expressing pro-Palestine views. In a 90-page ruling that Reuters described as “blistering,” she wrote that “in the United States, freedom of speech belongs to the people” and “is not the government’s to take.” As Conor Fitzpatrick of the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, counsel to the plaintiffs, told The Times (gift link), “Today’s ruling proves that free speech isn’t a privilege, but the inalienable right of every man, woman, and child.”

In other news about judges and the judiciary:

Josh Morrow, a partner at Lehotsky Cohn, conducted an interesting analysis (posted by Professor Eugene Volokh on the Volokh Conspiracy). Morrow ran 2,250 published opinions from federal appellate courts from 2026 through Pangram, an AI-detection tool, and found that more than 50 showed signs of AI authorship. He then took roughly 300 opinions published in January 2022 by federal circuit courts and fed them into Pangram—and found no signs of AI-generated text. Some folks I discussed this study with were troubled by its findings, but I wasn’t. First, 50 opinions out of 2,250 is a shade over 2%, a tiny percentage. Second, signs of AI authorship simply suggest that AI generated the prose; they don’t denote the presence of hallucinations or other errors.

Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito overlapped at Yale Law School for two years. Why weren’t they friends? As Thomas recounted to Senator Ted Cruz (R-Tex.) on his podcast, Alito said to Thomas, “Clarence, you were scary.” What did he mean by that? During their YLS years, Alito was the introverted, nerdy conservative that he still is today—while Thomas was “a left-wing radical,” in Cruz’s words, who wore bib overalls and combat boots around 127 Wall Street.

If you’re trying to get rid of your Indiana state criminal case by forging a dismissal order signed by a judge, pick a jurist other than Chief Justice John Roberts. A Colorado man named Joshua Culver learned this the hard way—and now he faces federal charges of impersonation and forgery as well.

In memoriam:

Judith Kreeger, who served as a judge in Miami-Dade’s 11th Judicial Circuit Family Division for more than 25 years, passed away at 85.

Barbara McDermott—who served for almost 14 years as a judge in Philadelphia’s Court of Common Pleas, spending a majority of that time handling homicide cases—passed away at 71.

May they rest in peace.

Job of the Week: an opportunity for an of counsel in trademark litigation.

text:
The third eyewitness to the fatal shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston by an immigration officer last month has been released from federal detention.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials released Victor Salgado Araujo, who is Lorenzo’s brother, from custody Sunday morning, after his attorney filed several legal petitions including a federal suit claiming he is wrongfully being detained. The government also indicated it would likely approve his application for a temporary legal status since he is a witness to a potential crime.

He had been held in the Montgomery ICE Processing Center, which is north of Houston, since the July 7 shooting.

That morning, Victor Salgado Araujo sat in the front seat of his brother’s van as they picked up two fellow workers for a construction job, when ICE officers started following them in unmarked vehicles.

ICE initially said Lorenzo Salgado Araujo rammed their vehicles as he tried to flee and an officer shot him in self-defense. But Victor Salgado Araujo and the two other passengers disputed that account.

Victor Salgado Araujo’s release comes just days after Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare publicly said he plans to bring the case to a grand jury in the “next few weeks,” partly to force the release of more evidence. And because there is no body camera or dash camera footage of the shooting, his testimony as one of just three eyewitnesses is even more crucial to the understanding of what happened.

The other two eyewitnesses, Daniel Tirado Pantoja and Jose Trinidad Rojas Pliego, have already been released from ICE custody.

“Victor’s release is an important moment, but it is not the end of this fight,” his attorney, Ruby Powers, said in a statement. “The pursuit of truth, accountability, and justice for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo continues, and we remain steadfast in protecting Victor’s immigration rights and standing alongside him and his family.”

Ronaldo Salgado, Lorenzo’s son, similarly called his uncle’s release “a key step” in getting justice for his father.

“His first meal was chilaquiles from his favorite restaurant, just as his usual Sunday routine called for,” he added in a Facebook post. “He is now with family, finally able to process the tragic loss he witnessed and the nearly two months spent in detention.

text:
A rally calling for Gov. Mike Braun to end a state contract to hold U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainees at a northern Indiana prison was held in Columbus on Saturday.

The rally was one of 62 actions — prayer vigils, teach-ins and rallies — held across the state as part of a “Weekend of Public Witness,” organized by the Indiana Organizing Project. Outside Columbus City Hall, people of faith gathered to pray and call on the governor to end the detention contract with ICE when it expires next summer, according to organizers. The state of Indiana currently holds approximately 800 ICE detainees at Miami Correctional Facility, a maximum-security prison in Bunker Hill.

Miami Correctional Facility has been holding ICE detainees since state officials signed a two-year contract last year that allows up to 1,000 immigrants to be held there. The state receives a daily payment of $291 per detainee — almost four times the $75 daily per-person cost for inmates at the prison, according to the Indiana Capital Chronicle.

At the rally, leaders noted what they described as the “cruelties and brokenness” of the immigration system in the U.S.

“Immigrants are frequently arrested on minor charges and then imprisoned for months without appearing before a judge. Children are left to fend for themselves when parents disappear,” local organizers said in a news release.

Organizers also cited what they described as “harsh and inhumane conditions” at Miami Correctional Facility. This comment points toward allegations raised in a series of lawsuits filed by the American Civil Liberties Union of Indiana on behalf of former inmates at the prison, the earliest of which was filed in 2021 before the state’s ICE detention contract was signed. The lawsuits alleged conditions at the prison included “spoiled food, lack of adequate clothing and basic hygiene, lack of access to legal advice and even solitary confinement.” Settlements totaling more than $1.2 million on behalf of 31 people were finalized earlier this year.

Braun has said Hoosier law enforcement agencies should “cooperate fully” with ICE to remove undocumented immigrants in Indiana. After it was announced that prison would house detainees last summer, Braun’s deputy chief of staff, Molly Craft, said Braun was ready “to deploy any and all resources” to assist in the Trump administration’s deportation efforts. After the Indiana State Police, Department of Homeland Security and Department of Correction signed up for federal immigration enforcement powers last year, Braun said the state is “not a safe haven for illegal immigration. Indiana will fully partner with federal immigration authorities as they enforce the most fundamental laws of our country.”

Following reports of medical backlogs and severe staffing shortages at the facility, as well as the deaths of two ICE detainees, Braun ordered an internal IDOC audit of the facility in late July. The ACLU also filed two lawsuits that month on behalf of an ICE detainee who alleges he suffered a severe seizure after not receiving prescribed medication and was later pepper-sprayed by correctional officers while recovering from his injuries.

Acting ICE Director David Venturella, in response to an inquiry from U.S. Rep. André Carson, D-Indianapolis, following reports of the audit, said that any death that occurs in ICE custody is a “significant cause for concern” and that the agency prioritizes the “health, safety and well-being of all aliens in its custody.” Venturella also said Miami Correctional Facility had not yet received a compliance inspection from ICE’s detention oversight office, and the initial inspection is scheduled for mid-September, the Indiana Capital Chronicle reported.

Community leaders with the Indiana Organizing Project say the audit ordered by Braun is not enough and that the state must terminate the contract entirely.

“Because Miami Correctional is the only state-run facility housing ICE detainees in Indiana, every Hoosier carries a shared responsibility for the treatment of those inside,” state organizers said in a news release. “This weekend, communities in 55-plus towns and cities across Indiana are rising in unified public witness to demand dignity, accountability and an immediate end to ICE detention at Miami Correctional Facility.”

Local organizers echoed this in their own news release.

“This is not only tragic; it is corrupt,” said Rev. Felipe Martinez, of First Presbyterian Church of Columbus, who spoke at the local rally. “No more lives should be placed at risk. Listen to the voices of these people who have been suffering through ICE Detention. Consider those who have lost their lives and the families who are suffering.”

Martinez also spoke about the state’s contract with ICE.

“Indiana is collecting your taxpayer dollars and clearly not using it for the humane treatment of detainees,” Martinez said.

In addition to Martinez, leaders of the event included Bro. Aelred Dean, St. Paul’s Episcopal Church; Ben Myers, the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints; Ashley Caceras, executive director of Su Casa Columbus; Rev. Mary W. Cartwright, the United Methodist Church; and Rhonda Baker of the Peace Church Coalition of Indianapolis. The event was sponsored by the Columbus Community United (CCU) Immigration team, the Indiana Organizing Project and Bartholomew County INDIVISIBLE.

“We call on Governor Braun to end the two-year contract with ICE, which now holds almost 800 individuals at Miami. The contract is up soon and now is the time to act. We must end ICE Detention at Miami Correctional Facility,” said organizer Mary W. Cartwright.

Victor Hugo Salgado Araujo, the deceased's brother, was in the passenger seat during the shooting and was detained the same day, July 7, alongside two other witnesses, Daniel Tirado Pantoja and Jose Trinidad Rojas Pliego. "It’s just been so wonderful – a lot of different emotions when I first heard it might be happening," his attorney, Ruby Powers, said. "So I first didn’t believe it, and then when I received an email from ICE that I knew it was real, so then it was about making sure he got out physically as soon as possible."

Sign up for the Hello, Houston! daily newsletter to get local reports like this delivered directly to your inbox.

Ronaldo Salgado, Lorenzo’s son, shared on social media the family reunited with Victor just before noon.

“Today is a key step in justice for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo,” Ronaldo wrote.

Powers told Houston Public Media the exact reason behind Victor's release was unclear.

"I don’t know what was the final thing that made it happen, but I don’t have a judge’s order or any definitive answer on what it was," Powers said. "I don’t have a definitive answer as to what was the final straw."

RELATED: Harris County DA's Office evaluating which charges to present to grand jury in ICE shooting case

The first two witnesses were released under orders in which federal judges said the men could not be re-detained unless the government demonstrated they are a flight risk or a danger to the community.

ICE did not immediately respond to requests for comment regarding Victor's release.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District had already filed a notice to appeal Pleigo's release and was expected to appeal Pantoja and Victor's release as well.

Powers said Victor is grateful to be home with this family.

"He’s out of detention after 50-something-odd days, and he’s able to start healing and sleeping and eating and trying to mourn and try to find some type of normalcy," Powers said.

On Thursday, Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said his office had collected most of the evidence in the Lorenzo Salgao Araujo case and was determining what, if any, charges would be presented to a grand jury.

In an appearance on Hello Houston on August 27, Teare said his office was at a “tipping point” with the evidence they’ve collected.

“We’re at a point where we’ve gotten just about everything we are going to get," Teare said. "There are back pieces of evidence that we still need from the federal government that we’ve requested and are effectively waiting on, but we’re now much more moving into the evaluation phase.”

text:
In Indiana, more than 60 events this weekend protested U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention in Miami Correctional Facility.

Across the highway from the prison Saturday, Aug. 29, about a dozen people engaged with drivers on their way to a nearby air show. Some drivers honked and pulled over to take pictures.

Indiana announced its two-year contract to house up to 1,000 male ICE detainees at Miami Correctional Facility Aug. 2025. In response, a group of multi-faith leaders launched monthly vigils at the prison that same month.

People traveled from all over the state Saturday to take part in a rally at Miami Correctional. Audri Svay drove from North Manchester. She said it was important to her to attend the rally outside the prison.

“I think it’s easy with everything that’s going on to get caught up in all the other things and to forget that there are injustices that are still happening, even though you may not see them, even though they may not be happening to you,” Svay said. “They are happening, and they’re happening in your community.”

Indiana Organizing Project, the American Civil Liberties Union of Indiana and Indivisible Central Indiana coordinated the rallies. Michael Polera helped arrange the one at Miami Correctional. He said even if some of the events have small attendance numbers, it’s important to have gatherings across the state.

“The travesties are going on all over the state. It’s our neighbors, it’s our coworkers, it’s families being affected, children being affected – and families matter,” Polera said. “So when we bring it to our hometowns and our small towns, then people kind of understand it’s all of us. We’re all in this together.”

State agreement with ICE to use prison to hold detainees

The first group of detainees arrived at the maximum security prison in October.

The ACLU of Indiana, politicians, churches and immigrant rights organizations have since questioned health conditions and called for the state to terminate the agreement.

Accusations focus on two detainee deaths and multiple inmate reports of mistreatment.

In February, guards found Lorth Sim, 59, from Cambodia without a pulse and not breathing. Intake forms show he had a history of diabetes.

In March, Tuan Van Bui, 55, from Vietnam died following a medical emergency in his housing unit. Guards also found him unresponsive. Van Bui reported a history of asthma and hypertension during intake.

Last month, the ACLU of Indiana filed a pair of lawsuits accusing healthcare providers and officers at Miami Correctional of “cruel and unconstitutional” mistreatment.

The complaints, filed in federal district court for detainee Andranik Grigoryan, allege a lack of medical care resulting in injury and the use of unreasonable force against the plaintiff.

The ACLU named the Indiana Department of Correction and private healthcare contractor Centurion Health of Indiana in the lawsuits.

IDOC declined to comment and referred questions to ICE. Centurion Health of Indiana did not respond to a request for comment by publication.

ICE did not answer WFYI's questions about conditions at Miami Correctional.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security did respond to a request for comment.

“Any claim that there are subprime conditions at ICE facilities are FALSE. In fact, ICE has higher detention standards than most U.S. prisons that hold actual U.S. citizens,” DHS told WFYI in an email.

DHS said detainees are provided with “proper meals, quality water, blankets, medical treatment, and have opportunities to communicate with their family members and lawyers.”

As of the date of publication, mistreatment has not been legally verified.

Following reports from IndyStar, Governor Mike Braun called for an investigation into operations at the facility.

Representative André Carson conducted a congressional oversight tour in April and joined faith leaders and immigrant rights advocates in their call to end the detention agreement.

“Weekend of Public Witness”

Indiana residents held protest events Friday, Aug. 28 through Sunday, Aug. 31. They included vigils, teach-ins and additional efforts to support immigrants in Indiana.

At the Indianapolis Public Library Michigan Road branch, dozens gathered outside Friday evening. That event featured a donation drive, specifically for participants to bring food and household items for Haitian immigrants.

Thousands of Haitians in Indiana lost their legal status to work and live in the U.S. in July, when the Trump Administration terminated Haiti's temporary protection status designation.

Amy Guzman is with Westside Indy Indivisible Resistance Movement and helped organize the rally. She said there are Haitian neighbors who can’t afford food or pay bills and are afraid to leave their homes. Donations will be delivered directly to them.

Guzman said it’s a starting point.

“We got a few things. I know the library probably has more, but it’s, to me it’s about awareness,” Guzman said. “And once you start the ball rolling … then hopefully more people will get involved.”

Sunday afternoon people strolled along the Monon Trail in Caramel. Just off the path, a self-guided walkthrough of educational signs explained U.S. immigration policy and outlined concerns about detention conditions.

At the end of the display several local organizations, including Indivisible Carmel, From Strangers to Neighbors and Food not Bombs, had information about ways to support local immigrant communities.

Courtney Osters with Indiana Organizing Project helped organize the event and said she felt it was well received.

“I hope we don’t need to have another event on this topic,” Osters said.

She also said she will continue to organize similar events if needed.

text:
MEMPHIS, Tenn. — MEMPHIS, Tenn. — An immigrant advocacy organization says more than 100 people were detained during an overnight federal law enforcement operation at a bar in Memphis’ Berclair neighborhood.

Vecindarios 901 said the operation happened around 1 a.m. Sunday at El Corralón.

According to the organization, Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents were involved in the operation along with other federal law enforcement.

The group initially said Memphis Police assisted with the operation by controlling traffic. However, MPD says its officers were not involved in the planning or execution of the federal operation and were called to the area later for traffic and crowd control.

According to MPD, officers were requested to Macon Street near Maria Avenue around 3:15 a.m., more than two hours after Vecindarios 901 says the operation began.

Police said officers were told Homeland Security Investigations and ICE had been conducting an operation in the area when a crowd began to gather.

“MPD was not notified of or involved in the planning or execution of this operation,” the department said in a statement.

Upon arrival, MPD officers established a perimeter on the south side of Macon Street and directed people to stay out of the roadway to maintain traffic flow and public safety.

MPD said its officers did not make any arrests or detentions. No injuries or property damage were reported, according to police.

The department has since cleared the scene and referred additional questions about the operation to the federal agencies involved.

Vecindarios 901 claims more than 100 people who were inside the establishment were detained and transported from the scene.

WREG has not independently confirmed the number of people detained or their immigration statuses.

The organization said agents arrived at the business with a search warrant connected to an investigation involving gambling machines and alleged drug activity.

Vecindarios 901 also alleges law enforcement officers attempted to interfere with people recording the operation and intimidated community members who gathered near the scene.

WREG has not independently verified those allegations.

The organization described the operation as the largest immigration raid in Memphis history and criticized the detention of people it says were not involved in criminal activity.

“Vecindarios 901 does not support businesses promoting criminal activities,” the organization said in a statement. “We also do NOT support the unconstitutional, unlawful search and detention of over 100 friends and family members without due process.”

The organization is encouraging people whose family members were detained to contact its community hotline for assistance.

The Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition condemned the operation. Executive Director Sherman Luna released the following statement.

“When more than 100 people are violently rounded up in the middle of the night it sends devastating shockwaves through the entire community. Fathers not returning home to their families, roommates left wondering where their friend is, businesses left shuttered and short-staffed as entrepreneurs and workers don’t show up Monday morning. When we say this administration is trying to reshape our nation in their narrow white nationalist vision, this is what it looks like: disappearing our families, neighbors, friends, and co-workers in the night with no regard for the devastation they leave behind.”

WREG is working to get additional information from federal authorities about the operation, including how many people were detained, whether anyone is facing criminal charges and the circumstances that led to the operation.

This is a developing story. WREG will provide updates as more information becomes available.

text:
Over a ten-day period, the Trump administration carried out the transfer of more than one hundred people in irregular immigration status to eight African nations, effectively expanding its third-country deportation program, according to internal federal government documents obtained and released by CBS News.

The logistics organized by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) included three deportation flights that transported men and women to Burundi, Cameroon, the Central African Republic, Equatorial Guinea, Eswatini, Liberia, Rwanda, and Sierra Leone.

None of the deportees held citizenship in the receiving countries. The list of those transferred included citizens from Afghanistan, Cuba, Nicaragua, Iran, Nepal, Turkey, and Venezuela, as well as detainees of African origin who were not nationals of the destination countries.

The legal framework for the deportations and the government's response

This operation is driven by third-country agreements, a mechanism through which more than 30 nations worldwide have agreed to receive foreigners expelled from U.S. territory.

While some countries in the region only accept people from their own continent, others, such as Eswatini, Liberia, and the Central African Republic, have received nationals from Latin America, Europe, and Asia.

In response to inquiries from CBS News about implementing these measures, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) defended the legality of the procedure and the responsibility of the individuals involved for their final destination.

"If an undocumented foreign national decides to file a lawsuit in court refusing to return to their country of origin, we are required by law to find a safe and secure country to which they can go. If an undocumented foreign national decides to go home, we will provide a free return flight and a check for $3,000," the DHS stated in an official press release sent to the media outlet. "The choice is theirs."

Among those deported are individuals with criminal records for serious offenses committed on U.S. soil, while others have accumulated removal orders for unauthorized entry or for failing to meet the legal requirements to remain in the country.

The scope of rulings in immigration courts

The case of a 24-year-old Afghan citizen identified as Khalil illustrates how this policy works. Khalil entered the country illegally via the southern border in 2024 after traveling through several Latin American countries.

In August 2025, an immigration judge granted him the protection known as "withholding of removal" after considering potential risks in his home country, although he was not granted asylum due to prior regulations that disqualify those who did not apply for protection in the transit countries.

WICHITA, Kan. (KSNW) — The case of former Coldwater Mayor Joe Ceballos has been stalled in immigration court.

In April, Ceballos pleaded guilty to three counts of disorderly election conduct, admitting to voting without citizenship. He previously said that he believed his green card allowed him to do so.

A month later, he was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement but was released after posting a $3,000 bond.

Ceballos was originally scheduled to appear in immigration court this month to determine whether he could keep his green card. But the case was postponed indefinitely due to a significant backlog in the court system, according to his attorney, Sarah Balderas.

One reason for the delays is the lack of attorneys available to take on the influx of cases.

"Another issue is people are proceeding with either representing themselves or they're saying, 'Nope, send me home. I don't want to be in detention anymore, and I can't find an attorney,'" Balderas said

'Welcome home, Joe!': Kansas town cheers former mayor's return from ICE custody

Despite the ups and downs, the Coldwater community has continued to support Ceballos.

Balderas said that she believes the media attention on the case has played a crucial role in the proceedings. She referred to a Department of Homeland Security article that highlighted the community's support

"They were talking about how much support that Joe was getting from the community, and that was exactly what we wanted because that's what we needed to show the judge was that the community wants him and he wasn't a danger to the community," she said.

Balderas said it remains unclear when Ceballos' case could be heard by a judge, with immigration courts booked through 2027.

text:
The Supreme Court's latest ruling on mail-in voting changes was a nakedly "partisan" move to please President Donald Trump, and one top legal expert explained how "the worst part" of the decision makes that clear.

Andrew Weissmann is a veteran attorney and legal counsel, having served over a decade as an Assistant U.S. Attorney, as well as in various legal roles at the FBI and former Presidents George W. Bush and Barack Obama. He now makes numerous media appearances where he offers legal insights into the various misdeeds of the Trump administration, including in his role as a legal analyst for MS NOW.

Over the weekend, he appeared as a guest on the latest edition of the "Fast Politics" podcast with host Molly Jong-Fast, with the conversation largely revolving around the Supreme Court's recent 6-3 ruling to allow Trump's executive order demanding changes to mail-in voting to proceed. The decision, coming down along familiar partisan lines, found that one of the lawsuits brought against the order was too early, as the changes had not yet been put forward.

After the new changes were put forward, however, the federal government tried to argue that a lawsuit brought against the order should be dismissed, as it was now too late and close to the midterms, which Weissmann described as a particularly galling but predictable switch-up after the Supreme Court's argument.

During the conversation, Weissmann also highlighted the part of the court's ruling that he found to be "the worst part," and one that gave away just how committed the conservative justices are to Trump's agenda.

"So let me just tell you the worst part of the Supreme Court decision: Even though I told you what its holding was, one of the things it did is it described the executive order as [saying] that the language of the executive order was to combat fraud," Weissmann said, which Jong-Fast agreed was a "ridiculous" description.

"I mean... that that was such a partisan description," Weissmann continued. "And then it also had language saying, well, this is just the president dealing with what his own executive branch can do."

Weissmann previously explained that Trump's efforts to impose new restrictions on mail-in voting were blatantly unlawful, flying directly in the face of the Constitution's intention for the states to run their own elections. If left up to the president in any capacity, Weissmann added, they could just decide that the race had been won by themselves or their party. Trump's anti-mail-in voting crusade could also conceivably see him deny Democrats the right to vote in the manner and reserve it exclusively for Republicans.

description:

text:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) on Sunday denied a report in The New York Times about harsh treatment of migrants in immigration detention facilities.

“Another day and another hoax about ICE detention from the @nytimes,” DHS wrote on social media. “The media is clearly desperate for these false allegations to be true.”

The Times reported Sunday on 10 deportees who said they experienced or witnessed what they described as abusive or violent treatment by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers.

The Trump administration later deported the migrants to third countries such as Liberia, despite them not having any ties to the African country. The administration has reportedly struck deportation deals with at least 35 countries.

Leonardo Sánchez, a Cuban migrant, told the Times that ICE officers forced him and three other deportees onto the tarmac in the Liberian capital of Monrovia, after they refused to disembark.

The federal agents then twisted the migrants’ handcuffs, pinned them to the ground and pressed their knees directly onto the their necks, Sánchez recalled.

“They didn’t treat us like people, like human beings,” Carlos Téllez-Sanchez, a Venezuelan whom the administration deported to Liberia, told the paper. “They can say or do anything to you and there’s nothing you can do.”

Other deportees said ICE officials denied medical care to migrants — including pregnant women — and housed detainees in detention centers where up to 50 people shared one toilet.

But DHS denied those claims, saying, “NO ONE is being tortured, denied medical care, or beaten in ICE detention facilities.”

The department also argued the report in the Times — which it called “GARBAGE” — is one of many “fueling” an increase in “assaults” against ICE officers.

title: U.S. human rights practices are taking a nosedive - Japan Today
description:
In the lead-up to the 2026 midterm elections, how is the U.S. government performing in terms of human rights?
Even accounting for the U.S.’s prior poor practices, however, new data from the Human Rights Measurement Initiative shows that in 2025 the country’s civil and political rights performance deteriorated even further.
As a human rights scholar who has been measuring human rights practices for 20 years – and as one of HRMI’s co-founders – I believe this data raises serious questions about the United States’ commitment to human rights.
Further, the Trump administration has changed one of the most important sources of human rights information, the U.S. State Department’s Country Reports on Human Rights Practices, to contain more bias in favor of the administration’s foreign allies and less information on human rights abuse overall.
Even starting from this poor position, the U.S.’s civil and political rights practices dramatically worsened in 2025.
text:
In the lead-up to the 2026 midterm elections, how is the U.S. government performing in terms of human rights? Listening to politicians, it can be difficult to know.

On one hand, some have pointed to a number of potential human rights abuses committed by the U.S. government inside and outside its borders in the past two years.

On the other hand, while marking the United States’ 250th anniversary this year, President Donald Trump called the country “the home of freedom,” “the land of liberty” and “the most extraordinary, most exceptional, most incredible nation ever to exist on the face of the earth.”

“We’re doing better now than we’ve ever done before,” he said.

So which is it?

According to many of the human rights data sources available, the U.S. lags behind most other high-income democracies – countries that are both members of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development and classified as high income by the World Bank. The U.S.’s poor performance spans civil and political rights, such as the right to be free from torture and the right to political participation, as well as economic and social rights, including the rights to health and food.

In fact, the U.S. has been a relatively poor performer across many of these rights for quite some time, regardless of the political party in power.

Even accounting for the U.S.’s prior poor practices, however, new data from the Human Rights Measurement Initiative shows that in 2025 the country’s civil and political rights performance deteriorated even further.

As a human rights scholar who has been measuring human rights practices for 20 years – and as one of HRMI’s co-founders – I believe this data raises serious questions about the United States’ commitment to human rights.

How are rights practices measured?

Governments rarely publish accurate information on their own human rights abuses, so the task of measuring them typically falls to advocates and scholars.

Historically, most international measures of civil and political rights have depended on public reports from the U.S. State Department, Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch or news organizations.

However, these reports cannot cover every human rights violation that experts know about, especially in countries with low government transparency or high levels of repression.

Thus, data produced using those sources will show fewer abuses than those that have actually occurred and will be more accurate about some places than others. Further, the Trump administration has changed one of the most important sources of human rights information, the U.S. State Department’s Country Reports on Human Rights Practices, to contain more bias in favor of the administration’s foreign allies and less information on human rights abuse overall.

Since 2017, HRMI has used a different approach. Recognizing the problems with public reports, we collect information directly from researchers for human rights organizations, human rights lawyers and others, asking them about governments’ practices across several rights and using a statistical model to assess their information and ensure that the resulting metrics are comparable across countries. The result is a robust dataset that includes information previously missing from public reports.

Today, HRMI’s civil and political rights dataset covers 62 countries, with more added every year.

How does the U.S. compare?

According to the Human Rights Scores dataset, which uses publicly available information to score more than 190 countries on physical integrity rights – such as the rights to be free from torture, killing, forced disappearance and political imprisonment – the U.S. never ranked higher than 81st from 2001 to 2021 or higher than 109th from 2010 to 2021.

Indeed, from 2003 to 2021, the United States’ score was either the worst or the second-worst every year among high-incomeOECD member states, which include the United Kingdom, Japan and New Zealand.

The Human Rights Scores dataset has not been updated past 2021, but HRMI’s data collected since that time suggests that the pattern has continued.

Among the six high-income OECD countries on which HRMI currently collects data, the U.S. has been the worst performer for physical integrity rights since 2017.

It has also frequently been rated as the worst performer on “empowerment rights,” or the rights to assembly, association, opinion, expression, political participation, religion and belief.

What changed in 2025?

Even starting from this poor position, the U.S.’s civil and political rights practices dramatically worsened in 2025. HRMI measures nine civil and political rights, and the U.S. significantly worsened on eight of them.

These were not small changes. Measured against every significant change HRMI has recorded since 2017, the U.S. showed the largest decline ever observed for the right to be free from forced disappearance and for the right to freedom of religion and belief.

The U.S. showed the second-largest decline ever observed for the right to be free from arbitrary or political arrest and for the right to opinion and expression.

The U.S. also showed major declines in the rights to be free from torture and extrajudicial killing, and the right to political participation – that is, the right to participate in one’s government via free and fair elections, to take part in public affairs and to have access to public service. U.S. scores likewise fell in the right to assembly and association, which are, respectively, the rights to peacefully gather in public or private and to form or join groups and organizations.

What caused the scores to fall?

Human rights experts raised several issues that led to these declines. For instance, the U.S.’s worsened scores for the rights to be free from arbitrary detention, disappearance and torture were tied to the expanded use of practices such as incommunicado detention and warrantless arrest by ICE and other immigration-related agencies.

While several killings occurred during ICE operations in 2025, the worsened extrajudicial killing score was also tied to the country’s use of airstrikes against boats in the Pacific and Caribbean, which caused the deaths of at least 123 people in 2025 alone.

Other changes enacted in 2025 contributed to large declines in the U.S.’s rights scores, including crackdowns on anti-ICE demonstrations and government pressure on universities, including limits on free speech and class subjects.

Last year also saw threats to television networks over political expression, restrictions on mail-in voting, state measures targeting American Islamic organizations by labeling them “foreign terrorist organizations” and an executive order focused on eradicating “anti-Christian bias.”

While current HRMI data does not yet cover 2026, early indicators are not promising, with continued abuses by ICE, further killings in international waters and allegations of attempts to use government powers to punish critics.

text:
SPRINGFIELD, Ohio — Members of Springfield’s faith community and groups from across the country marched Sunday outside City Hall to protest recent actions by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in the region, including the detention of two local pastors.

According to the faith organization G92, pastors Gilbert Joubert Adrien and Julio Dumano were detained by ICE in recent weeks. Rally organizers called for the pastors to be released and for ICE to end the use of ankle monitors in its enforcement.

Jewel Hall, a local resident who participated in the march, said they joined because many Haitian residents are living in fear.

“The fear is real,” Hall said. “I was scared for myself because it could be me.”

Pastor Carl Ruby, founder of G92, spoke during the rally and marched at the front of the group. Ruby said fear of ICE has affected attendance at his Haitian congregation, which he said had about 50 regular attendees a few months ago and now has three.

“We need Haitians to move us forward,” Ruby said. “It’s the first time we’ve grown as a city in 50 years when they arrived, and it just breaks my heart to see this happening.”

Not everyone at City Hall shared the group’s view. Phil Swanton, a local resident who watched the rally from the sidelines, said he supports peaceful protest and does not hold ill will toward Haitians, but says that it is time for them to leave.

“The Haitians are good people, but TPS is ending,” Swanton said. “And, you know, I just hope that there’s no violence and no bad things happen to them. But I do feel like it’s time for them to leave.”

ICE has previously said that it does not discuss ongoing operations.

According to jail records, as of Sunday afternoon, Pastor Adrien Joubert was still being held in the Butler County Jail on an ICE hold after being booked on the 20th. Dumano was no longer listed in the current jail database.

text:
The immigration offensive of Donald Trump's administration is in constant flux. The latest records from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) reveal a deeper transformation in how the system operates: the agency is expanding the pool of individuals targeted by its operations and relies less and less on taking custody of immigrants transferred from jails and prisons.

The majority of people arrested in July were charged with civil immigration violations, carrying no pending criminal charges or prior convictions, according to a New York Times analysis of new federal data. Meanwhile, the proportion of arrestees with a prior violent crime conviction dropped below 4%.

The records were turned over by ICE to the Deportation Data Project—an academic initiative co-directed by researchers from UC Berkeley and UCLA—following a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) lawsuit.

The new dataset includes information through August 6, 2026, offering an unusually detailed look into the mechanics of current immigration policy: it tracks ICE encounters, detainer requests, arrests, entries into the detention system, and deportations. In July, ICE carried out 49,571 arrests, up from 43,021 in June and 29,241 in February. Yet behind this overall growth lies a revealing trend: arrests of individuals without a criminal record are rising the fastest.

Most people arrested by ICE no longer have criminal records

The new records categorize arrestees according to ICE's own classifications: individuals with criminal convictions, those with pending charges, or those with neither. In July, more than half of those arrested had no criminal charges or convictions, according to the data analysis. These individuals were apprehended primarily under civil immigration laws—a significant shift from the profile that dominated ICE interior operations for years: immigrants handed over to the agency after passing through local or state jails and prisons.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) maintains that the government is fulfilling its pledge to arrest and deport criminals, but it has also made clear that anyone unlawfully present in the United States is subject to enforcement actions. The numbers reflect that broadened scope of individuals targeted by ICE.

Among those impacted by the surge in arrests are people married to U.S. citizens, asylum seekers who entered legally, and individuals whose temporary legal status the administration sought to revoke. At the same time, the proportion of arrestees with a prior conviction for violent crimes dropped below 4% in July.

Half of all arrests are now "at-large" community operations

Screenshot of the Deportation Data Project website

Data from the Deportation Data Project also highlights how these arrests are conducted. Graeme Blair, professor of political science at UCLA and co-director of the project, explained during a webinar on the new dataset that ICE distinguishes between different apprehension methods. One category is "custodial arrests," which occur when an individual already held in criminal custody at a jail or prison is subsequently transferred to civil ICE custody.

Another category is "at-large arrests," conducted directly by immigration authorities out in communities without an immediate transfer from a correctional facility.

In July, the last full month included in the release, 50% of all ICE arrests nationwide were classified as "at-large," Blair explained. The researcher noted that this represents a "major increase" compared to the final year of Joe Biden's presidency. The contrast is even sharper in certain regions: in California, 77% of July arrests fell into the at-large category, while only 22% were transfers from criminal custody.

This comparison helps explain why the profile of arrestees is changing. A system focused primarily on jail and prison transfers naturally encounters a high percentage of individuals with prior contact with the criminal justice system. When ICE ramps up direct community arrests, its ability to locate individuals who were not previously incarcerated expands. This shift coincides with an increase in the agency's staffing, funding, and technological resources.

ICE's workforce reached 29,000 employees in June, up from approximately 21,000 when Trump returned to the White House, according to Office of Personnel Management data cited by The New York Times. This growth occurred as the administration funneled billions of additional dollars into immigration enforcement and expanded the infrastructure needed to hold arrestees in custody. The combination enables the agency to run simultaneous direct operations, process jail transfers, and partner with state and local law enforcement.

However, the expansion has not been linear. Arrests surpassed 40,000 in December 2025 before slowing down following protests and controversies surrounding operations conducted in Minnesota earlier this year. They dipped to 29,241 in February and remained relatively stable over the following months. The upward trend accelerated again in June, recording 43,021 arrests, and reached 49,571 in July—an increase of approximately 15% in just one month and 70% compared to February.

Texas and Florida become central pillars of the operation

ICE is making more than 380 arrests daily in Texas. Photo: REUTERS/Paul Ratje

While the surge is visible across nearly the entire United States, Texas and Florida play an exceptionally prominent role. ICE is making more than 380 daily arrests in Texas and over 230 in Florida, according to the analysis, with daily totals in both states up by more than 100 per day compared to the spring. Both states home large unauthorized immigrant populations and have state governments that actively support the Trump administration's enforcement strategy.

Much of this operational capacity stems from the expansion of 287(g) agreements, which empower select state and local law enforcement agencies to perform immigration enforcement functions under ICE supervision. Participation in the program expanded rapidly during Trump's second term, and roughly 14% of current arrests are tied to this mechanism. Florida has accumulated at least 15,000 arrests through 287(g) since Trump took office, while Texas is approaching 10,000.

The program's importance is even higher in states where ICE maintains a smaller direct footprint. In Wyoming and West Virginia, more than half of all arrests are currently tied to 287(g). Yet the expansion is not limited to Republican-governed states or those fully cooperating with federal authorities. New Jersey and New Mexico saw arrests double despite passing legislation this year aimed at limiting certain forms of government cooperation with ICE, while smaller-population states like Montana and Vermont also saw arrest numbers more than double.

Over 66,000 people currently in ICE custody

The surge in enforcement is equally evident across the detention network. Blair explained during the Deportation Data Project webinar that the average daily population in ICE custody during July reached 66,094 nationwide. This figure does not represent daily new admissions, but rather the average number of individuals held in agency custody on any given day during that month—a distinction key to accurately interpreting the scope of the data.

While the administration has not yet reached its stated goal of securing 100,000 detention beds, signs point to ongoing capacity growth. Several facilities are scheduled to open during the fall, and plans to convert large commercial warehouses into detention centers have been re-evaluated. Simultaneously, deportations have maintained a pace exceeding 1,000 people per day since last summer, with removal flights picking up momentum again in the spring. At least 329 flights out of the U.S. were recorded in July, according to ICE Flight Monitor, an initiative by Human Rights First.

The Deportation Data Project also allows researchers to track an individual's journey from arrest through various facilities. Researchers link records using anonymized identifiers that trace movement without revealing personal details like names. A single detainee may appear at multiple facilities during a single stay in custody—for instance, passing through a short-term holding facility first, then a long-term detention center, and finally a departure facility prior to deportation.

The Deportation Data Project makes it possible to track a person's journey from arrest through their time in various facilities. Photo: REUTERS/Shannon Stapleton

Why researchers urge caution regarding overall deportation numbers

Not all records released by ICE share the same level of reliability. Project directors at the Deportation Data Project raise specific caveats regarding deportation totals. David Hausman, co-director of the project and law professor at UC Berkeley, explained during the webinar that establishing the exact number of deportations attributable to ICE remains a persistent challenge because different data releases from the agency itself have produced conflicting numbers for overlapping timeframes.

"One of our ongoing frustrations with the data is that we cannot be completely certain of the total number of ICE removals," Hausman explained. Recent releases include deportations that lack any link to a prior stay in an ICE detention facility. Researchers consider it plausible that some of these cases represent individuals expelled shortly after arriving at the border or those who self-reported for deportation, but they have been unable to confirm whether all such movements belong to ICE or if some were previously tallied as Customs and Border Protection (CBP) operations.

For that reason, the project considers it more methodologically sound to analyze deportations that can be explicitly linked to a prior stay in ICE custody. While this approach does not yield an exhaustive count of all removals, it provides a far more reliable picture of the full pipeline starting with an arrest, continuing through detention, and culminating in removal from the country.

New dataset reveals specific cities where ICE makes arrests

The latest data release introduces a field previously unavailable at this level of granularity: the specific city where each arrest occurred. Prior to this update, researchers could only study the geography of operations at the state level or through ICE's regional Field Office Areas of Responsibility, which in states like California and Texas cover areas far too vast to pinpoint operational hot spots.

This new field opens the door to localized analysis, though it carries certain limitations. According to Blair, city names appear to have been entered manually by ICE agents, leading to variations in capitalization and spelling for the same location. Furthermore, analyzing a metropolitan area requires aggregating data across multiple independent municipalities within the same urban region. In Los Angeles, for example, a researcher would need to compile separate entries for Santa Monica, Pasadena, and other municipalities across the county.

The project initially noted that roughly 4% of entries since 2025 lacked city information. During the webinar, Amber Qureshi, co-director of the Deportation Data Project, noted that for 2026 records, the missing data rate dropped below 1%, making recent entries significantly more complete. The team is currently working on a processed version that normalizes city names and aligns them with U.S. Census Bureau geographic units.

The existence of this database also highlights the ongoing hurdles in obtaining timely information about a rapidly evolving policy landscape. The Deportation Data Project received the files from ICE on August 21 and published them on August 24 following initial verification. "This is not data we generated; it comes directly from the agency itself, in this case ICE, and straight out of ICE's own databases," Qureshi clarified during the presentation.

Some of the hotspots are around ICE facilities: Oakdale, which holds an immigration court, is listed as the apprehension city in hundreds of ICE arrests.
text:
New Orleans became one of the Trump administration’s targets for immigration enforcement in December. Operation “Catahoula Crunch” led to a surge in ICE arrests before being scaled back in January, when agents were deployed to Minneapolis, having fallen far short of the agency’s reported arrest goals for the greater New Orleans area.

But following a slowdown this spring, ICE arrests have been climbing – though perhaps more quietly. In July, they reached all-time highs.

What’s driving these numbers, and who’s being impacted? To find out, The Lens analyzed public records obtained by The Deportation Data Project, an effort from academics and lawyers at UCLA and UC Berkeley.

First, a quick caveat: this data is drawn largely from DHS and ICE records obtained through FOIA requests, and ICE’s recordkeeping is imperfect. Some records are incomplete, or incorrectly filled out. And ICE agents sometimes misspell the names of Louisiana towns. The data, therefore, is limited, and some of these arrest figures are likely an undercount.

The arrests are sorted into three categories: custodial, at-large, and 287(g).

Custodial arrests: ICE agents take over cutody from a jail or prison.

At-large arrests: ICE agents arrest someone at their home, workplace, traffic stop a check-in, or elsewhere in public.

287(g): Local law enforcement officers arrest someone and process them for ICE, thanks to a signed agreement between the agencies.

Here’s five takeaways.

1. ICE arrests in Louisiana are at an all-time high and rising.

ICE arrest figures have been trending upwards since the start of the current Trump administration. Louisiana saw a spike in December, around the time of the “Catahoula Crunch” surge, though the operation led to only a fraction of the agency’s reported goal of 5,000 apprehensions.

Louisiana ICE arrests slowed in January, as the agency’s attention turned to Minneapolis, where public pushback escalated after ICE agents shot and killed two residents in separate incidents.

But arrests have been steadily rising again since the spring. In June, the U.S. Congress approved $70 billion in ICE funding. By July, the arrest figures in New Orleans —

and across the nation — reached an all-time high.

2. Kenner has seen the highest total number of arrests.

Louisiana has a few hotspots for ICE arrests. The map above includes all arrests, including when ICE takes someone into custody from local law enforcement or prison.

Some of the hotspots are around ICE facilities: Oakdale, which holds an immigration court, is listed as the apprehension city in hundreds of ICE arrests. So is St. Rose, where ICE moved their regional field office, previously in New Orleans, in November. Pollock, home to a federal correctional institute, is also a hotspot.

Other hotspots include the New Orleans, Baton Rouge, and Lafayette metro areas. Kenner, whose police department signed a 287(g) agreement with ICE last March, has the single highest figure for overall arrests.

Since January 2025, there have been at least 725 ICE arrests in Kenner, 570 in Gretna, 549 in New Orleans, 274 in Metairie, and 508 in St. Rose, where the ICE field office now sits.

3. New Orleans has seen the highest number of “at-large” arrests.

This map shows only “at-large” arrests, meaning ICE did not formally take custody of the detainee from law enforcement or prison.

In other words: when only looking at arrests by ICE agents at home, work, or in public, New Orleans’ figures are higher than Kenner’s. That suggests that Kenner’s arrests figures are being driven at least in part by their 287(g) agreement, which New Orleans doesn’t have, while New Orleans arrests are the result of more proactive targeting by ICE.

4. ICE is mostly arresting people with no criminal history.

The Trump administration, the Department of Homeland Security, and Gov. Jeff Landry have frequently justified the surge in immigration enforcement – and the ballooning budget behind it – with claims that the operations are targeting people with violent criminal histories.

ICE’s own records suggest the opposite is true.

ICE has arrested and detained only a handful of people with convictions for violent crime, while arresting thousands of people with no criminal history at all.

In July, ICE arrested just 10 people in Louisiana who had a conviction for a violent crime, and 629 with no criminal history at all. Nationally, July was the first month in Trump’s second term where a majority of people arrested by ICE — 51% — had no criminal charges.

That trend appears to be deepening, with non-criminal detainees driving much of the increase in arrests.

5. The surge in ICE arrests is due in part to local law enforcement.

Louisiana’s increase in ICE arrests appears driven in part by a recent increase in ICE apprehensions stemming from 287(g) agreements with local law enforcement. That’s new: a year ago, there were essentially zero ICE apprehensions resulting from such agreements.
