text:
A federal judge in California has ruled that the Trump administration cannot use federal immigration law to revoke visas or pursue deportation against international students because they expressed pro-Palestinian views, criticized Israel or engaged in other political speech protected by the First Amendment.

U.S. District Judge Noël Wise issued the 90-page decision Friday, August 28, finding that portions of two provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act violate the First and Fifth Amendments when the government uses them to target noncitizens for protected speech.

The ruling follows a campaign that began in March 2025 in which federal immigration officials revoked visas, arrested and detained noncitizen students involved in pro-Palestinian campus advocacy. Among the high-profile cases were Columbia University graduate Mahmoud Khalil, Tufts University student Rümeysa Öztürk and other students whose protests, writings or associations became part of federal immigration proceedings.

Wise concluded that lawfully present noncitizens do not lose First Amendment protection because they hold student visas or other immigration status.

“Stated plainly, in the United States, freedom of speech belongs to the people,” Wise wrote. “It is not the government’s to take.”

The case, Stanford Daily Publishing Corporation v. Rubio, was brought in August 2025 by the organization that publishes The Stanford Daily and two noncitizen students. One student was later dismissed from the case.

The plaintiffs argued that international students had begun censoring themselves because they feared that writing about Gaza, attending pro-Palestinian demonstrations or criticizing Israeli policy could lead to the loss of their visas and eventual deportation.

The Stanford Daily said some noncitizen journalists declined assignments involving protests or the Israel-Palestine conflict, asked that previously published articles be removed and avoided publishing commentary because of those concerns. Wise had previously ruled that those allegations were enough to establish a concrete First Amendment injury and allow the case to proceed.

Friday's ruling reached the merits.

The lawsuit focused on two parts of federal immigration law that provide the secretary of state with substantial authority over noncitizens.

One allows a noncitizen to be deemed deportable when the secretary of state has reasonable grounds to believe the person's presence or activities could have potentially serious adverse consequences for U.S. foreign policy. Federal law ordinarily protects lawful beliefs, statements, and associations from serving as the basis for such a decision, but contains an exception when the Secretary personally determines that the person's presence would compromise a compelling U.S. foreign policy interest.

The second provision, 8 U.S.C. § 1201(i), gives the Secretary of State or a consular officer discretion to revoke a visa after it has been issued. Visa revocation can then contribute to the government's effort to place a noncitizen into removal proceedings.

The Trump administration argued that the government needs broad authority in immigration and foreign affairs and that noncitizens do not necessarily possess constitutional protections identical to those of U.S. citizens.

Wise rejected that argument as it applied to lawfully present noncitizens and protected political expression.

The judge distinguished between people already living lawfully in the United States and foreign nationals seeking admission from outside the country. Supreme Court precedent has historically given the political branches especially broad authority over people seeking initial entry, but people who have entered the United States can invoke constitutional protections that do not depend on citizenship.

Wise cited Ninth Circuit precedent recognizing that student visa holders can bring First Amendment claims. She also found that the Fifth Amendment's protection against unconstitutionally vague laws applies to noncitizens in immigration proceedings.

The First Amendment problem, Wise concluded, arose because the government was using speech itself as the reason for immigration action.

When protected expression becomes the reason for a visa revocation or deportation decision, she wrote, the government is treating speech differently because of its content or viewpoint. Such restrictions are generally subject to strict scrutiny, one of the Constitution's most demanding tests.

Wise found that the government failed to show the challenged provisions, when applied to protected speech, were narrowly tailored to accomplish a compelling government interest.

The ruling does not prevent the federal government from enforcing immigration or national security laws against international students who engage in conduct that provides an independent legal basis for action.

Wise specifically pointed to existing provisions permitting the government to pursue removal of people engaged in terrorist activity, espionage, sabotage and certain conduct threatening national security. The Supreme Court has also distinguished constitutionally protected political advocacy from prohibited material support provided to foreign terrorist organizations.

That distinction limits the reach of Friday's decision. An international student is not immune from immigration enforcement simply because a case has some connection to political activity. The ruling instead prevents protected speech itself from becoming the basis for punishment under the provisions Wise reviewed.

The judge also found a separate constitutional problem under the Fifth Amendment: vagueness.

A law can violate due process when ordinary people cannot determine what conduct it prohibits or when it gives government officials so little guidance that arbitrary or discriminatory enforcement becomes possible.

Wise found both concerns in the challenged immigration provisions when they were used against speech.

The foreign-policy provision left noncitizens unable to determine which otherwise lawful beliefs, statements, or associations might prompt the Secretary of State to conclude that their presence threatened a compelling U.S. interest, the court said.

The visa-revocation provision presented a similar problem. The government acknowledged during the litigation that the law grants the secretary broad discretion to revoke visas. Wise found that, when that discretion is applied to protected expression, the lack of defined standards opens the door to enforcement based on which views government officials favor or oppose.

The factual record was central to the ruling.

Wise relied in part on findings from a separate Massachusetts case that examined the administration's enforcement campaign. According to those findings, federal officials reviewed thousands of names associated largely with campus protests and relied on sources including Canary Mission, a website that tracks people and organizations it describes as hostile to Israel or supportive of antisemitism.

Immigration authorities prepared reports on some individuals based on protest participation, associations with pro-Palestinian groups, social media posts and opinion articles. The record cited by Wise found that the cases involving several prominent students did not rely on violence or material support for terrorist organizations.

A federal judge in Boston had already ruled in September 2025 that the administration violated the First Amendment through a policy of targeting noncitizen students and faculty involved in pro-Palestinian advocacy. Wise's decision goes further in one respect by directly addressing the constitutionality of the statutory provisions themselves when applied to protected speech.

The California ruling does contain an important procedural limitation.

Wise issued a declaratory judgment stating that the challenged portions of both the deportation and visa-revocation provisions violate the First Amendment and are unconstitutionally vague under the Fifth Amendment when enforcement is based on protected speech.

She did not issue a permanent injunction against enforcement of the deportation provision. Under 8 U.S.C. § 1252(f)(1), lower federal courts generally lack authority to issue injunctions restraining operation of certain removal provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act; that power is reserved to the Supreme Court.

Wise also determined that a separate injunction concerning visa revocation was unnecessary at this stage in light of the declaratory judgment, although she said the plaintiffs otherwise had established the factors needed for such relief.

The decision therefore should not be read as a nationwide injunction against immigration enforcement or as a ruling that every past or future deportation involving a campus activist is unlawful. It establishes that the specific statutory powers challenged in the case cannot constitutionally be applied on the basis of First Amendment-protected speech.

The Justice Department had not announced an appeal as of Saturday, and neither the State Department nor the Department of Homeland Security immediately commented on the ruling, according to Reuters and The Associated Press.

An appeal would place the dispute before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit and could eventually present the Supreme Court with a broader question about the intersection between two powerful areas of federal authority: the government's historically broad control over immigration and the Constitution's prohibition against punishing people inside the United States because officials disapprove of their political views.

For international students and universities, the immediate significance is clearer. The ruling recognizes that lawful immigration status does not give the government a free hand to make political conformity a condition of remaining in the United States.

As Wise wrote near the close of her decision, constitutional protection for speech includes speech the government itself strongly opposes.

text:
The White House “border czar,” Tom Homan, denied on Sunday that deporting British far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos just a day after being arrested by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) amounted to preferential treatment.

Homan said it was his understanding that Yiannopoulos, 41, had overstayed what he believed to be a visitor visa, had not appeared at an immigration hearing and was issued a final order of removal on 22 July.

“He didn’t show up,” Homan told CNN’s State of the Union. “The judge ordered him deported. So, once ICE gets an order of deportation from a federal judge, their job is to execute that order, and that’s what they did.”

He added: “He had his due process, ordered removed by a federal judge, and ICE removed him. It’s that simple.”

Yiannopoulos’s removal one day after his arrest, when many others who have been deported had first endured lengthy detention center incarcerations, has prompted questions about whether he received preferential treatment in that respect. Homan said the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, was trying to speed up the deportation process.

“Once a judge orders them out, rather than being in detention, waiting for travel documents and flight arrangements, we – ICE, along with the [border patrol] and [DHS] – [are] working really good on the efficiencies of the removal process,” Homan remarked.

He continued: “As soon as we get an order removal, our goal is remove them as quick as possible, regardless of who they are. Get them out quick. Open those beds up for more detainees.”

DHS had quickly publicized Yiannopoulos’s arrest on Thursday at an airport in New Orleans – where he may have travelled to attend a concert by rapper Ye, formerly Kanye West, on Friday at the city’s Caesars Superdome.

Officials with DHS touted Yiannopoulos’s arrest on Friday. By Saturday morning, Yiannopoulos’s name was removed from a list of people in ICE detention, and DHS confirmed that he had been deported to the UK on Friday – one day after his arrest.

“He chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws,” a DHS release said, adding “The administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport”.

CNN host Dana Bash asked Homan if the rightwing influencer Laura Loomer had, as she claimed, tipped off ICE that Yiannopoulos’s permission to be in the US had expired.

“A lot of people tipped ICE off,” Homan replied. “There are a lot of people who’s calling ICE, and she says she’s one of them. She probably was.

“But bottom line is, it doesn’t matter. He was ordered removed by an immigration judge, and ICE’s job it to execute that order.”

Loomer and Yiannopoulos – who had sanguinely cheered the Trump administration’s deportation efforts before his expulsion from the US – had publicly fallen out.

Homan, meanwhile, denied that the Trump administration had made an example of Yiannopoulos to send a message. “We don’t deport people based on political affiliation,” he said.

text:
The official landscape of global mobility experienced a significant shift when the United States officially lifted a months-long immigrant visa hold affecting seventy-five countries. This particular administrative pause was initially introduced in January by the US Department of State as an enforcement measure directed at screening applicants who were deemed potentially more likely to depend on public benefits within the United States. Such individuals are traditionally evaluated under public-charge provisions outlined in federal guidelines.

However, the policy faced immediate scrutiny and legal challenges from advocacy organizations. A pivotal lawsuit was filed by the Catholic Legal Immigration Network against Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The litigation contested the legality of the blanket restrictions based purely on national origin. The directive was ultimately brought to an end on August 21 after U.S. District Judge Jeannette Vargas of the Southern District of New York delivered a decisive ruling against the policy. The court concluded that the implementation of restrictions solely based on nationality exceeded the statutory authority granted to the Secretary of State under the Immigration and Nationality Act. Consequently, the State Department updated its official digital portal to confirm that the hold was no longer legally enforceable.

Impact on Travellers

The abrupt cessation of the policy has cast widespread effects across prospective immigrants originating from the affected seventy-five countries, which span diverse geographic regions including nations such as Afghanistan, Albania, Algeria, Belarus, Brazil, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Nigeria, Pakistan, Russia, and Syria, among many others. While the hold was active, applicants from these designated territories were legally permitted to submit documentation and attend scheduled interviews, but the final authorization and physical issuance of permanent residency visas, colloquially known as Green Cards, were systematically frozen.

With the policy being struck down, final visa issuances have been authorized to resume, provided that applicants satisfy all standard immigration requirements. It is noted that dual nationals possessing a valid passport issued by a sovereign state outside the designated seventy-five countries list were previously granted exemptions. Furthermore, minor children undergoing adoption procedures by American families were protected through specific exemptions under a National Interest Exception tied to Presidential Proclamation 10998. Conversely, nonimmigrant categories, encompassing short-term tourists, international students, and temporary workers, were unaffected by this specific administrative pause.

Industry Insights

Immigration lawyers and international mobility analysts have closely monitored this legal battle, highlighting the delicate balance between executive administrative authority and judicial oversight in immigration policy. Legal experts argued that blanket nationality-based bans create severe backlogs and administrative unpredictability for individuals who have spent years navigating complex bureaucratic pipelines. The ruling by Judge Vargas is viewed by legal professionals as a reaffirmation of statutory limits, establishing that sweeping directives cannot bypass established legislative frameworks defined by the Immigration and Nationality Act.

Employment agencies, family reunification advocates, and global relocation networks have expressed relief regarding the judicial intervention. Analysts suggest that the resumption of visa issuance will gradually alleviate the emotional and financial strain experienced by thousands of affected families and sponsored workers. Nevertheless, immigration experts caution that consular processing centers may encounter temporary administrative congestion as they work through the backlog of cases that accumulated while the hold was enforced.

Practical Information

For prospective applicants seeking entry into the United States, navigating the current consular environment requires careful attention to distinct administrative categories. Individuals who belong to the list of seventy-five countries can now expect their immigrant visa applications to proceed toward final issuance, subject to routine background checks and standard administrative processing protocols. Applicants are advised to monitor official consular notifications and communicate directly through designated governmental communication channels to verify the status of their specific files.

It must be emphasized that this specific development is distinct from other ongoing immigration directives. For instance, while India was not included in the seventy-five countries list—meaning Indian nationals were exempt from this particular issuance pause—Indian applicants must navigate a completely separate global measure. Earlier reports confirmed that the United States paused immigrant visa interviews worldwide while consular personnel underwent specialized training regarding public-charge evaluations. Therefore, the lifting of the multi-country restriction does not automatically signify the resumption of regular immigrant visa interviews on a global scale, and applicants are instructed to await further official announcements from consular posts.

Comparison with Previous Policies or Developments

When compared with historical immigration measures implemented by previous administrations, the January policy represented a targeted approach focused heavily on public-charge assessments tied directly to national origin classifications. Traditional immigration enforcement has typically relied on individualized case-by-case determinations rather than broad, nationality-wide halts on final visa issuances.

While past policy shifts often focused on expanding security screening measures or adjusting financial thresholds for sponsors, the January directive was unique in completely suspending the final issuance phase for a specific group of nations while permitting preliminary administrative steps like interviews to continue. The swift legal challenge and subsequent invalidation by the federal court mark a notable departure from historical precedents, demonstrating that sweeping executive actions targeting specific lists of countries remain highly vulnerable to successful judicial review under existing federal statutes.

text:
British far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported to the United Kingdom after his arrest by American immigration authorities.

The Department of Homeland Security said Saturday that Yiannopoulos was returned to his home country Friday after being accused of overstaying after entering the U.S. legally in May 2019. An immigration judge issued a final order of removal July 22 after he failed to show up for an immigration hearing, a Homeland Security spokesperson said.

Yiannopoulos was arrested Thursday at Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport in Louisiana and detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

“He chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws,” a Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement.

Yiannopoulos and his representatives did not respond to requests for comment, and he has not posted on the social platform X since Thursday.

Yiannopoulos is a well-known champion of conservative causes and has frequently taken provocative public positions criticizing feminism, Islam and immigrants. He has been especially supportive of President Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement policy, aimed at people in the country illegally.

“Zero immigration for the next 20 years. No ifs, no buts,” Yiannopoulos said on X last year.

Yiannopoulos’ arrest and deportation come amid a nationwide uptick in detentions as part of Trump’s immigration crackdown.

In social media posts, the Department of Homeland Security touted Yiannopoulos’ arrest and posted a booking photo of him. It added that it encourages people in the country illegally to leave voluntarily, saying the U.S. offers “$3,000 and a free flight to self-deport.”

“We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream. If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return,” the department said.

text:
KABUL, AFGHANISTAN – The United States has deported dozens of migrants, including 12 Afghan nationals, to the Central African Republic.

According to The Associated Press, the migrants arrived on Saturday in Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic.

Savi Arvey of Human Rights First said the deportation flight included 12 Afghans, eight Iranians, and several migrants from Nepal and Nicaragua.

Among those deported was an Afghan man in his early 20s whose brothers had worked with the U.S. military in Afghanistan. His lawyer, Alma David, said a U.S. judge had previously prevented his deportation to Afghanistan because of fears that he could face persecution by the Taliban.

According to court documents reviewed by AP, the young man’s family in Afghanistan had received threats from the Taliban because of his brothers’ work in support of the U.S. military. One of his brothers lives in the United States and previously served in the Afghan National Army, while another was a U.S.-trained pilot who was killed by the Taliban.

Afghan refugee advocacy organizations, particularly groups involved in evacuating former Afghan military personnel and U.S.-affiliated Afghans, continue to urge Washington to protect those who risked their lives in support of the U.S. mission in Afghanistan between 2001 and 2021.

The latest findings come amid broader shifts in U.S. immigration and foreign policy under President Donald Trump. Shortly after taking office in January 2025, Trump signed an executive order pausing refugee admissions to the United States, including for Afghans who had assisted American forces.

In November 2025, following a shooting in Washington involving an Afghan national who killed a US National Guard member and injured another, Trump ordered a halt to all Afghan settlement programs and visa issuance for Afghan passport holders. He also directed a full review of Afghans admitted to the United States during the Biden administration.

These policy changes affected thousands of Afghans awaiting relocation to the United States from third countries, including former interpreters, contractors, and civil society workers who supported U.S. operations over two decades. Many remain at risk under Taliban rule or are stranded in neighboring countries with limited legal protections.

Refugee advocacy groups, US lawmakers, UN officials, and human rights organizations have expressed concern over the US approach, urging the administration to continue offering protection to Afghans at risk and reverse policies that block their resettlement to the United States.

Against this backdrop, a new poll indicates that a large majority of Americans support admitting Afghans who previously worked alongside U.S. forces in Afghanistan. AfghanEvac, a coalition of U.S. military veterans advocating for Afghan refugees, said in a poll published on August 29 that 72 percent of Americans support admitting Afghan allies.

The figure rose from 52 percent after respondents were informed about the role Afghan partners played in supporting the U.S. mission in Afghanistan.

text:
When she has access to a phone inside the Leavenworth ICE detention center, Katsiaryna Bartko calls her partner regularly throughout the day to let him know she’s still alert.

Dmitry Shyshov lives in fear of a day when no call will come. If Bartko slips into a myxedema coma due to severe hormone deficiency, she might never regain consciousness.

“It’s very hard to hear every morning her voice fading,” Shyshov said.

Sometimes, he said, Bartko can barely speak because of the spasms in her throat.

The 33-year-old Belarusian asylum seeker and cancer survivor had her thyroid and parathyroid glands surgically removed in her early 20s. Without those organs, she has relied for the last 11 years on life-sustaining calcium and hormone replacement treatment in precise daily doses.

Bartko, who earned degrees in civil engineering and law in Belarus, fled her home country on a student visa to avoid political persecution over her vocal opposition to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

She has been detained by federal immigration authorities for more than 12 weeks following her arrest in Miami and the dismissal of a low-level charge against her.

Now, Bartko fears death in a Kansas prison cell or deportation to Belarus, where her friends have been prosecuted as political agitators. Her partner has launched an online fundraiser to help cover her legal and medical expenses.

Hospital visits before relocation

After allegedly being denied access to medication while detained in a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Florida, Bartko had to be hospitalized three times in four days from June 6 to June 9, medical records show.

Then federal immigration authorities moved her to Leavenworth.

Since her transfer on June 18 to the Midwest Regional Reception Center, which CoreCivic runs for ICE, Bartko has not been evaluated by an endocrinologist or any other outside physician, ICE acknowledged in a federal court filing.

Her treatment has been handled exclusively by the for-profit prison company’s medical staff, despite a referral for an endocrinologist signed by the head of the medical unit at the last ICE facility where Bartko was held in Florida.

“CoreCivic’s medical staff has determined that Petitioner’s offsite consultations are routine — not an emergency or urgent,” deportation officer Aaron Wendler wrote in a sworn court filing on Aug. 11.

Based on CoreCivic’s policy, Wendler wrote, “offsite consultations should be performed within 12 weeks.”

Medical neglect allegations

Representatives for ICE and CoreCivic both said Bartko is receiving proper care for her highly specialized medical conditions within the walls of the concrete fortress that houses roughly 500 immigrant detainees awaiting deportation proceedings, according to the warden’s most recent count.

But medical records included in federal court filings show that Bartko’s hormonal deficiencies have worsened considerably in the two months since she was moved to the privately run Kansas facility.

In the Aug. 11 filing, the ICE deportation officer acknowledged that a blood test from the same day indicated Bartko’s thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels were well “outside the normal range” and had nearly doubled since her last blood draw nearly a month earlier.

Higher-than-average TSH readings occur when the body attempts to compensate for low hormone levels by alerting the thyroid to produce more. Bartko, who no longer has a thyroid, had a TSH reading of 148.77 mIU/L on Aug. 11 — roughly 30 times the healthy upper limit.

Sarah Raza, a board-certified trauma and vascular interventional radiologist with Physicians for Human Rights, wrote multiple sworn court statements requesting outside medical intervention for Bartko after reviewing her lab tests.

“Her hormones have been — I mean, it’s an understatement to say extremely poorly regulated,” Raza said in an interview. “It’s obvious if we just objectively look at the blood work.”

Citing medical privacy laws, Ryan Gustin, a spokesperson for CoreCivic, declined to answer questions about Bartko’s allegations that her medication was confiscated and withheld from her for nearly two weeks.

“I can share that the individual you asked about is being regularly monitored by facility medical staff, with all known medical issues being addressed,” Gustin said in an email statement.

Raza said she has reviewed lab results that establish Bartko is suffering from “severe overt biochemical hypothyroidism” — a condition that indicates extreme hormone deficiency.

“I would worry about neglect because she’s having multiple hospitalizations, multiple blood works that are showing she’s not being adequately treated with medications for this,” Raza said.

She added that based on the trajectory of Bartko’s lab work, risk factors are increasing for the worst possible outcome in a patient suffering from poorly regulated electrolytes and hormones: a myxedema coma.

“If you do develop myxedema coma, that is a serious, significant percentage of those patients who unfortunately don’t make it,” Raza said, noting that it can only be diagnosed in a clinical setting.

The fatality rate for people who go into a myxedema coma is between 25% and 60%, according to the American Thyroid Association.

“People with those symptoms, with those conditions, they are not screaming for help,” Shyshov said. “She will just not wake up in the morning or her throat will spasm so hard she cannot say a word. It will be silent.”

Fleeing Belarus over political speech

As a pro-democracy activist in Belarus, Bartko demonstrated against the brutality and corruption of the country’s longtime authoritarian leader and objected publicly on social media when Belarus aided the Russian military in the early days of its Ukraine invasion, Shyshov said.

Her participation in protests and her online activity put her in danger, he said.

“She spoke about (the Ukraine War) loudly, and she decided that it would be safer for her to leave the country because there were already rumors that she might be a person of interest,” Shyshov said.

Bartko entered the U.S. legally on an F-1 student visa in March 2022, according to a copy of her passport. She arrived in New York and made her way to the University of California San Diego to study the English language through an international student program.

After she left Belarus, several people in her friend group who had been sharing anti-war messages were swept up in the government dragnet when President Aleksandr Lukashenko cracked down on opposition voices, Shyshov said. He said Belarusian agents came to Bartko’s parents’ house to ask where she was and when she would return.

Going back home wasn’t an option for Bartko, he said, so she applied for political asylum. If that application is denied, deportation could be a death sentence. Death by medical neglect in Belarusian prisons is well documented.

Shyshov still hopes to build a life with Bartko in America.

“She is everything good that a person can be — thoughtful, devoted and full of warmth toward the people around her,” Shyshov wrote in a June letter to the court.

Medical records provide timeline

Daniel McIntosh, an organizer with Leavenworth Community Response, said that in the more than five months since the Kansas immigrant detention center has been operating, detainees and their families have reported persistent medical neglect and malfeasance.

On several occasions, he said, community organizers were notified of detainees’ acute medical needs and persuaded the city to intervene to ensure they received proper care. The Leavenworth City Manager’s office declined to speak to the city’s role in securing treatment for patients in ICE custody earlier this month.

Shyshov, who is legally authorized to review all of Bartko’s medical records, said his partner’s limited command of the English language and CoreCivic’s inconsistent use of translating services have made it remarkably challenging for her to communicate her needs to medical staff. He said at times, staff have been negligent and indifferent to her suffering.

Bartko’s twice-daily calcium doses must be timed properly to ensure they don’t counteract her daily hormone medication, Shyshov said.

When she first arrived in Leavenworth, Bartko was allowed to keep her hormone medication, levothyroxine, in her cell and administer it herself, Shyshov said. But he said it was confiscated on June 23 and withheld from her until July 10, when CoreCivic staff took over its administration.

CoreCivic medical records reviewed by The Star show that within days of allegedly losing access to her hormone medication, Bartko made her symptoms known to medical staff.

On a June 26 form filled out in handwritten English, Bartko reported experiencing severe pain “under my heart in chest.” She also reported dizziness and blurry vision when she woke up.

Beneath her report, the provider wrote, “No medical intervention required at this time. Detainee stable, no acute distress noted.”

A July 2 clinical note from a physician who spoke to Bartko without a Russian interpreter asserted that, “During the face-to-face she stated she is allergic to levothyroxine” — the medication that she has been prescribed for over a decade and relies on for life-sustaining hormone replacement.

“I have now been provided additional information that a facility record states that levothyroxine and calcium were not administered because Ms. Bartko reportedly identified herself as allergic to both,” Raza, the physician, wrote to the court. “Her signature does not appear on that notation, and the notation conflicts with multiple prior medical records documenting continuous use and tolerance of both therapies.

“An allergy to calcium itself is not a medically coherent basis for withholding all calcium replacement,” Raza added.

In a translated copy of Bartko’s sworn deposition in support of her motion seeking release from detention, the cancer survivor recounted that on July 3, a nurse brought her a dose of calcium and the hormone medication she had been going without for more than a week.

Bartko said she attempted to explain that calcium is taken after food and levothyroxine is taken on an empty stomach. She said she asked the nurse to bring back the levothyroxine in about an hour. A CoreCivic medical record shows the incident was logged as a “refusal to accept medical treatment.”

“I am not refusing medications — I want to take them correctly and safely,” Bartko recalled writing in a grievance she filed that night.

‘Put her life in danger’

Before she was taken into custody this spring, Bartko was staying on top of her treatment regimen, Shyshov said. Medical records predating her stint in ICE custody show that her calcium and hormone levels were stable in March.

But her condition has deteriorated significantly in the months since she was first arrested in Miami-Dade County on May 5 and booked on a misdemeanor battery charge. Shyshov said the arrest stemmed from an argument involving the couple and other people at a birthday party.

That charge was dropped by the state attorney’s office on June 2, according to a filing reviewed by The Star. It was resolved as “no action” with no conviction.

But ICE, the primary immigration enforcement agency within the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, placed a detainer on Bartko due to her expired student visa, and she was handed over to immigration authorities in early June.

“Since Florida cooperates, this criminal illegal alien was turned over to ICE,” said Robert Hughes II, a DHS spokesperson, in an email statement.

He said Bartko is “receiving proper medical care and treatment for hypothyroidism and hypocalcemia,” adding that she “will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings and will receive full due process.”

The statement twice refers to Bartko as a “criminal illegal alien,” despite the fact that in federal court filings, ICE says she is only being held on civil charges related to her immigration status. Shyshov said his partner filed an asylum application before her student visa expired in March 2023.

“Note that ICE’s statement promises she ‘will receive due process’ in the same breath that it pronounces her guilty,” Shyshov said.

Bartko’s bond was denied on July 22 by an immigration judge on the basis that she was a flight risk.

“We’re not against any immigration proceedings that she’s facing right now because she’s from Belarus. She’s facing political persecution,” Shyshov said. “We are OK with having the immigration court. But the problem is that it doesn’t give any reason to mess with her health, her body and put her life in danger.”

text:
Over a 10-day period, the Trump administration sent more than 100 deportees from Afghanistan, Cuba, Nicaragua and other nations to eight countries across Africa, expanding its "third country" deportation campaign, according to internal U.S. government documents obtained by CBS News.

Three Immigration and Customs Enforcement deportation flights, the government documents show, dropped off dozens of men and women expelled from the U.S. in Burundi, Cameroon, the Central African Republic, Equatorial Guinea, Eswatini, Liberia, Rwanda and Sierra Leone.

None of the deportees were from the countries where they were deported, according to the documents. In addition to Afghans, Cubans and Nicaraguans, the ICE flights over the past week and a half included deportees from Iran, Nepal, Turkey and Venezuela, as well as African detainees who are not from the nations where they were sent.

The federal documents, which have not been previously reported on, offer a window into the Trump administration's intensifying campaign to use "third country" deportation agreements to banish groups of deportees to far-flung countries where they have no ties.

More than 30 countries across the globe have agreed to receive such deportations from the U.S., including some in Latin America like Costa Rica, Panama and Paraguay. But a growing number of African countries have brokered third-country deportation deals with the Trump administration, including nations like the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and South Sudan, plagued by armed conflict, political tumult and human rights abuses.

The international agreements have largely been shrouded in secrecy, but it appears some countries, like Ghana and Sierra Leone, have only agreed to accept deportees from other places in Africa. Countries like Eswatini, the Central African Republic and Liberia have received detainees from Latin America, Europe and Asia.

Some of those deported to Africa by the Trump administration have criminal records in addition to immigration violations, including the detainees sent to Eswatini and South Sudan, where officials have imprisoned deportees convicted of violent and serious crimes in the U.S. But many of the deportees sent to other countries lack any criminal histories, beyond entering the U.S. illegally or not having the proper documents to stay in the country.

The latest of three ICE flights to Africa dropped off detainees in Sierra Leone and the Central African Republic, where longstanding armed conflict and Russian mercenaries have made the landlocked country one of the most dangerous in the world. A "Level 4" U.S. State Department advisory warns Americans to avoid traveling there for any reason, given widespread violence and insecurity.

CBS News reached out to the Departments of Homeland Security and State seeking comment on the deportations to Africa.

"If an illegal alien chooses to file a claim in court refusing to go to their home country, we are required by law to find a safe and secure nation for them to go to. If an illegal alien chooses to go home, we will give them a free flight home and a $3,000 check," DHS said in a statement to CBS News on Sunday. "The choice is theirs."

Among those deported to the Central African Republic on the most recent flight was an Afghan man whose family helped American forces fight the Taliban and who won legal protection in a U.S. immigration court, according to his lawyer and brother.

Khalil, the 24-year-old Afghan deportee, crossed the U.S.-Mexico border illegally in 2024, after traveling across Latin America, according to his immigration lawyer. He was held by ICE in custody during his entire time in the U.S. His immigration lawyer said Khalil came to join his brothers, one of whom was brought to the U.S. in 2014 because of his work alongside American military forces while in the Afghan Army. Legal documents indicate another of Khalil's brothers fought the Taliban as a pilot and was killed during the war.

In August 2025, while detained, Khalil was granted a legal protection, known as "withholding of removal," by a U.S. immigration judge who found he could face persecution in Afghanistan, legal documents show. He did not get asylum, a more permanent legal protection, because of a Biden-era policy that disqualified asylum-seekers who failed to seek protection in other countries before reaching American soil, according to the documents.

While that protection barred ICE from returning Khalil to Afghanistan, it did not legally prevent his deportation to a third country. And the Trump administration has increasingly sought to deport those who've won limited protections in immigration court, like withholding of removal, to third countries.

"The goal is to obliterate the global refugee protection system, and his case should serve as a warning of the unconscionable consequences," said Alma David, Khalil's immigration lawyer. CBS News is not disclosing Khalil's surname due to concerns from his family that he or relatives could be targeted by the Taliban.

Zachary Schmidt, an active-duty Marine colonel who supervised Khalil's brother during his deployment to Afghanistan, said he's concerned about Khalil's safety in the conflict-ridden Central African Republic and the prospect that he could be returned to his homeland. He said he's seen threats made by Taliban militants against Khalil's family.

"It is my belief that if Khalil gets sent back to Afghanistan, that he will be killed," Schmidt told CBS News, speaking in his personal capacity.

Schmidt, who testified in Khalil's immigration court case, noted the U.S. made a "deal" with Afghans who agreed to aid the American war effort in Afghanistan.

"The deal is that if you help us, and help rebuild your country, we will look out for you. We'll help you and your family," Schmidt said. "We have to keep that promise."

text:
White House border czar Tom Homan on Sunday pushed back on the idea of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arresting parents at bus stops in Connecticut, as alleged by Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) this week.

“I pointed out, the last two years, no one can point to one single incidence we arrested anybody in elementary school. We haven’t arrested anybody in the hospital. We haven’t arrested anybody in the church. ICE is real good at their job,” Homan told CNN’s Dana Bash on “State of the Union.”

“Now, did they arrest somebody at a bus stop? I’m not aware of that, but ICE is out there to enforce law against those that have been ordered removed by a federal judge. And especially if they’re a criminal or if they’re a national security threat, there’s no safe harbor for them in this country,” he added.

Earlier this week, Murphy said in a post on the social platform X that “ICE was arresting parents at school bus stops” in Danbury, Conn.

“But it’s more sinister. ICE waited until the kids were on the bus so when they are dropped off at the end of the day, they are alone, scared to death they can’t find their parents. I’m heading to Danbury,” the senator added in his Wednesday post.

Throughout President Trump’s second term in office, his administration has faced backlash over its strict immigration agenda. That backlash boiled over earlier this year when two U.S. citizens were killed in Minneapolis by federal immigration authorities, and since then, more people have been killed in confrontations with immigration enforcement in other states including Maine and Texas.

Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont (D) said in his own post on the social platform X on Thursday that he was “horrified by the stories shared by activists in Danbury.”

“Parents detained dropping their children off at the school bus. 3 year old children watching ICE forcibly detain someone outside their daycare window. Rounding up people at random to meet a quota doesn’t make our communities safer,” he added.

title: ICE arrests are surging as the administration targets more immigrants - WYSO Public Radio
authors: Vanessa Romo, Joel Rose, www.wyso.org, joel-rose
description:
Newly released data show the number of arrests by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement climbed to nearly 50,000 in July.
Here to talk about what's going on is NPR immigration correspondent Vanessa Romo.
VANESSA ROMO, BYLINE: Hi, Joel.
ROSE: Let's start with new data showing that ICE has made more arrests in July than any other month during the current administration.
ROSE: NPR's immigration correspondent Vanessa Romo.
text:
JOEL ROSE, HOST:

The Trump administration's crackdown on illegal immigration is yielding big results. Newly released data show the number of arrests by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement climbed to nearly 50,000 in July. It's part of a broader crackdown on illegal and legal immigration during Trump's second term. Here to talk about what's going on is NPR immigration correspondent Vanessa Romo. Hey, Vanessa.

VANESSA ROMO, BYLINE: Hi, Joel.

ROSE: Let's start with new data showing that ICE has made more arrests in July than any other month during the current administration. How has the agency been able to do that?

ROMO: Well, it's sort of a combination of factors. One, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has shifted ICE's strategy, and he's really broadened when and where people are being arrested. So yes, it's still raids, but it's also happening a lot more quietly. It's happening at airports and ICE check-ins and immigration court.

And then second, ICE has a lot more manpower now. This year, they've added more than 12,000 new hires, doubling the size of the force. And many states and local law enforcement are actually now participating in the effort to arrest people through a program that's called 287(g). And these are agreements where ICE works with local law enforcement to make those arrests.

ROSE: Who are the people who are being arrested? I mean, I know a lot of Haitians lost protections from deportation recently. Is that showing up in these numbers?

ROMO: Yes, definitely. The Supreme Court ruled back in June that the Trump administration can strip 300,000 Haitians of what's called temporary protected status. And so that has shown up in the July figures. But the experts I spoke to say we're actually likely to see a lot more of those in the August data.

ROSE: With all of these arrests, there are also a lot of people being held in detention, right? Exactly, you know, where are all of these people being held?

ROMO: So you're right. As of July 11, there were nearly 66,000 immigrants being held in detention across the country, and that's according to the TRAC Project at Syracuse University. And that's really, really concerning for immigrant rights activists who say that detention center facilities are already overcrowded.

I've spoken with a lot of people in detention and their lawyers, and I've heard about how overcrowding exacerbates so many of the problems that already exist. You know, overcrowding can lead to unsanitary conditions and inconsistent medical care. Now, both the government and the private companies running these facilities have repeatedly defended their level of care that they provide. But with the massive infusion of cash from Congress to DHS and ICE specifically, the government is also planning on acquiring new detention centers to address that.

ROSE: Shifting to legal immigration, I know the State Department announced plans to potentially revoke up to 200,000 visas. Why?

ROMO: Right. This could be the largest visa revocation effort in U.S. history. And to be clear, it's not all visas. It would target tourist and business visas that were held by people who then later filed for asylum. And Tommy Pigott, the State Department spokesman, was on Morning Edition this week explaining that this, at least from the Trump administration's point of view, is really about eliminating what it calls fraudulent asylum cases.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)

TOMMY PIGOTT: Fundamentally, this is meant to ensure that if someone is here on a short-term visa but indicates a desire to stay permanently, then that short-term visa no longer reflects actually what their desire is here. But it is important to point out that we do see a large number of frivolous asylum claims.

ROMO: So Pigott says that this change is intended to allow the government to get a better handle on who's in the country and for what purpose.

ROSE: Vanessa, in about 30 seconds that we have left, what will this mean for people who came to the U.S. under a short-term visa and then applied for asylum?

ROMO: So Pigott said that DHS will continue with those active asylum cases until they are adjudicated, but it is widely anticipated that the department's going to use those revoked visas against individuals during the interview process. But, you know, since the start of Trump's second term, ICE has been directed to arrest, detain and deport as many immigrants as possible. That has included instances where people who are legally present in the U.S. or in the process of adjusting their status have been detained.

ROSE: NPR's immigration correspondent Vanessa Romo. Thanks for your time, Vanessa.

ROMO: Thank you. Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

text:
British far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos was deported to the United Kingdom after being arrested by U.S. immigration authorities, officials said Saturday.

What they're saying:

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said Yiannopoulos was returned to his home country on Friday after being accused of overstaying after entering the U.S. legally in May 2019. A immigration judge had issued a final order of removal on July 22 after he failed to show up for an immigration hearing, a Homeland Security spokesperson said.

Yiannopoulos was arrested Thursday at Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport in Louisiana and detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

RELATED: Milo Yiannopoulos arrested by ICE, held at major deportation hub in Louisiana

"He chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws," a Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement.

The other side:

Yiannopoulos and his representatives did not respond to requests for comment. He has not posted on his X social media account since Thursday.

Big picture view:

Yiannopoulos is a well-known champion of conservative causes and has frequently taken provocative public positions criticizing feminism, Islam and immigrants. He has been especially supportive of President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown.

"Zero immigration for the next 20 years. No ifs, no buts," Yiannopoulos wrote on X last year.

The British national has most recently worked for the rapper Ye, formerly known as Kanye West, who performed in New Orleans on Friday evening.

Yiannopoulos rose to fame in the early 2010s as an incendiary writer for the conservative website Breitbart News. He resigned from the company in 2017 after a video of him endorsing pedophilia resurfaced online. He later apologized for the remarks and said he himself was a victim of sexual assault as a minor.

Yiannopoulos’ arrest on Thursday comes amid a nationwide uptick in detentions as part of Trump’s immigration crackdown.

Controversy around Yiannopoulos ballooned in 2017 when he carried out what he called his "Troll Academy Tour" across college campuses nationwide. Fights broke out when some students protested Yiannopoulos’ appearances and accused him of hate speech, while others celebrated him as a champion of free speech. Around that time, Buzzfeed reported on Yiannopoulos’ cozy relationships with self-proclaimed white nationalists.

In recent years, Yiannopoulos continued to work in the orbit of conservative activism. In 2022, he was an intern for former U.S. Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, according to the Washington Post. He subsequently ran the short-lived 2024 presidential campaign for Ye.

Most recently, Yiannopoulos has worked as a spokesperson for Ye, who has been beset by controversy of his own following antisemitic comments that the rapper has since apologized for.

text:
Washington, Aug 29: A US federal judge has temporarily vacated three Trump administration policies that halted Diversity Visa processing and immigrant-visa approvals for nationals of 75 countries, ordering immigration authorities to resume ordinary adjudication of affected applications.

US District Judge Edward J. Davila of the Northern District of California issued the preliminary injunction on Friday in Medani et al v. Trump et al, a class-action challenge brought by fiscal year 2026 Diversity Visa selectees and their families. Davila granted part of the applicants’ motion for class certification and part of their request for a preliminary injunction. The order will remain in place while the litigation continues.

The court temporarily set aside a US Citizenship and Immigration Services hold on Diversity Visa adjustment-of-status applications, the State Department’s suspension of Diversity Visa issuances and its separate pause covering immigrant-visa applicants from 75 countries.

The State Department was ordered “to the extent practicable and in good faith” to take reasonable steps during the remainder of the Diversity Visa fiscal year to reconsider applications refused solely under the two State Department suspensions. It must also resume the ordinary adjudication of pending Diversity Visa applications.

The court separately directed USCIS to resume processing pending adjustment-of-status applications without applying its Diversity Visa hold. Davila certified three subclasses covering fiscal year 2026 Diversity Visa selectees and their derivative beneficiaries affected by each of the challenged policies.(IANS)

description:
Before he arrives, he checks social media to make sure there are no Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents in the vicinity.
According to Hernández, ICE raids keep crews on alert and scare away those with irregular immigration status.
This fear is not unfounded: ICE has shown up at various construction sites in Altadena and arrested several workers.
“Some believe that white construction workers are going to come and rebuild their house.
However, these three men have refused to go quietly and have filed a lawsuit against the federal government flagging up alleged racist language used by the ICE agents during their arrest.
text:
The sound of hammers, drills and Mexican music herald the rising from the ashes of Altadena. Just over a year ago, only the charred remains of homes blasted by the Eaton wildfires were in evidence. Now, the wooden skeletons of houses are multiplying and gradually recovering their shape. As one of the most devastating wildfires in California’s recent history, it claimed 19 lives, leveled thousands of homes and reduced an entire neighborhood to rubble. But on one construction site, manager Ian Hernández has a task that goes beyond supervising the workers. Before he arrives, he checks social media to make sure there are no Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents in the vicinity. That morning, he says, he checked that the coast was clear.

According to Hernández, ICE raids keep crews on alert and scare away those with irregular immigration status. This fear is not unfounded: ICE has shown up at various construction sites in Altadena and arrested several workers. Others have been detained on their way to work. According to organizations that defend migrants, ICE has been seeking undocumented migrants since reconstruction began.

“In February, a car on Mendocina Street let us know that ICE was just around the corner. Some workers hid and others stayed. Nothing happened. It was Friday. On Saturday, no one came to work,” says Hernández, an Oaxacan foreman who supervises the construction of 10 houses. Mendocina Street was one of the last to be engulfed by the Eaton fire in January 2025. It is now part of an area of vacant lots where a middle-class neighborhood once sprawled across the foothills of the Angeles National Forest. Previous fires had never reached so far south.

Almost all the houses being rebuilt in Altadena have chained and padlocked the two-meter-high fences that surround them, even during the working day. “It’s so that ICE doesn’t have access,” explains another foreman. “God willing, they will never come here, and nothing will happen.”

Billboards warn: Do not enter without authorization. Private property. Other factors accounting for the slow progress of reconstruction include bottlenecks in processing permits from the local government, a process that can take up to 125 business days; indemnities from insurers that fail to cover the total cost of construction; and the increase in the cost of materials and labor.

“ICE agents were in Altadena and Pasadena [a neighboring city] for five consecutive days,” says José Madera, director of the Pasadena Community Labor Center, an organization that functions as a safe meeting point for employers and day laborers, as well as cleaners. “The owners of the houses have told us that the builders no longer want to come to work. That affects families because they cannot return to their homes.”

But the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) maintains that ICE raids on workplaces are “a fundamental pillar” of its strategy to protect the public and the country’s economy. The agency also claims it seeks to rescue possible victims of labor trafficking and exploitation. “These operations aim to dismantle illegal employment networks that harm U.S. workers, destabilize labor markets, and threaten communities,” DHS said in a written statement to EL PAÍS.

“I pray they leave them alone”

The new home of African American Damon Blount is half-built. The work began in April and now a crew of construction workers is putting on the roof. It will take eight to 10 months to complete, but Blount is confident his family can settle there before Christmas — that is, if ICE doesn’t show up.

“There are a lot of Hispanic workers in the community right now, and I just pray they leave people alone, that they allow them to rebuild, and that they let us go home,” Blount says. Some of his neighbors have been unlucky. “They said that ICE agents have taken three or four workers, and that has caused delays.”

Immigrant advocacy organizations, media, and politicians have reported ICE raids at construction sites, bus stops, area coffee shops, and at traffic lights. Last January, the day that Altadena commemorated the first anniversary of the Eaton Fire, ICE returned to the streets of the city. “These chaotic raids are never justified, but they are especially cruel when they target our friends and loved ones, including the people who do the physical and specialized work needed to help us recover from this disaster,” said state Senator Sasha Renée Pérez, a Democrat who represents the area.

Volunteers patrol the streets in a bid to detect ICE vehicles, but their efforts have not been enough. “The migra [ICE] comes here often. The agents ride in private cars and it is difficult to identify them,” explains Andrés Rivas, a 70-year-old Salvadoran who is looking to be hired by one of the properties in Altadena. Rivas is a U.S. citizen, but he still fears he could be detained and spend some time in immigration custody. “They come very early. The risk exists,” he says.

A slow business

The resurgence of Altadena, where the Eaton fire destroyed 6,746 homes, has been, above all, lacking in funds. As of June 19, the Los Angeles County government had issued 2,845 building permits, but only 89 homes were habitable. More than 1,600 houses were still under construction, from laying the foundations to the final finishes.

Marialyce Pedersen hopes her home will be ready soon. Right now, there’s just a plot of land. For two decades, she lived in a house in Altadena that she bought from a friend and that, over the years, she filled with memories. Among the most precious were her grandmother’s piano and dozens of children’s books that she dreamed of reading to her grandchildren. Everything went. “It was horrible, it’s the worst thing that has happened to me,” said Pedersen, 62, who has worked as an environmental consultant and adviser to the Walt Disney Company.

Pedersen has already reached out to her trusted builder, a Salvadoran migrant who has been in the U.S. for 25 years. But she fears that he or one of his workers could be detained by ICE, either on her property or at one of the Home Depot stores where they buy materials.

“Some believe that white construction workers are going to come and rebuild their house. Well, good luck with that. It is not going to happen. Hispanic migrants are the ones who are working reconstruction and the ones who are here in our community,” Pedersen says. “They are willing to work, even in this heat.”

The day laborers who never made it to Altadena

Out of nowhere, four pickup trucks screeched to a stop in front of a bus stop next to a coffee shop in Pasadena. Several masked officers got out. It was the morning of June 18, 2025, amid the intensification of raids in the LA metropolitan area — part of the Trump administration’s mass deportation offensive. Among those arrested were three day laborers who were on their way to work on a house in Altadena: Pedro Vázquez Perdomo, Isaac Antonio Villegas Molina, and Carlos Alexander Osorto. The three were handcuffed. One of them, who tried to escape on foot, had a taser pressed to his head. “Stop or I’m going to use it,” the officer shouted, according to court documents.

Instead of arriving in Altadena, the three day laborers ended up in the parking lot of a CVS pharmacy. There, they had their immigration status verified. They were then transferred to the ICE detention center in Adelanto, about 60 miles from L.A. However, these three men have refused to go quietly and have filed a lawsuit against the federal government flagging up alleged racist language used by the ICE agents during their arrest.

Pablo Alvarado, leader of the National Day Laborer Network (NDLON), says that this is one of the clearest examples of how ICE operations are affecting a city that is trying to get back on its feet. “Contractors can’t find enough labor. Although it was said they would not carry out raids here, the migra has been in the vicinity and has detained workers,” Alvarado says. “It’s clear that, in the literal sense, migrants are rebuilding communities and ICE is disrupting this through immoral, inhumane, cruel and illegal operations.”

text:
Tarrant County booking records show that the county booked 278 defendants from January 1 through August 3, 2026, who had U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement holds. The file associates those defendants with 480 coded criminal charge entries apart from the holds, according to county data The Dallas Express obtained.

The spreadsheet contains 497 non-ICE charge rows for those defendants. Of those, 477 name an offense, while three additional rows carry a first-degree felony code without naming the offense. The remaining 17 contain only an “other offense” or administrative description.

Because the export omits case numbers and repeats rows with the same visible fields, the 480 figure counts charge entries as the county supplied them, not 480 confirmed unique cases.

The county marked 355 of the 480 coded entries as first-, second- or third-degree felonies or state jail felonies. The file lists 42 entries for aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, 28 for assault causing bodily injury involving family violence and 26 for assault of a family or household member by impeding breath or circulation.

The records also list 16 entries for sexual assault of a child, five for aggravated sexual assault of a child, 11 for indecency with a child by sexual contact and 10 describing continuous sexual abuse of a child under 14. Other entries include aggravated kidnapping, aggravated robbery and 57 involving driving while intoxicated.

The charges listed in the file represent allegations, not convictions. The law presumes each defendant innocent unless a court enters a conviction. An ICE hold does not establish a conviction or a final removal order. The spreadsheet does not include immigration-court records sufficient to independently determine each person’s final immigration status.

How Tarrant County’s 287(g) program works

The Tarrant County Sheriff’s Office describes its 287(g) partnership with ICE as a jail-based program. The agency says it limits the program to illegal aliens facing high misdemeanor or felony charges.

ICE defines a detainer as a request that a law enforcement agency notify ICE before release and maintain custody temporarily so federal officers can assume custody. The Dallas Express previously reported that Tarrant County has participated in the 287(g) program since 2017.

State Rep. David Lowe (R-District 91) told The Dallas Express that the records demonstrate what he believes is at stake in the political debate over immigration enforcement.

“The Tarrant County data shows exactly what is at stake. ICE holds include illegal aliens charged with sexual assault of a child, kidnapping, and other violent offenses. Democrats are running on abolishing ICE, and that agenda would make Tarrant County families, especially our children, more vulnerable. I stand with ICE and the safety of American families,” Lowe said.

Democratic commissioners opposed ICE grant

Tarrant County commissioners voted 3-2 on February 10 to approve an application for a $140,000 state grant supporting the county’s 287(g) program. Tarrant County Commissioners Alisa Simmons (D-Precinct 2) and Roderick Miles Jr. (D-Precinct 1) opposed the application.

The state grant program covers 287(g) costs that the federal government does not reimburse, including personnel, required reporting, equipment, training and confinement expenses, the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts said.

“I do not support ICE. I do not support this grant, and I do not support expanding immigration enforcement at the county level,” Simmons said during the February 10 meeting.

Simmons also pointed to two recent jail escapes and what she described as 76 deaths in custody. “Tarrant County has its own problems to fix and deal with operationally,” Simmons said.

The Dallas Express contacted Simmons and Miles to ask whether the criminal charges in the records affect their positions on ICE enforcement but did not receive a response by publication.

text:
Gov. Kathy Hochul and New York Attorney General Letitia James have filed a lawsuit against the Rensselaer County Sheriff's Office, alleging it failed to comply with a new state law requiring local law enforcement agencies to end certain agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The lawsuit centers on New York's Local Cops, Local Crimes Act, which required local law enforcement agencies to terminate agreements made under Section 287(g) of the federal Immigration and Nationality Act by Aug. 25, 2026.

The law prohibits local governments and law enforcement agencies from entering into or remaining in such agreements with ICE.

What are 287(g) agreements?

Section 287(g) agreements allow state and local law enforcement officers to perform certain federal civil immigration enforcement functions.

Depending on the terms of an agreement, local officers may be authorized to question, arrest and detain people suspected of violating federal civil immigration law.

The Local Cops, Local Crimes Act, signed by Hochul on May 27, gave agencies with existing agreements 90 days to begin the process of ending them.

Under the law, covered agreements that remained in effect after Aug. 25 are considered void and unenforceable under New York law.

Why is New York suing the Rensselaer County Sheriff's Office?

The Rensselaer County Sheriff's Office has maintained a 287(g) agreement with ICE since March 2020, according to the governor's and attorney general's offices.

After the new law was enacted, the attorney general's office contacted the sheriff's office seeking information about the status of the agreement. State officials said they did not receive confirmation that the agreement had been terminated or would be terminated by the Aug. 25 deadline.

On Aug. 19, the attorney general's office issued a formal investigative demand seeking documents showing what actions the sheriff's office had taken to end the agreement, according to the state.

State officials said they still have not received confirmation that the agreement was terminated.

"Compliance with the Local Cops, Local Crimes Act is not optional," Hochul said in a statement. "Today, we are taking action to ensure the Rensselaer County Sheriff's Office performs the duties required of it under state law, because no one in New York State is above the law."

James said the lawsuit is intended to enforce the state's law.

"All law enforcement agencies are expected to uphold New York's laws," James said. "The Rensselaer County Sheriff's Office has been given every opportunity to follow the law, yet has chosen not to."

Rensselaer County is the only agency that has not indicated it will end its agreement

Of the 12 law enforcement agencies in New York that had 287(g) agreements before the new law took effect, the Rensselaer County Sheriff's Office is the only one that has not indicated it intends to end its agreement, according to state officials.

The lawsuit asks the Rensselaer County Supreme Court to order the sheriff's office to exercise the termination provisions in its agreement with ICE and declare the agreement void and unenforceable under state law.

What is New York's Office of Immigrant Trust?

The lawsuit is the first legal action brought by the attorney general's newly established Office of Immigrant Trust.

The office was created to enforce New York laws limiting state and local involvement in federal civil immigration enforcement. It is authorized to investigate potential violations and bring civil lawsuits when appropriate.

Federal government also challenged New York's law

The U.S. Department of Justice filed a federal lawsuit in June challenging New York's Local Cops, Local Crimes Act.

Earlier this month, however, the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of New York denied the federal government's request to block the state's ban on 287(g) agreements, allowing the Aug. 25 deadline to remain in effect.

text:
August 30, 2026 - New York — Immigrant families, workers, and legal assistance groups harmed by the Trump-Vance administration’s 75-country ban on immigrant visas filed an emergency motion to enforce Friday’s court order and judgment in CLINIC v. Rubio. The filing directly responds to reports that the U.S. State Department ordered a global “pause” on immigrant visa appointments, citing a training program as the reason after the court issued its order. On August 21, 2026, a federal court struck down the Trump-Vance administration’s blanket ban on immigrant visa processing for people from 75 countries and found the Secretary of State had no authority to “pause” or suspend visa processing.

“The August 21 ruling created an important path forward for families who have been waiting for their immigrant visa cases to move ahead,” said Adriana Coppola, supervising attorney of emerging issues at CLINIC. “CLINIC’s emergency motion is focused on ensuring that the court’s decision is implemented in a way that allows those cases to proceed fairly, individually, and with respect for the dignity of each person and the importance of family reunification.”

“The Administration cannot keep circumventing the legal system. This ban is unjust, and the court has agreed. We won’t let the Administration continue separating families and targeting our communities. It must resume processing visas and follow the law,” said Diana Konaté, Deputy Executive Director, African Communities Together.

“The court’s orders were crystal clear – the Trump-Vance administration’s Visa Ban is unlawful and cannot be enforced,” said Skye Perryman, president and CEO of Democracy Forward. “Yet the administration is egregiously and flagrantly ignoring a duly issued court order and enforcing unlawful policies that continue to inflict enormous harm on families and communities across the country. On behalf of our brave clients, we are asking the court to enforce its judgment and ensure that the government stops this abuse of power.”

“Families who have waited for months to be reunited with their loved ones continue to be separated across oceans as a result of the government refusing to abide by the court’s order and lift the blanket visa ban,” said Efrén C. Olivares, vice president of litigation & legal strategy at the National Immigration Law Center (NILC). “We continue to seek justice for our plaintiffs and have sought relief from the court to ensure the government complies with the order and judgment immediately.”

“The court was clear: the State Department cannot simply stop processing immigrant visas because it chooses to. Yet days after that ruling, the administration appears to be doing exactly that under a different name,” said Antionette Dozier, senior attorney, Western Center on Law & Poverty. “This blatant attempt to sidestep the law continues to keep families separated, disrupt lives, and leave people who have already endured months of uncertainty in limbo. A court order is not a suggestion. The administration must follow the law and resume processing these visas.”

“This administration’s seeming default is disorder and lawlessness, wherever that serves to hurt and exclude families of color,” said Baher Azmy, legal director of the Center for Constitutional Rights. “The executive branch shouldn’t have to be forced, again, to follow the law, yet we need additional judicial intervention to protect those families the administration seems determined to punish.”

“Legitimate global training programs are not rolled out in this manner,” said Sarah Wilson, partner & federal immigration litigation practice leader at Colombo & Hurd. “We are optimistic that the court will see this for what it is: blatant noncompliance with a thoughtful and well-reasoned court order.”

“The court’s decision made clear that the ban is unlawful and that the processing of visas for the families and workers impacted directly by the ban should proceed,” said Susan Welber, supervising attorney in the civil practice at The Legal Aid Society. “The Defendants’ outrageous attempt to thwart the processing of such visas worldwide smacks of animus and pretext.”

Plaintiffs include Catholic Legal Immigration Network, Inc. (CLINIC), African Communities Together, and individuals whose lives were upended by the ban. They are represented by Democracy Forward, The National Immigration Law Center, The Legal Aid Society, the Western Center on Law & Poverty, the Center for Constitutional Rights, and Colombo & Hurd.

The lawsuit argued that the U.S. Department of State imposed an unlawful, discriminatory, nationality-based barrier to legal immigration that strips families and working people of the process guaranteed by law. The Trump-Vance administration baselessly cited “public charge” risk as its stated justification for the ban, after relentlessly and cruelly smearing immigrant communities, particularly communities of color.

The case is CLINIC v. Rubio, and the legal team at Democracy Forward includes Erez Reuveni, Catherine Carroll and Elena Goldstein.
